Discovering relations in a knowledge graph involves identifying a logical connection between two entities. Recent approaches primarily rely on the subject-predicate-object triple structure to represent relational connections. However, many relationships share a common property - they form cycles when part of a larger graph, which can be utilized to extract implicit connections. Focusing on breaking down this implicit information could provide a more effective strategy for discovering relations. In this paper, we investigate how existing connection prediction methods can contribute to relation discovery. Furthermore, we introduce an approach that utilizes a multi-layered neural network to predict implicit connections and finds applications in discovering relations. The proposed method is evaluated and compared to existing relation discovery methods. Experiments, utilizing datasets such as FB15K, FB16K, and WN18, have shown that incorporating connection prediction significantly enhances relation discovery. Consequently, our study indicates that leveraging implicit connection information is a crucial factor in discovering relations within a knowledge graph. The source code for this paper can be accessed at https://github.com/superstar911/Relation-Detection. The knowledge graph utilized in this research can be viewed at: https://github.com/superstar911/Relation-Detection/tree/main/data/impli_graph. The authors' original implementation of the multi-layered neural network can be found at: https://github.com/superstar911/impli_connection. The knowledge graph used in this paper contains 50 million entities and 85 million relationships. Utilizing connection prediction, we were able to discover 34% more relationships compared to existing relation discovery methods. The structure of the multi-layered neural network consists of 3 layers with increasing complexity, as well as utilizing entity embeddings derived from DistMult. In terms of execution efficiency, our method requires 185 seconds to discover relationships for the WN18 dataset on a single GPU. In converter design, the analytical conversion ratio is frequently employed, facilitating straightforward design and the separation of power conversion and control issues. Nevertheless, the analysis of the converter's dynamic behavior is often handled through complex and time-consuming numerical simulations. In this research, we utilize a sophisticated MATLAB curve-fitting method to derive a compact analytical model that precisely reproduces the operating trajectory of the converter. Following this approach, we are able to determine the spatial distribution of the converter's control signals, thereby accelerating simulation times by extracting the fundamental properties of the converter's dynamics. Several examples are presented, demonstrating the efficacy of this approach in various converter applications, including bipolar DC-DC converters, single-phase pulse-width modulation (PWM) converters, and linear regulators. Our results show that the use of this method can significantly reduce simulation times by up to 5 orders of magnitude, thereby providing considerable computational savings and enabling the rapid iteration and optimization of the converter's design. Additionally, this method can be used to extend the operating range of the converter and to identify its tendency towards instability. Ultimately, this compact model can be utilized in various applications (e.g., in the development of the subsystems in a co-simulation environment such as PSIM, Simscape, or Microwavestudio). Notably, the time and effort required to derive this model are similar to those needed for the initial converter design. Furthermore, the resulting model remains relatively robust across variations in the device's data sheet parameters, thereby requiring minimal adjustment for practical applications. In this study, we have focused on the continuous-converter convention; however, similar results are expected for other converter topologies and modulation schemes. Moreover, it should be noted that this method can be used for identification and analysis purposes even if an in-depth understanding of the converter's dynamics is not available. Our code and data have been publicly released and can be accessed through the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/bas-naija/Curve-Fitting-Converter-Delay-Analysis. Similarly, a pre-built MATLAB package has been developed to facilitate the easy and efficient application of this method to various converter systems. This package can be downloaded from the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/bas-naija/Converter-Delay-Analysis. A detailed video demonstrating the application of this method to a DC-DC converter can be found at: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8m5N9D2HAr4. Similarly, a video illustrating the identification of the linear regulator is available at: https://www.youtube

We introduce a novel concept of projective $L^{p}$-smoothness, a more generalized and flexible variant of the commonly used Recht and Balduzzi's smoothness in the learning theory and machine learning domains. Specifically, we define the projective $L^{p}$-smoothness of a function $f:X\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ as its tendency to have similar values on nearby balls of a given radius within a metric space. Furthermore, we show that this new smoothness concept leads to optimal rates for non-parametric regression and supervised learning in general metric spaces when the value of $p\geq 1$. Interestingly, we found that different values of $p$ can lead to significantly differing rates of convergence. In the context of MDPs within the $L^{q}$-Fubini space and under the condition of Lipschitz $q$-regularity, we demonstrate that our smoothness concept leads to the optimal rate of $\mathcal{O}(1)\cdot T^{1/(2p)}$, thus generalizing the findings of Giroir et al. (2020) and verifying the roughness of some functions in the learning theory domain. We also illustrate that our new smoothness concept leads to tighter rate bounds compared to those obtained from the classical $\ell_{\infty}$-smoothness and that it is resistant to perturbations. Furthermore, we found that functions with lower values of $p$ tend to have more restrictive smoothness conditions, thus reducing their applicability. Lastly, we show an example of how functions with exponential tails can be smoothly updated using perturbations. The findings of this research are published in a recent paper titled "Rough-Grained Smoothness for RL in Metric Frameworks". The related code can be accessed at https://github.com/damien-moulin/nest-rl-smooth. A recent study employed a stochastic framework to evaluate the animacy arrangement by combining bottom-up low-level image characteristics and high-level semantic information. In this work, we seek to understand the stochastic principles governing the animacy continuum and reveal the underlying essence of the animacy arrangement process. To do this, we develop a statistical model that integrates visual and semantic factors to predict human animacy judgments on a continuum from non-living to animal entities. The model consists of two stages: the first leverages a low-level feature extractor to extract visual animacy cues, followed by a fusion of these cues with semantic animacy information to generate animacy predictions. The results demonstrate that our proposed model surpasses existing analyses in capturing the essence of the animacy arrangement in human visual and semantic space. Notably, when the model's parameters are fixed, our study indicates that human VTC employs a spatial strategy to differentiate between nonliving and animal entities by utilizing low-level visual features, and that the fusion of these features with semantic information in the second stage enables nuanced distinctions between animate entities. This study proposes an intelligent demand side management system that utilizes game theory to efficiently organize load schedules. The system combines load aggregation with distributed optimization to produce energy usage plans that adhere to various participants'state of mind regarding energy usage. The study also introduces a billing system that factors in both scheduled and actual load, yielding a win-win situation for the grid and consumers. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is demonstrated using a 52-bus test network and compared with a flat pricing system. We investigate how radiation and black hole mass decay are respectively affected, under the assumption that charge conservation holds true. Additionally, we explore the connections between spin, charge, and gravitational feedback in this theoretical context. Our findings show that, in the absence of gravitational feedback and considering equilibrium conditions, the energy emission spectrum follows a Planck distribution. However, equilibrium conditions are not strictly maintained when gravitational feedback is included, which instead modifies the energy emission spectrum and introduces a damping effect, resulting in reduced Hawking radiation energy transmission. We also found that the Hawking radiation energy release is inversely related to the string's gravitational feedback strength and, in the absence of such feedback, this energy is completely absorbed by the black hole, causing it to shrink. To mitigate this energy loss, the string's gravitational feedback effect must be intensified, which can be accomplished by increasing the string's parameters, such as its length, mass per unit length, or the product of charge and length. Furthermore, our research indicates that the Hawking radiation energy release is directly dependent on the spin parameter and Hawking energy. We have also verified that, in cases where the string's gravitational feedback is not significant, the spin and charge relationships between these solutions and those in the original Einstein theory remain intact. This paper investigates the convergence rates in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem, making use of spectral metrics. By doing so, we shed light on the relationship between convergence speed and the smallest eigenvalue of the transition matrix. In particular, we obtain estimates for the rate of convergence in terms of the spectral gap, as well as examples illustrating the conditions under which this spectral gap may tend to zero. We also consider an illustrative example with an almost discrete spectrum. Furthermore, we extend our methodology to analyze convergence speeds in a more broad context of random operators, encompassing (multi-dimensional) Markov chains, stochastic processes, and operators defined on abstract Hilbert spaces. In doing so, we introduce the concept of p-spectral gaps for p > 0, demonstrate its relation to the best constant in a p-Hölder inequality, and display its significance in determining the rate of convergence in the Ergodic Theorem. We also provide illustrative examples of Markov chains involving both discrete and continuous-state spaces. Lastly, we confirm that our method of analysis is independent of any assumptions regarding the structure of the state space, which may be either countable or uncountable, or even comprise an arbitrary measure space constructed in an arbitrary manner. Consequently, the findings presented here may be considered highly general. We extend our scope of investigation even further by applying the same methodology to analyze operator semigroups in a more broad context, though we do make certain assumptions regarding the semigroup's regularity. Our approach is, however, entirely arithmetical in nature. By doing so, we establish a connection between the smallest eigenvalue of the semigroup's generator and the best constant in the p-Hölder inequality. We also obtain a detailed description of the behavior of norms of powers of (q, p)-Hölder norms for q + p ≠ 1, 2, with the goal of distinguishing between the limiting behavior of those norms when p < 2 versus the case in which p ≥ 2. In the former case, we obtain a degenerate limit, corresponding to a convolution semigroup characterized by a compactly supported Lipschitz function. In the latter case, we obtain a semigroup characterized by a Gaussian distribution. In addition to these illustrative examples, we also confirm that our method of analysis is applicable to a wide range of contexts, encompassing the dissipative one-dimensional Schrödinger operator on the real numbers, the classical heat equation, the Poisson equation, and the Laplacian on a manifold

This research aims to analyze and forecast blaze intensity on a global scale, using data from the Operational Linesearch Database. By developing and using an alternative metric for blaze intensity, we're able to evaluate and compare different types of sparks and reactors. In addition, we're training a BPE tokenizer to translate labels into numerical codes, which we're using to train a headless GameMaker engine to generate physics-based rendering of sparks. This rendering is being integrated into a TensorFlow model, which we're training to predict intensity on a logarithmic scale. Notably, we're training our model without using labeled data, instead using a reconstruction autoencoder to pretrain the encoder, followed by a nearest-neighbor lookup to find similar data points for each sample, which we're using to calculate reconstruction errors for each encoder dimension. By adding L1 regularization at training time, we're preventing overfitting and optimizing our model's hyperparameters. In addition to spatial intensity prediction, we're exploring two novel directions: first, using audio cues from listeners to gauge blaze intensity; second, using spatially unaligned 2D drawing data to forecast 3D blaze intensity in the absence of sufficient 3D training data. Overall, we're proposing the first global blaze intensity prediction framework, which has numerous applications in multiple fields. We're assessing our model's performance using both manual evaluation and crowdsourcing. In related work, we're examining and comparing the perceptual and cognitive blaze intensity metrics used in the past. In particular, we're evaluating and proposing a new GameMaker-based metric for automated intensity judgment. Furthermore, we're testing the feasibility of our framework for other physics-based simulation tasks. In addition, we're examining the trade-offs between the benefits of incorporating user input, namely listener response, to aid intensity prediction. Lastly, we're investigating and discussing the implications of leveraging drawn 2D drawings to forecast 3D blaze intensity in the absence of sufficient 3D training data. In summary, we're presenting a unique fusion of machine learning, computer vision, signal processing, and signal genetics to tackle the challenging problem of global blaze intensity prediction. This note examines two elliptic equations related to surface metrics, specifically with $W^{2, p}$ and $W^{1, p}$ norms on compact manifolds. We provide a unified proof for the existence and smoothness of solutions in these metrics, drawing on ideas from elliptic theory and Lorentz spaces to establish appropriate estimates. Our approach encompasses not only surface metrics but also $C^{0, \gamma}$ norms on compact surfaces and even extends to study partial differential equations. Moreover, we explore an intrinsic equation in relation to surface metrics, providing potential applications in geometry and calculus of variations. We also consider an alternative form of this equation, namely the Euler-Lagrange operator of a surface variational problem. We demonstrate that solutions to this operator are smooth and explore their potential use in establishing $C^{1, \gamma}$ estimates for conformal metrics. Ultimately, our approach offers a novel perspective on surface metrics and their applications, though we do regretfully overlook the critical case of $p = 2$ in our estimates due to issues related to the degeneracy of the second derivative. Estimates in this case would require modification to avoid the singular terms that arise, as was done in related works by Vainchtein and Giga--Bouchittouche. We hope to address this case and expand our findings in a future study. Conversely, we can readily establish the $C^{0, 1, 1, 2, p}$ estimates for all $p > 1$, as desired, through the use of a simplified approach that relies on the $W^{1, p}$ norm in this context. Our specific findings concern an equation of the form $\mathrm{div}_{g} (Y^{ij} \partial_{j} u) = 0$ in the surface metric $g$, which we determine to be solvable for $1 < p < q < q + n$, with $n$ dimensions, and offering a unified framework for surface metrics that draws on ideas from potential theory and the use of Lorentz spaces, calder\'{o}n-Zygmund operators, and other relevant systems. We can explore the potential use of these theorems in the context of surface conformality in geometry and calculus of variations, while our findings on the Euler-Lagrange operator and conformal metrics are more novel in nature and not directly related to existing works in these fields. We can thus use these theorems in the context of surface conformality in geometry

Furthermore, our predictions also suggest the potential existence of many unknown cobalt-abundant compounds in the Co-B-YSZ system, which could be verified by experimental validation. This paper investigates the most effective strategy for display advertising bid management when taking into account the risks associated with winning ads without knowing their values. We focused specifically on a specific type of value uncertainty where the possible values for each ad are drawn from a known distribution. Our approach involves creating an innovative bounded adaptive dynamic program that tailor bid amounts to the specific characteristics of each auction, such as the number of competing bidders and the estimated ad value ranges. We also examined various scenarios to understand how different factors like the distribution of ad values, the number of participating auctions, and the available budget affect our proposed method. Additionally, we compared our approach with a widely used bidding algorithm and conducted several experiments to measure its performance under different conditions. Our results indicate that our approach can achieve up to a 56% reduced risk compared to a standard bidding algorithm for display advertising, and also remains robust against uncertainties and budget limitations. Establishing secure communications over insecure channels is the primary goal of Quantum Key Exchange (QKE), which achieves this through the implementation of quantum physics principles, primarily ensuring that eavesdropping attempts will disrupt the communicated data, making it unreadable after the exchange. Although QKE can provide optimal security, in practice, factors such as non-ideal source reliability and non-uniform random source privacy enhancement impact the achieved security, thus compromising the complete security of the communicated data. To address this, we introduce a reliable transmission metric and propose the operation strategy of "first-bound then-bound" for QKE, first enabling a bound evaluation of the source's unreliability and subsequently allowing for legitimate parties to use this bound as a reference to determine the maximum possible eavesdropping loss, thereby ensuring the remaining data remains secure. Our research confirms that with non-uniform random source privacy enhancement, "first-bound then-bound" offers better performance than the "always-bound" approach, providing greater total reliable data transmission and enhanced overall system resilience. Compared to "always-bound", it can achieve a 66.89% and 64.35% increase in total reliable data transmission in cases of non-uniform random source privacy enhancement of 0.5 and 0.7 respectively. We have further verified that the "first-bound then-bound" strategy outperforms "always-bound" and can establish QKE in scenarios where "always-bound" fails to do so, providing greater total reliable data transmission and overall system resilience. To showcase its applicability, we have implemented the "first-bound then-bound" strategy on the BB84 QKE and plain QKE systems, achieving promising results. Our research notably indicates that "first-bound then-bound" and "always-bound" obtain the same total reliable data transmission in some cases, thereby making "always-bound" a reliable choice when contract negotiation priority is crucial, whereas "first-bound then-bound" offers superior system resilience when contract negotiation priority is crucial. A typical reward learning process typically begins with an algorithm that ranks candidate rewards and ends with a model that uses the selected reward to guide policy learning.
This research focuses on finding a faster alternative to most existing methods, which evaluate rewards in a vacuum and struggle with the sheer number of potential rewards.
Our proposed solution groups rewards together then asks the learner to identify the best batch, reducing the need to evaluate rewards one by one.
To achieve this, we utilized the insights from human feedback to develop a more efficient clustering algorithm, which combines constraint propagation and clustering to produce high-quality groups.
Our method outperforms existing reward learning methods by using an optimized algorithm that speeds up the process, resulting in more accurate reward learning in our experiments. 
Ultimately, this research makes reward learning faster and more robust, enabling it to be used in real-world applications, such as robotics.

Research on topological phenomena in disordered systems has garnered significant interest due to their remarkable characteristics. Within the realm of classical spin models, a group of Toric code-inspired patterns has emerged as ideal candidates for exhibiting topological features. This family of models incorporates a new frustration element, leading to the assumption that their behavior may be similar to that of the non-trivial topological models despite being classical in nature. However, this assumption is challenged when analyzing the models' ground states, as we demonstrate our findings by focusing on the triangular-lattice-based Livan-Luscher model. Our study reveals that this model possesses only a single ground state characterized by a zero-energy double dipole. Although this outcome may suggest the presence of a topological edge state, our in-depth analysis shows that this edge state disappears once a small perturbation is applied, revealing that the model's behavior is actually that of a standard frustrated spin model. As such, we can conclude that these typical models do not adequately represent the desired Toric code patterns. We then extend our research by introducing a new modified Livan-Luscher model, incorporating a cosmological constant term, and successfully verify the presence of a topological edge state within this modified model. This achievement marks an important breakthrough in the search for topological features in classical spin models. Furthermore, our research has significant implications for the development of quantum surface codes, as the understanding of their classical counterparts may either validate or refute their potential use in efficient information processing. We provide an in-depth analysis of the possible applications of these models, recommending further study into the development of phase-separated Livan-Luscher patterns as a potential solution to decompose the complex ground state into its individual cluster components, thereby enabling the effective characterization of their properties. We also explore alternative approaches such as the use of constraint cycles or the addition of coherent dynamics to differentiate between the standard and the topological behaviors of the models. Ultimately, our research has rendered the existence of topological features in classical spin models questionable, a conclusion that may also significantly impact the broader theories of topological quantum dynamics. Furthermore, our cross-validation findings indicate that BERT- MeaningEncoder achieves more robustness in handling inaccuracies in text, as compared to a baseline model using BERT. Our proposed BERT- MeaningEncoder also exhibits superior performance and more stability in comparison to a state-of-the-art model called MesoTRG. One such method is the Isolation Forest algorithm, which works by incorporating two random forest classifiers in series, one responsible for separating and the other for isolating anomalous data. By utilizing two forests, Isolation Forest exhibits faster computation and improved parallelization opportunities. Building upon this concept, we've created TiWS-iForest, a loosely supervised anomaly detection method that combines the efficiency of Isolation Forest with enhanced performance capabilities, facilitated through data augmentation and weighted sampling. Our results demonstrate that TiWS-iForest significantly outperforms the standard Isolation Forest, achieving a 25% or greater improvement in remote sensing anomaly detection tasks. Furthermore, we've made the WS-iForest version of this method open-source for the community to use and continue developing anomaly detection innovations. A statistical framework is proposed to compare the 'Poisson by choice' approach with traditional methods, where simulations are conducted to assess how well different models accurately capture extreme event patterns. A detailed study of the metal-rich globular cluster NGC 2808 has provided precise measurements of critical properties for 8 red giant stars within the cluster. Our research, which took into account the complex interplay between temperature, pressure, and chemical composition in star formation, led to accurate determination of key elements including helium, carbon, and nitrogen levels. Our results also suggest that the cluster exhibits a notable yet subtle gradient in chemical composition. A notable aspect of our findings is the detectable difference in helium levels across the cluster, which is a rarity among old stellar clusters. Our work confirms the long-held theory that the cluster's multiple populations arise from distinct formation episodes rather than a single uniform star-forming event. Additionally, our data indicate that the cluster's initial chemical spread, accounting for He variation, was approximately 0.2 dex, a degree of spread that is comparable to recent findings for the young $\omega$ Centauri star cluster, rather than the more extreme variations seen in younger globular clusters. Computational data in modern scientific applications typically exhibits sparse or irregular patterns with varying levels of local correlation. Leveraging this structure, techniques like parallel recursive partitioning and cut-sampling have been successfully applied to tackle virtual machine (VM) placement issues in cloud computing. Nonetheless, existing implementations have failed to effectively harness the potential of data sparsity and local correlation in customizing VM allocations. This study proposes the Prepartition method to address VM placement by incorporating a novel, data-driven approach called preference. Based on user-specified preferences, Prepartition partitions and maps spare resources accordingly, resulting in better resource utilization, increased efficiency, and greater flexibility. Evaluations using real-world applications, matrices and various types of user preferences have demonstrated the effectiveness of Prepartition in achieving these benefits. In contrast to traditional methods, results show that Prepartition can achieve up to a 25% reduction in communication cost, 30% greater performance, and increased user flexibility. Compared to other parallel partitioning-based methods, Prepartition can achieve up to a 90% speedup while using up to 94% less memory. Moreover, Prepartition outperforms cut-sampling by providing more efficient and accurate allocations. This research marks the first study to explore the sparsity and local correlation in customizing VM allocations, and its innovations have been patented. In graph theory, an upward planar drawing can be visualized as a two-dimensional layout where edges are directed upwards without intersecting other edges in the drawing. Upward planarity has numerous applications across various fields including astronomy, biology, medical genetics, and software engineering. The main challenge in checking if a graph can be drawn in an upward planar format revolves around identifying whether the given graph's edges can be realigned to form a planar diagram with all edges pointing upwards. Due to the complexity of solving this issue using traditional approaches, researchers have developed parameterized solutions that efficiently solve this problem for specific types of graphs. Notably, researchers have developed a technique to solve the problem in a linear time framework if the graph in question has a relatively small number of vertices that violate the upward planar condition. Using the concept of contraction decomposition, researchers have further refined this approach to narrow down the complexity to a more manageable subset of these vertices - specifically to the k most "connected" vertices within the graph. Theoretically, this technique allows for solving upward planarity problems in O(n/k^2.5) time. Another variant of this concept, known as Additive Increase, exposes an even smaller subset of these problematic vertices, to be gradually increased over the course of the contraction process, yet an efficient algorithm eludes us. The final technique, known as Progressive Increase, has its own algorithmic implications. The main issue with Additive Increase and Progressive Increase is that they fail to offer the same kind of guarantee as the Contracting Decomposition - that the number of vertices needing special handling decreases gradually as the contraction process advances. The Progressive Increase technique has some potential in that its input-based vertex selection could potentially be combined with Contracting Decomposition's, yet an efficient algorithm remains elusive for the latter. The paper delves into these techniques, discussing their inspirations, connections, differences and similarities in an effort to improve our understanding of upward planarity. The research was fueled by real-world data, showing that in nearly 80% of the tested graphs with 20 or fewer problematic vertices under the Progressive Increase criterion, the graph in question could be easily drawn in an upward planar format. The remaining 20% proved more challenging to solve - whether or not to develop an efficient algorithm for these more complex graphs remains an open question. The researchers argue that the search for an efficient algorithm to solve these more complex "challenging" graphs has merit, while also acknowledging that the current techniques allow for solving simpler graphs in the majority. We investigate a multi-player game where players' actions are determined by private variables with possibly correlated values, and the player with the highest or lowest value wins. The specific scenario we examine involves four players with publicly drawn, randomly sampled, three-value indicators from a shared, normally distributed pair of variables, and the player with the lowest draw wins. In this study, a replication of a previous investigation into the directed genetic algorithm is conducted to further explore its effectiveness in generating failures for software systems.  By utilising practical approaches within real-world contexts, the researchers aim to enhance the directed genetic algorithm's efficiency in producing failures and increase its potential for linking those failures to existing bugs.  Their search for optimal failures was concentrated on just one fault, choosing strategies to control the algorithm that were suggested in the original research as particularly successful in generating failures for it.  Notably, by restricting the search to a single fault, the team were able to produce detailed system state records, thereby gaining insight into the algorithm's operation, a resource missing from the original research.  Their experiments with the directed genetic algorithm, applying it to a practical Java-based software system, revealed mixed results, suggesting further research is needed to fully understand its potential for failure reproduction.  Consequently, a decision has been made not to carry out further investigations focused on producing a comprehensive map of system failures, instead advising against such a focus in the present state of knowledge.  Their data and program can be accessed at github.com/fathahussain/dga-failure-reproduction.  Finally, through an evaluation involving three experts in software testing, suggestions for enhancing the directed genetic algorithm's performance were suggested.  Specifically, several potential enhancements were identified which may cause the algorithm to search less randomly, thereby presenting potential avenues for growth and development in this field.  Their search logs and other supporting information is available online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.infsof.2021.102434.  A particular thanks is expressed for the original research's lead author's willingness to engage with these replication efforts and share further details of their research, which was greatly valued.  Ultimately, further investigations should seek an integration of the directed genetic algorithm with existing failure reproduction techniques.  One such failure which the algorithm was unable to replicate involved linking the system's crash to an unexpected data type mismatch, a potential bug which the team were able to confirm existed within their test system, underscoring yet another compelling reason for ongoing research in this area.  Their findings serve to expand the body of knowledge surrounding this directed genetic algorithm, which was initially studied in depth by its lead author Alkhatib et al. This phenomenon was noted in the first report of static magnetoresistance in a cuprate superconductor and has since been observed in additional systems.  In an study on the interplay of magnetism and superconductivity in \textit{Y$_{1-x}$Ce$_x$Ba$_2$Cu_3$F_7$}, a similar vortex grid transition from a square to a square-square pattern is reported.  The new pattern exhibits a higher degree of periodic disorder and is linked to the appearance of a substantial and unusual magnetoresistance.  The Ce dilution needed to achieve this transition is significantly lower than previously required for observation in the similar $T_\textrm{c}$ system \text{YBa$_2$Cu_3$F_8$}.  The Ce distribution is shown to break the full $P$4/$mmm$ point group symmetry of optimally doped \text{YBa$_2$Cu_3$F_8$} yielding an isotropic magnetoresistance and reducing charge $w$ waviness in the square grid of vortices.  The Ce distribution forms local antiferromagnetic (La) sites acting as magnetic scatterers, providing insight into the physical mechanism of the vortex grid transition and suggesting an new class of systems to search for this transition. Thermal photons, produced early in the collision, can reveal the initial conditions and help understand how collective flow emerges. Research shows that thermal photons cross the critical viscosity threshold, transitioning from an ideal fluid to an interacting fluid, exhibiting collective behavior. Furthermore, studies reveal that thermal photons align in the same direction as other collective particles at lower viscosities but shift to oppose them at higher viscosities. experiments have two key differences. Firstly, the interventions are highly
correlated. Secondly, the experiments have a regulated false discovery rate
(FDR). Given these factors, the standard routine of testing individual
hypotheses one by one using Bonferroni to control FDR is less optimal. 
  - Optimality is achieved when FDR is controlled and the number of tests

by comparing groups in a hierarchical manner and using family groups to test the
null hypothesis of no effect. The method's performance is demonstrated in a
simulated experiment and the technique is applied to analyze real-world data

The wave function that describes spatial expansion was interpreted as a multi-dimensional "gas" whose pressure is negative, resulting in negative energy density, thereby facilitating further expansion. The wave function was normalized to obtain the energy density per mode of the wave function, which was found to be negative energy density due to the non-zero spatial components of the conformal tensor in the given model. In human-computer interaction, question-answering systems can benefit from providing conceptual support to enhance user comprehension, but not all questions require such intervention. Determining which questions do benefit from conceptual support and finding the optimal way to present it are key challenges in this area. To address these challenges, we introduce the QUICKAR system, which uses a multi-stage approach with various machine learning models to reformulate given questions in a way that highlights specific concepts, with the goal of supporting a variety of concepts and text formats. Our results, based on crowdsourced feedback, demonstrate that QUICKAR outperforms competing approaches with a significant improvement of over 23% in their performance. Additionally, we explain how QUICKAR's recent integration with Google's web interface has contributed to its success by leveraging web-based information to inform its decision-making process. Our findings highlight the various strategies that QUICKAR uses to adapt to different concepts and text formats, as well as the key characteristics that distinguish its question reformulations from those of other systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that QUICKAR's ability to effectively formulate questions about specific concepts depends on the quality of training data, which can be positively affected by incorporating web-based information. Using these insights, we outline a range of potential future research directions in this area. Our results also illustrate the various strategies that users employ to answer questions, which can inform the design of more effective human-computer interaction systems. Using these insights, we demonstrate at Google's Developer Day how QUICKAR's integration with Google's web interface can be used to inform the design of more effective human-computer interaction systems. Entrainment in conversations is a phenomenon where interactants adjust their communication strategies to synchronize with each other, which can be achieved through several methods, including altering speech tempo, using concise or elaborate language, selecting specific vocabulary, or varying the frequency of interruptions. Prior studies on entrainment in conversations often rely on measures of similarity between speakers' utterances, such as word frequency or part-of-speech distributions, but these measures may not capture the dynamic nature of entrainment, especially lag effects. Alternatively, studies have used correlation analysis to assess the consistency between speakers, but correlation does not directly indicate the timing or magnitude of shifts in speaking styles. In order to develop a more effective method of identifying entrainment without relying on manual annotation, we created a training corpus using text data from conversations and natural conversations as they naturally occur. Using this method, we calculated the average word embedding distances between speakers over varying time intervals from the conversation corpus, then trained a neural network to predict the speaker who used each sequence of words based on the average distances between speakers. By testing the performance of our model, we found that speaker identification becomes more challenging as the time interval lengthens, but our model can still achieve speaker identification with reasonable accuracy when the analysis window is several minutes long. This method could be used to automatically detect entrainment in conversations without needing human reviewers, provided the analysis window is long enough, offering a potential computational solution to identify and analyze entrainment in conversations. This study was conducted to explore entrainment as it relates to conversational lags and may have implications for developing AI systems that can adapt to the tempo of human conversations. Our proposed model presents an alternative to traditional statistical methods of analysis, offering a more direct measure of lag effects in conversational entrainment. While this study focused on word embeddings, researchers could also investigate other statistical measures, such as analyzing the frequencies of speaker interruptions or assessing consistency in part-of-speech usage, in order to develop a more comprehensive characterization of entrainment that can be used to predict or manipulate speech patterns at the lexical, syntactic, and semantic levels. Most existing approaches to unsupervised temporal action segmentation rely heavily on frame-level hand-crafted features and memory-basis attention mechanisms. Nevertheless, these methods have significant drawbacks, including high computational cost for feature extraction and failure to capture the complex relationships between actions due to their focus on individual frames. To overcome these limitations, we introduce SSCAP, a novel self-supervised action parsing method, which utilizes a graph neural network to incorporate inter-action relationships. SSCAP also incorporates a novel attention mechanism called Temporal Self Attention (TSA), which enables the network to accurately determine start and end frames of actions and effectively avoids relying on hand-crafted features. Furthermore, we suggest an unsupervised loss function for training the entire parsing network without ground truth. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that SSCAP outperforms state-of-the-art methods on action segmentation and segmentation-to-classification tasks. SSCAP also shows excellent generalization capabilities across across categories and datasets, and its source code is available at https://github.com/fuqianghe/SSCAP. Students learn software testing concepts best by actively using them, not just studying, so instructors. As part of the testing education initiative, we offer two educational tools: the Testing Confusion Experiment and the Testing Debugging Experiment. These tools apply inquiry-based learning to help students understand testing ideas in an empirical setting. We found that students who used these tools improved their problem-solving skills and had fewer confusions about testing concepts than students who received conventional study materials. They also performed better in an actual testing project. Since its introduction in 2018, the Testing Confusion Experiment has been used by over 500 students, demonstrating its effectiveness in helping students learn and overcome testing challenges. Our comparison of inquiry-based learning and conventional study methods shows that students who used the Testing Confusion Experiment outperformed those who received a study guide in terms of reduced conceptual confusions (81.4% vs. 55.9%), better debugging skills, and higher team effectiveness in a actual project (87.1% vs. 81.3%). These differences were statistically significant. Given its effectiveness and wide adoption, we believe that the Testing Confusion Experiment is a valuable educational tool for teaching software testing concepts. It can be applied to other programming and software engineering education domains as well. As proof of its practicality, we have successfully applied this concept to a actual practical project in the past at CUI. As a result, the students involved in this project demonstrated their ability to design and carry out actual testing strategies for that project. Our results were confirmed through an A/B testing analysis, providing empirical validation for this concept in an educational setting. Currently, the Testing Debugging Experiment is helping over 200 students improve their debugging skills as part of an actual project at CUI. We look forward to expanding this concept to a larger audience in the future. Domain adjustment, the task of adapting a model's performance across related datasets, has been extensively used in various medical imaging applications. Despite its significance, this approach often struggles when there are no target data available for direct training, a scenario known as source-free domain adjustment. This paper presents a novel and robust framework for addressing this limitation by identifying and transferring key statistical patterns, or domain features, between two different datasets. To prevent overfitting in our method, which relies on two unsupervised approaches to estimate domain features, we employ a semi-supervised transfer strategy utilizing a large amount of unlabeled target data. Our proposed framework significantly improves upon existing source-free domain adjustment techniques and delivers superior performance in cross-hospital brain segmentation exercises. For more information on our experiments and results, please visit our project page at https://sites.google.com/view/supconvergence. To facilitate further research, we have also made our source code and pre-trained models publicly available at https://github.com/whhu2000/Source-Free_Domain_Adjustment. Our research demonstrates that by leveraging domain features, we can achieve state-of-the-art source-free domain adjustment performance that rivals that of supervised domain adjustment methods. To the best of our knowledge, this work presents a groundbreaking solution to the problem of source-free domain adjustment. We hope that through our research, the medical imaging community can enjoy more benefits from domain adjustment techniques. Lastly, we have explored the theoretical boundaries of our framework and obtained several novel insights that may contribute to the understanding of domain adjustment methods, as detailed in our paper. We are particularly excited about the potential applications of our research and eagerly anticipate the feedback and collaborations of fellow researchers in the future. A particular system that has received limited attention is the Gas Core Nuclear Reactor, largely due to the complexity of its design and the challenges posed by its seven-fold increase in size compared to other nuclear systems. This paper aims to introduce the GCR concept, evaluate its advantages and disadvantages compared to other space nuclear power systems, and present recently completed design studies of the GCR initiated at the University of Tennessee. Building upon their work, this paper proposes a comprehensive design plan with detailed design specifications of the GCR's various components, including its reflector and fuel modules, fuel, tritium, and plenum. A thorough examination of these systems, along with estimates for their weights, will be provided, along with an assessment of the remaining challenges that need to be addressed to move the GCR concept forward. A critical analysis will be provided on the current status of GCR development and the steps required to advance this system further. Lastly, this paper will present an overview of the remaining hurdles that need to be overcome for NASA and other space agencies to consider deploying the GCR in various space missions. It is expected that the detailed design and weight estimates will facilitate the implementation of the GCR system, potentially propelling its development forward at a faster pace. An executive summary of this paper will be provided to the NASA Mars Exploration Directorate to gauge their interest in incorporating the GCR concept into their future mission plans. Similarly, a copy will be shared with NASA Nuclear Systems Division to explore the interest of NASA Centers in further research and development of the GCR concept. A comprehensive set of graphics, including 3D models, cross sections, flow charts, and schematics, will be created to aid researchers and engineers in visualizing the GCR system and to facilitate their understanding of its various components. It is anticipated that the engagement of industry participants and researchers involved in the GCR concept or other nuclear power systems for space will be obtained to incorporate their feedback and to identify potential collaborators in further research and development of the GCR system. A series of lectures will be delivered at the University of Tennessee, as well as at the Texas A&M University, to introduce the GCR concept to students and researchers, with a view of gauging their interest in further research and development of the GCR system. Furthermore, a series of webinars will be conducted at the Texas A&M University to raise awareness of the GCR

Novel methods in deep learning have made significant contributions to astroparticle research, particularly in identifying scattered particles and their original sources. Deep learning approaches, however, often require large datasets and experimental validation, making them poorly understood and difficult to inform with existing scientific knowledge. This research proposes a neural network architecture that seamlessly integrates scientific research findings, thereby Monte Carlo data used in the astrophysics community. The architecture's flexibility allows for a flexible balance between data-driven and physical science approaches, providing insight into the complex relationships between particle inputs. With its adaptable nature, the architecture can accommodate various input data such as particle depths in the ground or energy levels, allowing for simultaneous prediction of multiple parameters, including energy, direction, and depth of origin. We present several examples of the architecture's applications, covering neutrino sources, ultra-high energy cosmic rays, and gamma rays, illustrating the effectiveness of scientific research informing neural networks through domain-informed learning techniques. The accompanying code can be found on the 'informnn' repository on GitHub. 

Domain-informed learning has numerous applications and benefits, particularly in astrophysics and related fields. Domain-informed learning networks recognize patterns within data but also make connections to the underlying physical world, providing a deeper understanding of the relationships between inputs and outputs. This paper presents a general framework for informing neural networks using physical domain knowledge and applies it to the prediction of ultra-high energy cosmic rays' depths, energy spectra, and arrival directions. The networks can simultaneously make these three predictions based on the same feature set. Experiment results using Standard Large Ensemble Monte Carlo shows that the informnn method significantly improves energy reconstruction, achieving a root-mean-square error nearly an order of magnitude lower than traditional methods, while the impact on depth and direction prediction shows substantial potential with further optimization. Consequently, domain-informed learning has the potential to enhance the accuracy of many astrophysical experiments and data-driven investigations.

The study of exoplanet atmospheres, particularly those of brown dwarfs and giant exoplanets, relies heavily on models that use various astrophysical data and molecular absorption cross-sections. Despite its vital role, there's no comprehensive database available to date for this data. We've developed EXOPLINES, a repository of high-accuracy absorption cross-sections for key atmospheric molecules (N2, CO2, H2O, CH4, NH3, and H2S) at room temperature and pressure. To ensure precision, our cross-sections are compared against experimental and simulated data, with many showing less than a 1% discrepancy. We've also derived plausible range extensions for each cross-section. By providing accurate and up-to-date absorption cross-sections, EXOPLINES serves as a valuable resource for researchers working with atmospheric models. As such, we plan to regularly update our database with new cross-sections to reflect the latest research developments. Additionally, we've illustrated the utility of EXOPLINES through the analysis of its potential application in studying heavy metal sulfides within giant planet atmospheres. We've demonstrated its capability to forecast consistent absorption properties for these species across various pressure conditions. We believe EXOPLINES will play a significant role in advancing our understanding of exoplanet and brown dwarf atmospheres. We invite the community to reach out and collaborate with us to further develop this essential tool. Currently, EXOPLINES and related materials are accessible for free at our dedicated Git repository at https://git.lde.oaubo.edu/astroalex/exoelines. In the future, we also intend to integrate it into the C2RY framework. Furthermore, we will integrate our repository into the remixed C2RY Version 2.0, which is scheduled for release in mid-2023. We welcome users to reach out to us at https://astroalex.lde.org for technical support and feedback. We're pleased to provide feedback and support to the community to ensure successful integration and implementation of this repository, ultimately facilitating cutting-edge research in the field of exoplanetary science. Currently, key molecules covered by our repository include those found in the H2O-CH4 atmospheres of giant exoplanets and their associated sub-Neptune planets, providing essential insights into their internal heating mechanisms and overall planetary mass distributions. We also provide comprehensive support for the study of telluric species (CO2, NH3, and H2S) in vast interstellar medium and planetary environments.

The idea behind boson sampling suggests that measuring the density matrix of a boson sample in a specific state might not reveal any information about the underlying interaction Hamiltonian, and thus the outcome might be entirely determined by the wavefunction of the source photons. In this paper, we investigate whether there exists a wavefunction for the input photons that would consistently produce sample outcomes independent of the interaction setup, and assess whether this wavefunction is entangled. We find that, in general, this wavefunction must be entangled and, further, that it is impossible to determine its entanglement using measurements on the sample output, regardless of their specificity or number of trials. We further explore the notion of "fair" boson sampling, in which the probability distribution of output photons remains unchanged under all possible wavefunctions, and demonstrate that it is impossible for boson sampling to be fair if all possible input wavefunctions are either pure or mixed states. However, when input wavefunctions are restricted to being pure, we identify a criterion for a boson sampling setup that allows it to be fair if and only if it is implementable with a wavefunction that is not entangled. This insight is similar to a known property of entanglement-free clonning, and we show that both concepts are actually equivalent, albeit with a specific restriction of the underlying systems, and thus can be extended to our consideration of boson sampling. We conclude by discussing how these findings relate to recent experimental results. Our work provides theoretical support for boson sampling, and helps to further clarify its underlying physical implementation. Moreover, in conjunction with Stierhof's work on entanglement in the wavefunctions for general quantum states, we obtain complete information about the entanglement in the wavefunction for the source photons that participates in a boson sampling process. We demonstrate that, in a boson sampling process, this wavefunction is either not entangled or is a specific type of tripartite entanglement, and we identify necessary and sufficient conditions under which it must be entangled. In various life science applications, researchers often work with high-dimensional temporal data that are brief and noisy in nature. Examples of such data include microarray time course analyses and microscope imaging in cells. Problems with such data types are complex: they involve processing complex temporal patterns with many variables, noisy data, limited sequence lengths, and incomplete or missing values. Existing machine learning techniques, however, have been shown to be ineffective in handling these complexities on their own. Therefore, a novel approach is presented, combining monitored learning with Echo state network, resulting in the MoESN model. This model was successfully tested on simulated and real-world microarray time course data. Experimentation revealed that MoESN performs substantially better than traditional methods. Moreover, an advanced variant of MoESN, the Selective MoESN, was developed, employing all relevant data in a thoroughly systematic manner. Preliminary studies indicate that selective data choice has a major impact on the accuracy of temporal networks, and that choosing relevant data based on temporal relationships can greatly enhance temporal system comprehension. Overall, the integration of monitored learning and Echo state networks has shown promising results and further research is recommended for leveraging temporal network characteristics to improve temporal data analysis and understanding. Recurrent neural networks are remarkably effective at handling time-series data at a systemic level, but their ability to interpret internal state changes for tasks in partially observable environments is less clear. We investigated this question through a new approach that involves a direct method to assess a recurrent neural network's perception of its own state in tasks with hidden variables. Using this more realistic model, we found that recurrent networks often reach a high level of confidence in their decisions even when there is no direct evidence available, but their understanding of their own state remains remarkably poor. Additionally, we discovered that this lack of state self-awareness does not hinder their overall performance in environmental tasks. These findings are highly relevant to the development of future artificial systems, particularly those that are designed to operate in uncertain or unpredictable real-world environments. One potential implication is that the creation of safe and reliable intelligent systems that operate in partially observable environments may require significant changes to their underlying architecture. In order to achieve this goal, we would recommend developing algorithms or systems that are capable of learning to accurately recognize and adapt to changing states over extended periods of time. In this research, we found that recurrent networks, which are widely used in many AI systems, are not naturally designed to do this effectively. Therefore, we would recommend exploring alternative architectures that are capable of learning and interpreting their own internal state in a more effective manner. One such example is the relatively new 'differentiable neural layer' which has been proven to be an effective tool for learning and interpreting internal states. In future, we intend to continue investigating these topics and answering the question of whether it is possible for artificial systems to truly 'know what they are thinking'. Our research is taking a step towards addressing this question by developing new systems that learn and interpret their own internal states in a more effective manner. One such example is the'Knowledge-Optimising Recurrent Network' which has been successfully tested in a range of difficult tasks. By developing systems that are capable of learning and interpreting their own internal states in a more effective manner, we believe that we are one step closer to answering this key question. Ultimately, we are committed to advancing the latest AI technologies in a responsible and effective manner in order to address some of the key challenges that are currently holding back the development of trustworthy and intelligent systems. In this case, we are working to develop new systems that place equal emphasis on both optimisation and state transparency, which we believe is key to realising the full potential of recurrent architectures in tasks with hidden variables. Our proposed solution is designed to address these key challenges

Current action detection methods heavily rely on strong and expensive annotation guides. This leads to a common issue of scarce annotated data. Our novel framework addresses this problem by developing a system to identify key video segments based on the entire context, rather than relying on expensive guides. We utilize a graph to represent the association between spatial-temporal actions and learn this relationship with a graph convolutive network to produce a context-aware memory. This memory then facilitates the inference of action detection. Our spot-based approach can learn from guides of various strengths (bounded from above by box-based methods) and outperforms existing action detection methods on HLMTA. Our code is available at https://github.com/cz660/spot. Extensive experiments on HMDB51, UCF101, Kinetics SALiency, JHMDB, and ActivityNet have shown superior performance compared to baseline methods. We also report state-of-the-art detection results on the ActivityNet dataset. For the UCF101 23 dataset, our method achieves a mAP@50, 75, and 100 that is 2%, 4%, or 6% higher than the baseline memory-less model. We demonstrate large performance improvement over diverse guides types, validating the value of developing this framework. Our framework yields mAP@100 that is 3%, 5%, 8%, 11%, and 14% higher than the baseline method on the ActivityNet dataset when using 1, 5, 10, 20, and 50 guides per video, respectively. Our method also shows great resistance to noisy guides, recovering performance when the guide noise ratio is set to 0.5. Furthermore, our method yields state-of-the-art detection results on the ActivityNet dataset. Specifically, using five guides, our method reaches a mAP@100 of 20.39%, outperforming the existing top method on the dataset by 14.25%. This study highlights the effectiveness of developing this framework, which has the potential to greatly boost action detection performance, thereby saving the labor and cost associated with box guides. We also conducted a cross-database cross-validation, where our method performed well when tested on different datasets, indicating robustness and a well-generalized model, which further confirms the value of this framework. This study demonstrates that spot-based action detection yields higher mAP@100 than box-based methods, reaching a mAP@100 of 40.44%, representing a 33.07% increase over the top action detection method on the ActivityNet dataset. Tables are highly readable and searchable components within documents but are often difficult to locate in disorganized structures such as archives and old manuscripts. Research has shown that graph neural networks are more effective than traditional retrieval methods at understanding table layouts and extracting table data from unstructured documents. To improve table structure recognition, we suggest using graph neural networks in combination with distinct representation encoding. Specifically, we recommend using Lightweight Lightweight Word Embedding for text analysis within table cells and the Dense Tensor Train for compact table representation encoding. As a result, tables can be accurately identified and their contents can be efficiently extracted and made searchable. Experimental data collected from various open-source archives demonstrates that combination of these methods surpasses existing table retrieval techniques in terms of both structure and content understanding. Classification models trained on recognized table data also outperform other methods in search tasks. Our findings illustrate the practical applications of graph neural networks and cutting-edge representation encoding in real-world search engineering applications. The research highlights the value of graph neural networks in searching and analyzing complex, historically significant documents such as archives and manuscripts. We investigate complex cognitive structures in multi-phase mixed signal games where players lack complete information. Our focus is on two-step and three-step games. To tackle these incomplete games, we develop a new approach by incorporating stochastic Markov chains and dynamic reinforcement learning into cognitive modeling. Our results demonstrate that both two-step and three-step mixed signal games can be represented by stochastic Markov chains. Additionally, we prove that dynamic reinforcement learning fails to optimize cognitive structures in these games, leading to suboptimal results. Therefore, we utilize our own method of reinforcement learning with backtracking to identify the optimal cognitive structure for each game. Our approach is effective in generating stochastic equilibria and significantly outperforms dynamic reinforcement learning in three-step games. Furthermore, we found that two-step games exhibit distinct characteristics compared to three-step games in terms of efficiency and behavior. Our findings contribute to the understanding of cognitive structures in multi-phase games of incomplete information. They are also practical, as well as relevant for real-world applications. For instance, such games have been used to model complex sales strategies in research by Rand and Shterna (2020). It's worth noting that one possible limitation of our method is that it may not be suitable for games with an extremely large number of phases. In response, we propose an alternative method of representation for multi-phase games, which we discuss in more detail in the accompanying paper. In addition to the theoretical analysis, our approach demonstrates its practical capabilities through numerical examples and comparisons, which can be accessed via the associated GitHub repository. The relevant code has been included to facilitate reproduction of our results and demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. We investigate how quantum machines can enhance machine learning techniques, particularly in the areas of classification and clustering, using two approaches: a single qubit training method and a multi-qubit testing method. The training method involves creating classifiers directly within the quantum circuit or by transforming data into binary kernels for support vector machines. On the other hand, testing is done using a specially designed verification circuit that processes input samples to yield output results. Both the training and testing processes take place simultaneously in an uncontrolled environment. Furthermore, a classical correction technique is applied to correct errors that occur during the processing cycle. By combining the principles of unsupervised learning and the principles of Bayes' theorem, a clustering algorithm is developed within a quantum computer and tested using the dataset for iris flowers with successful classification results. Additionally, a method for determining quantum error probability is developed from the measurement outcomes. With the application of this correction technique, an impressive 71% accuracy is achieved from the processed sample dataset. Furthermore, the processing time for iris data on a quantum computer under real-world conditions is found to be several orders of magnitude greater than that of a classical computer. Consequently, further optimization techniques are being developed to refine the processing time and accuracy. Finally, a classical verification method for determining multi-qubit states is outlined along with an analysis of measurement accuracy in a multi-qubit system. An upcoming experiment will combine unsupervised and supervised learning to classify data and determine quantum error probabilities on a 54-qubit processor, respectively. Consequently, future research will likely lead to achieving parity with classical computers in processing time and surpassing classical performance in classification accuracy. Consequently, the development of quantum machines may indeed outperform their classical counterparts in data analysis and understanding. Unfortunately, existing large-scale datasets collected through crowdsourcing and automatic methods are contaminated with pitch variations that make it challenging for models to mimic human-like pitches naturally.
To combat this issue and further refine the pitch control of models, we've developed a technique that preserves the tone characteristics during pitch adjustment and enhances the manageability of pitches in existing TTS frameworks.
We've also introduced a simple yet effective method to augment fastPitch's pitch space, making pitch variations more distinguishable.
Through experiments on the Libri-TTS dataset, we've demonstrated the effectiveness of our approaches in enhancing pitch variability and control. 
We've also created a new augmented dataset called augmented-LJSS3 with twice the speaking characters to compare the performance of TTS models on natural and artificially expanded datasets.

Hopper efficiently encodes the evolution of target values over space and time by relating local and global factors through hop connections. Extensive experiments validate Hopper's performance on diverse tasks, surpassing previous state-of-the-art models for K-means, Action Resumability, and Video Classification metrics. Our analysis demonstrates Hopper's ability to learn complex temporal and spatial patterns through its hop connections and latent state representation. Hopper's effectiveness is further illustrated in our novel application: forecasting future COVID-19 cases based on geographical maps of confirmed cases. Hopper's source code is publicly available at https://github.com/asharakeh/Hopper. Our related work is documented at https://www.acm.org/binaries/588774. Hierarchical linear forecasting models, specifically Bayesian hierarchical linear models (BHLFs), offer a robust solution by filling the gaps left by Gaussian Process (GP) models, which often come with significant computational costs. The BHLF approach consists of two main parts: a hierarchical structure that forms a GP and a regression model combined with the GP, allowing for the incorporation of spatial and temporal characteristics in the prediction process. Our goal is to provide an in-depth, easy-to-understand explanation of the BHLF method by first introducing the underlying techniques and concepts, including hierarchical structures, GP definitions, and gradient boosting. We'll also offer a comprehensive overview of the BHLF algorithm and provide example illustrations using Python's OpenCV and scikit-learn libraries, in addition to examining the method's efficiency through model selection and hyperparameter optimization experiments. Our findings demonstrate that the BHLF has the potential to outperform traditional machine learning and Bayesian models such as GPs and forest random survival models in terms of accuracy and execution speed. The proposed method is expected to find applications in computational biology and medicine where historical data on time series is available for analytical purposes. The source code of our model has been made accessible at https://github.com/mayez/bhlf-ILFM-Code on GitHub. The illustrations' visual content and the numerical data used in our study are hosted on an image sharing platform at https://image.net/bhlf-ilfm-signature-models. The data generated during our execution of the experiments is also available for review at https://github.com/mayez/bhlf-ILFM-Data-Exchange. The paper is also compatible with screen readers for users with disabilities. Our model's performance has been verified on multiple platforms, including Windows, Linux, and macOS. The suggested model's training algorithm relies on the PyMC3, XGBoost, and sklearn libraries, which are compatible with the mentioned operating systems. The findings of our model selection and hyperparameter optimization experiments indicate that execution times of approximately one to two minutes are typical for the BHLF method on workstations with reasonable specifications. The paper also includes a copy of the related execution time statistics in its Appendices. Our model's performance has also been tested on the Google Cloud platform. The BHLF model generates results distinct from those of GP and forest models, with accuracy and execution times that may vary depending on factors such as the quantity and quality of training data, as well as the computational capabilities of the machine on which it is running. The Mafia game, also known as Versus or Mafia Versus, is a role-playing social game that incorporates both cooperative and competitive elements. Players are divided into two teams; one team consists of townspeople while the other is comprised of townspeople and mobsters. Each team has distinct objectives; the townspeople aim to eliminate the mobsters through deduction, and the mobsters strive to outnumber the townspeople in a killing spree. 

A previous analytical study solved a simplified version of the game to provide an optimal strategy but was limited due to its computational inaccessibility. To better understand this game, we developed a simulation model that mimics the game's rules and conditions. Using this model, we tested different scenarios, calculated exact probabilities, and validated previous analytical findings, ultimately confirming that the town's survival probability can exceed 50% with a sufficient number of townspeople. Additionally, we obtained an expression for the killing probability's asymptotic behavior but were unable to determine its exact value due to the complexity of the calculations involved. Notably, we discovered that certain patterns of mobster death can affect the town's survival prospects and established a system to measure this impact, known as efficiency. An unexpected outcome of our study was the discovery that certain patterns of mobster activity could increase the town's survival chances, which contradicts previous assumptions that the mobsters' behavior had no bearing on the game's outcome. Lastly, we analyzed the average number of townspeople killed in each iteration of the game, found it to be finite, and presented an expression describing this average in terms of the game's current state. We concluded our study by addressing variants of the game, for which we developed a model to simulate and calculate exact probabilities, ultimately finding that the average killing spree duration is inversely related to the number of remaining townspeople. All calculations were performed using the obtained numerical model, and we verified its accuracy by comparing it to a probability-amplification algorithm, demonstrating that the model-generated results and algorithmic results converged to one another as the town and mobster populations became increasingly balanced. An additional variant of the game involved integrating liars into the game, for which we developed a simulation at the base of our model to determine liars' influence on survival probability and discovered liars to have a negative effect on this probability, contrasting with our previous finding that the mobsters' behavior could aid the town's survival prospects. The electronic properties of carbon nanotubes make them an ideal material for building the next generation of high-performance interconnects and data storage devices. However, achieving low electrical conductivity in nanotube-based films has proven to be a significant challenge. Despite the numerous benefits offered by carbon nanotubes, a major obstacle to reaching their full potential has been the high electrical resistance exhibited by films composed of these nanotubes. By harnessing the phenomenon of wave function folding, which is supported by the quantized vibrations of the films' phonons, we have demonstrated the feasibility of transferring electrical current between individual nanotubes within a film. Utilizing both experimental measurements and theoretical modeling, we have established that the conductivity of these nanotube-based films can be explained by the incorporation of phonon-assisted processes in a modified Chaplygin model. The incorporation of these phonon-assisted processes significantly enhances the films' electrical conductivity, thereby revealing the critical role played by the collective vibrations of the films' lattice at low temperatures. Our findings from this research not only offer a previously unexplained explanation for the high conductivity of these nanotube-based films but also highlight the importance of incorporating the effects of collective modes into the electronic transport phenomena occurring within these materials. Furthermore, our method of supporting electrical current transfer between individual nanotubes has also offered a new framework for the design and development of nanoscale interconnects. Importantly, these advances in nanotube-based technology could potentially be applied to the development of novel transistors and data storage devices, thereby bringing us closer to realizing the full performance potential of these materials. Our research has further motivated the exploration of the role played by collective modes in the electronic conductivity exhibited by atomic-scale materials, which could open up new avenues of investigation in the rapidly evolving field of quantum nanotechnology.
