In numerous scientific fields, clustering is a crucial technique used to identify similar data points, determine natural groups, and dimensionally reduce complex datasets. Fuzzy k-means, however, has limitations that affect its accuracy, particularly when dealing with tightly packed clusters, computationally intensive calculations, and unevenly distributed data points across features. Therefore, a pre-processing approach was developed to tackle these issues by stepwise eliminating irrelevant features, varying feature weights to give equal importance to all clusters, and using entropy to ensure proper initial placement of fuzzy points within each cluster. These fuzzy points, representing the center of each cluster, were determined by applying a weighted averaging algorithm, where the weights were computed based on the distance between data points and their respective fuzzy centers. Additionally, to achieve more accurate results, the fuzzy positions of all data points were refined by iteratively updating their assignments and affiliations to one of the predefined clusters. Experiments were conducted using both synthetic and real-world datasets, resulting in substantial improvements in clustering accuracy, comparable to state-of-the-art algorithms like Hierarchical and Spectral clustering. Notably, the proposed approach can effectively handle high-dimensional datasets, such as those found in drug discovery and medical informatics. Therefore, the proposed entropy-based variable feature weighted fuzzy k-means method provides a valuable Dr. clustering strategy for high-dimensional information systems. The proposed algorithm has been successfully implemented in a shared repository, available at https://github.com/ContF/EntropyFkMeans. The technical documentation, including step-by-step descriptions and example usage, can be found at https://contf.github.io/EntropyFkMeans. The user can easily install the Dr. Clustering Node module by running the command 'npm install --save dr.clustering.str' within the project's node_modules folder, followed by importing the Dr. Clustering module in their JavaScript code using the command 'import clustering from "dr.clustering.str"'. Subsequently, the user can utilize the provided Dr. Clustering library to perform clustering operations on their dataset. Furthermore, the Dr. Clustering module offers additional features, such as automatic feature weighting and fuzzy center initialization using entropy, to name a few. Consequently, the proposed approach sets a new standard in fuzzy k-means clustering, addressing the aforementioned issues and demonstrating significant improvements in accuracy and efficiency, resulting in state-of-the-art clustering results at a relatively low computational cost. We develop a general approach to identifying the topological properties of the stable equilibrium sets, known as attractors, for a broad class of discrete-time systems that are based on permutation actions. This methodology has practical applications in understanding the theoretical underpinnings of circuit analysis, which relies heavily on combinatorial principles. Furthermore, we provide a clear definition for the Jacobian variety associated with a proper attractor and outline the rules for its formation. We also explore the concept of a dual attractor and demonstrate that its relationship with the original attractor mimics the mathematical structure of a covering map. This results in the attractor being classified as a non-Riemann surface, with properties of non-hyperelliptic nature. Moreover, we identify the attractor's modular properties and establish a clear connection to a specific type of curve double covering model known as a Jacobian curve. This curve has a unique property allowing it to support a high degree of embedding capabilities into other types of curves, specifically those of genus 2. To illustrate the effectiveness of our theoretical framework, we conduct a detailed examination of a specific system defined by its triangular complex structure, which trially embeds within the genus-2 curve of study in [12]. This specific system corresponds to the firing of tokens at specific time frames across three distinct stages, with rules governing their interstage transition established. The associated curve of study in [12] corresponds to the system's equilibrium state, with properties defined by specific combinatorial principles, even though this paper demonstrates that these principles fail to comprehensively define the system's topological properties. The paper also highlights the systematic discrepancy between the theoretical study of its triangular structure and the practical applications of its associated curve of study in [12], where the former significantly surpasses the latter. To rectify this discrepancy, we propose a novel systematic approach to identifying the topological properties of a broad class of token-firing games with graph structure. This novel approach has far-reaching practical applications in circuit analysis, which we also discuss within this manuscript. Finally, the paper conducts a detailed comparison with results recently established in [10], leading to a clear demonstration of how our theoretical framework can seamlessly integrate with the existing token-firing games of study. Our framework has also inspired a new class of curve double covering models with interesting and varied structural properties, which we also discuss within this manuscript. Moreover, the paper has led to a clear definition of a new class of proper attractor varieties, which have the inherent property of being non-hyperelliptic

insensitive to data augmentations, their performance actually fluctuates in
response to certain types of augmentations. We propose a new concept called
Performance-Reproducibility (PR) agreement, which is based on a model's
reproducibility in case-sensitive training and testing and its consistency in
performance across different training methods.

Under certain conditions, the ergodic index of a Lagrangian submanifold in a symplectic manifold can be evaluated using a simplified formula, building upon Thomas-Yau's conjecture. This formula scales linearly with the Euclidean volume of the Lagrangian submanifold and incorporates an error term that depends on the next differential invariant in syzygy, as shown using a modified version of Hamilton's perturbation method combined with Guillemin's formula. Consequently, the error term's growth rate defines a new metric on the space of Lagrangian submanifolds, which we refer to as quantitative Thomas-Yau distinctiveness. Furthermore, applying this distinctiveness to simple abstract tori reveals distinctiveness patterns that separate conjugate Lagrangian submanifolds based on two distinct criteria, involving Guillemin's formula and the bar complexity of toric symplectic manifolds, respectively. Notably, the ergodic index exhibits growth and divergence characteristics reminiscent of the Hamiltonian action functional in Floer theory, providing fresh insights into its nature. These findings address an open question posed by Guan and Zhang and complement recent work by Anatharaman and Mathematischen Annalen. Moreover, they offer novel connections among ergodic flows, Lagrangian submanifolds, and Hamiltonian dynamics, as well as potential applications in physics and the development of a ergodic reformulation of Thomas-Yau's conjecture and Floer theory, which are expected to expand our understanding of Lagrangian submanifolds and their role in symplectic geometry and mathematics. (This is a companion paper to arXiv:2102.12717.)

The classical formula used in time domain for unamplified optical fiber links has been widely applied in practice, yet its validity for arbitrarily wide bandwidths has not been thoroughly investigated. Consequently, a discrete-time version of this formula is introduced, allowing for its analysis and comparison with its continuous-time counterpart, especially in its applicability to widely bandwidths. By comparing these formulas, the exact conditions under which they produce accurate results are identified, revealing that certain constraints must be implemented to ensure reasonable approximations are met. Furthermore, a method of calculating the delay that appears in the formula is presented, using a quantity that accounts for the position of the signal of interest within a symbol period. Utilizing these insights, a method of designing optical fibers with transfer functions that minimize distortion is proposed, taking into consideration the trade-off between bandwidth and delay, in an effort to optimize the interpolation and sampling process for a specific bandwidth. Additionally, the effects of self-phase modulation are investigated in a discrete-time framework, in which the FDSD formula is shown to accurately describe the distortion produced by self-phase modulation over broad bandwidths. In particular, the FDSD formula is seen to closely match a discrete-time approximation of the continuous-time phase-mapping formula, with both accurately modeling the output of a photodetector across various frequencies. Analysis reveals that the FDSD formula possesses certain desirable properties, including discrete-time convexity and a bounded error, compared to its continuous-time counterpart, in which the difference between them is depicted as a function of frequency and considers the position of the signal within a symbol period. The FDSD formula is shown to provide accurate modeling of the process over broad bandwidths, in which the total combined effect of amplifier noise and bandwidth is investigated, in order to identify the maximum bandwidth at which accurate modeling can be achieved. The FDSD formula is seen to provide effective modeling of the process up to 5.0 times the symbol rate, in which the error is found to be near the noise floor up to a distance of 0.2 times the channel bandwidth. Furthermore, the FDSD formula is found to outperform the classical formula, in which the error is found to be up to one order of magnitude higher at equivalent bandwidths, in order to provide compensation for dispersion and thereby improve performance. In conclusion, the FDSD formula is found to provide a rigorous mathematical description of the process in the context of wideband transmission, in which the error is found to be near the noise floor up to a distance of 0.2 times the channel bandwidth.

The dial-a-ride problem (DARP) demands efficient coordination of door-to-door passenger transportation in low-density areas with sparse demand. Enhancing the service quality in DARP requires significant reduction in both passenger travel time and the trip duration, leading to the definition of the metropolitan dial-a-ride problem (MDARP). This study formulates MDARP as an integer program but instead of solving it directly, they devise a practical branch-and-bound algorithm to yield high-quality solutions quickly. The algorithm's capability to generate tight lower bounds results in minimal solution search, thereby reducing computation time in branches. The efficiency of this approach is demonstrated through its application on six DARP instances and a large MDARP instance showcasing its applicability and solution quality. The results indicate that this algorithm can provide high-quality solutions within a reasonable computation time, thereby making it a viable option for passenger transportation optimization in metropolitan areas with dense demand. The proposed algorithm represents a new class of efficient decision-making tools for DARP. The study's solutions can be downloaded from https://github.com/MaMe-Skript/macmahon_tilp/tree/master/2022_DCARPD.

We design three datasets for insight recognition: a simple set for "what", a geographic dataset for "where", and a seasonal dataset for "when". We also introduce two categorical product datasets for product categorization. As computers increasingly interact with humans through language, the ability to accurately determine the meaning of individual words or sentences within a given context remains crucial. Unfortunately, existing machine translation techniques frequently fall short, often producing humorous errors in translation, as exemplified by Google's attempts to translate "The exact recipe is unknown." In contrast, human translation yields "the recipe is unclear." This study presents a model of human language comprehension, drawing from psycholinguistics research, where a sequence-to-sequence model, accompanied by a recurrent neural network, incorporates contextual information through repeated iterations of calculation and interactive dialogue. Simulation results reveal that, when allowed to periodically "speak," the model exhibits improved performance in understanding word meanings within sentences, while the produced words influence the interpretation of subsequent sentences. Our model's ability to emulate distinct word usage in scenarios with updated knowledge and artificial conversation is demonstrated. Furthermore, our model outperforms existing baseline models in understanding sentence contexts. These capabilities suggest that, through interaction, the model develops a dynamic, coherent understanding of language. This study offers a new perspective on how to modulate the internal workings of neural networks to facilitate human-like comprehension." With the rapid advancement of AI healthcare tools, more complex models are being developed to outperform existing solutions, frequently at the expense of explanation and reliability. In order to create greater trust in these models, researchers are identifying ways to measure the reliability of AI-powered diagnostic tools for medical image analysis. Past studies have primarily focused on evaluating model performance on seen data, but we propose a novel approach to estimate performance on unseen data, particularly when the distribution has shifted. We propose an adaptive forecasting technique called DistShiftCF that leverages learned probabilistic models to simulate a range of label assignments for a single image. By evaluating this method on two medical image datasets against established benchmark metrics for single-dataset and cross-distribution evaluation, we demonstrate its superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we utilize our approach to evaluate the performance of top-ranked submissions to the Medical Image Learning for Glaucoma Analysis (MILA) 2020 challenge not only on the training dataset but also on an unseen test dataset, showing the effectiveness of our method in detecting distribution drift. We have introduced a novel method, combining force field adjustments with advanced DNA structure constraints, yielding superior results for double-stranded DNA segments in relation to reference data generated through neutron scattering. This advanced biasing technique is effective in achieving convergence for critical DNA structures within reasonable simulation timeframes. We have also demonstrated its capability to simulate DNA unbinding processes in the absence of an explicit solvent environment. Future paths of numerous moving entities such as people, vehicles and clogs in traffic are hard to predict accurately in crowded environments. To tackle this challenge, we develop a novel probabilistic model called SocNet, which uses learning-based techniques to forecast the future movements of multiple entities in crowded places. This model uses a sequence of past interactions among entities to understand and predict social behaviors. By incorporating a socially-aware attention mechanism, SocNet captures and conveys the ongoing social interactions between entities and adapts to changing environmental conditions over time. This mechanism, by utilizing self-supervised technique, self-adjusts the importance of past interactions dynamically. Experimental results show that our approach outperforms other methods significantly in forecasting the movement of entities in crowded environments, as demonstrated by superior performance on public and self-created datasets. Moreover, qualitative analysis confirms that the socially-aware attention mechanism plays a crucial role in the success of our approach. Measuring Performance (MP), a widely used performance measurement in Finance, is highly dependent on the method and structure of the performance evaluation set used in practice. To address this challenge, the field of Operations Research and Optimization has developed sophisticated tools like Slice Regression, a technique for regressing Performance on selected variables while maintaining the feasible set's convexity and avoiding infeasibility. To facilitate the use of these tools, we present pyStoNED, a Python library based on SciPy that implements the StoNED method for Convex Regressions and related convex optimization techniques to assess and analyze sets in MP. Through a practical example involving fund data, we demonstrate the library's capabilities, offering users a novel approach to perform performance evaluations within Python. Additionally, the library's integration with popular Financial libraries makes it an essential tool for empirical research in the field. You can install the library from the PyPI repository at https://pypi.org/ext/pyStoNED/. Furthermore, the source code is available at https://github.com/sta-sta/sta-stoNED/. Lastly, the original paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.01333. Feel free to reach out to us via email at sta-sta@uninomadia.it for any further information. 

The library provides the following key features:
- Implementation of the StoNED method for Convex Regressions and related convex optimization techniques to assess and analyze sets in MP.
- Ability to perform Slice Regression, Convex Regression with Gaussian errors, and Convex Optimization with both black-box and black-box-free formulations for Performance evaluation sets.
- Support for the following types of feasible sets: Affine, Euclidean, L1-Ball, Linf-Ball, Second-Order Conic, and Positive Semidefinite.
- Integration of the most commonly used libraries in Empirical Finance, including scikit-learn, pandas, statsmodels, yfinance, and wind (for Chinese A-share data access).
- Demonstration of the library's capabilities through a practical example involving fund data.

- docstrings: to facilitate the usage of the library through its docstrings.

- release: to release the library's source code to the community for a better understanding of its implementation

This study presents UFA, a pioneering approach for developing safe and reliable PTMs with minimal requirements for labeled data. UFA leverages natural language-based information-extraction mechanisms to define safe coding practices and assesses PTMs' compliance using a degree-of-safety metric. This metric evaluates the safety risk associated with a given piece of code and does not require any human supervision. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of UFA in promoting the use of safely-generated code, even in scenarios with limited human involvement. UFA's performance was evaluated in a competition against alternative methods based on supervised learning and reinforcement learning, yielding superior results across various experiments. Unlike these methods, UFA successfully ensured models could correctly generate correct code based on few examples. Moreover, UFA's adaptability was further demonstrated through its application in a knowledge-based coding challenge. This study represents an important step towards developing safe and understandable generation capabilities for future coding powerhouses. Nonetheless, their responsiveness to individual inputs within a sequence can be somewhat limited, leading researchers to assign distinct names to sequences and use reference points to contextualize each instance.  A key innovation in this study is the NFT-K model, which uses a reference context system to process sequences as stand-alone entities.  In processing a task, a sample is drawn from a stored database, and then a reference context is selected from another pre-trained database and fused with the sample to create an executable model.  Notably, the choice of reference context is based on a measure of similarity between the sample and a pair of key values drawn from the database, making this a Bayesian-type model that estimates a target distribution of desirable key values. The task of designing robotic controllers that are able to withstand uncertainties during execution has been found to be extremely challenging. In order to tackle this issue, our research focuses on developing robotic controllers that not only optimize their performance but also satisfy a broad range of constraints and requirements during task execution. In this context, we view the controller as a uncertain parameter within a probabilistic framework. Our approach generates numerous policies through the combination of reinforcement learning and model analysis, with each policy represented as a probability distribution across the controller's uncertain parameters. The resulting distribution enables the reduction of performance variability when adapting to changing conditions, while maintaining task-specific characteristics. We implement this concept on a robotic arm with two degrees of freedom and demonstrate its effectiveness through the achievement of consistent results across multiple experimental scenarios, with the additional benefit of being resistant to adversarial perturbations. Our findings demonstrate the immense capability of model analysis in policy-based reinforcement learning and its potential to be widely applicable in various robotic applications, with a particular emphasis on tasks that require low variability in performance. Our approach's source code has been made publicly accessible at https://github.com/maydell/unc-stmp-e. Additionally, a video illustrating the findings is available on https://youtu.bevideo3_bxkxw3m. Our research further highlights the interest of our findings from a formal verification perspective, with potential applications in designing robotic controllers that can withstand uncertainties during execution, with extensions to the design of controllers using planning-based methods to generate the policies and with the additional benefit of demonstrating the importance of model analysis in improving the robustness of learned policies through the use of adversarial perturbations in experimental settings. A Larmor clock is conceived and developed to measure the infamous tunneling time. The clock works by monitoring a system in a $A$ state tunneling to a system in a $B$ state under specific conditions. The tunneling process is linked to a Larmor frequency shift in the system, which is detected through its sideband activity during a monitored oscillation. The duration of this tunneling event is found to be the average time it takes for the system to go through three distinct phases - an initial rise, a maximal point, and the beginning of its down cycle - based on the applicable Hamiltonian. The developed Larmor clock is tested on a particle model inspired by the Böhmian view of quantum mechanics. When applied to the originally proposed by Bohm original tunneling model, the sideband activity exhibits a more complex pattern, however, a duration can still be defined. Additionally, with sufficient monitoring resolution, the Larmor clock can also measure the pre-tunneling time, which corresponds to the system reaching its maximal point and beginning its down cycle in its oscillation. To further clarify its results, the Larmor clock is used to measure tunneling times on an anisotropic "Mexican Hat" potential. Ultimately, these findings support the idea that macroscopic particles may exhibit finite, albeit long, tunneling times even in quantum mechanics. It's also noted that other particle models, such as those inspired by weak measurements, may reveal different results, leading to new research avenues on the topic. A relevant experimental project is proposed in the conclusion. The Larmor clock concept challenges the established view that quantum tunneling occurs instantaneously and may have potential applications in the development of new, fine-tuned quantum algorithms. Its development also highlights the potential use of monitoring and sideband activity as an experimental tool to study quantum tunneling. Two distinct approaches, represented by the Groenewold criterion and a more recent theory of deformed classical operators as proposed by Tsallis et al., exist to define nonlinear quantum operators corresponding to classical phase space coordinates. Although both methods can facilitate the completion of a quasi-extension of the classical Hamiltonian system, the first approach adheres to a strict extension and can derive the quantum analogue of classical thermodynamic properties in a straightforward manner. In contrast, the second approach results in a complex, non-Hermitian quantum system, the validity of its results often being obtained at the cost of its own inconsistency. This research uses the first approach to investigate how the quantum behavior of a Bose-Einstein condensate influences its thermodynamic properties. It has been observed that, unlike classical systems, the non-Hermitian quantum model fails to exhibit negative temperature or the finite-size singularity characteristic of the Bose-Einstein condensate. Instead, the non-Hermitian quantum model presents a continuous evolution of its thermodynamic properties from the classical Boltzmann limit to a novel temperature regime characterized by a continuous decrease in entropy. This result is supplemented by an approximate analytical solution and corresponding numerical simulations. These findings support the idea that the non-Hermitian quantum model fails to provide the correct thermodynamic properties due to its inherent inconsistencies. Consequently, the non-Hermitian quantum model should not be employed to investigate the influence of quantum behavior on the thermodynamic properties of a Bose-Einstein condensate. Instead, the use of accurate quantum operators allowing for a strict extension of the classical Hamiltonian system is recommended. This research also outlines a theoretical framework for the interpretation of the quantum behavior of a Bose-Einstein condensate and suggests avenues for future investigations. These involve experimenting with alternative nonlinear quantum operators, investigating other condensed matter systems, and examining the influence of various deformation parameters on the thermodynamic properties of a Bose-Einstein condensate. By pursuing these avenues, the understanding of the quantum behavior of complex systems and the thermodynamics of condensed matter can be advanced. Preliminary results indicate the successful application of this research in the achievement of its objectives. To tackle this issue, we present a neural framework that achieves a 95.8% reduction in forgetting, using minimal assumptions and without influencing the online classifier. This framework operates on a low computational budget, suitable for real-time applications. Additionally, we introduce the MOON benchmark, a collective learning dataset with five interconnected tasks and comprehensive evaluations, demonstrating the efficacy of our method across various scenarios and leading baseline methods. The framework is available on GitHub at https://github.com/fhatembenai/neoclim. For technical reasons, the collaborative training of the encoder is disabled by default, as detailed in the repository's README file. Our research is the first to use neural architecture search in the online collective learning setting, aiming to mitigate catastrophic forgetting and open the doors to further research in this field. The encodings produced by our method exhibit not only superior stability but also improved coherence and relevance, facilitating task adaptation. As such, our method offers a versatile tool for applications like image classification, where subcategories often have an intrinsic relationship. Our theoretical analysis of coherence and relevance (Appendix C) sheds light on the design of the architecture using the Koopman operator, offering a novel perspective on the encoding dynamics. Our method can be adapted for other online collective learning scenarios, such as domain adaptation, semi-supervised learning, and generative modeling. Lastly, the stability of the encodings plays a pivotal role in mitigating the intrinsic bias present in the MOON dataset, as detailed in Appendix D. Human intestinal parasitic infections cause significant global issues, contributing to inadequate nutrient absorption, direct health issues, and increased risk of other diseases. A significant challenge in addressing these issues is accurately diagnosing parasitic infections, a process complicated by the vast number of intestinal parasitic species, their rapid reproduction, and the risk of misdiagnosis from faulty diagnostic tools. Advances in digital microscopy and machine learning suggest a potential solution, with recent research demonstrating the effectiveness of artificial intelligence in categorizing intestinal parasites. This study focuses on utilizing Deep Belief Networks (DBNs) to classify various intestinal parasites found in the Philippines. Our contribution involves providing DBN training data, with detailed information on the morphology of 19 intestinal parasite species. From this dataset, we conducted a thorough analysis of the impact of feature quantity on model accuracy. Our analysis revealed that introducing a selective feature elimination method can improve classification results, with the overall top-classification accuracy amounting to 93.52%. Our study aims to contribute valuable knowledge to the medical community by detailing the morphology of intestinal parasites and introducing a relatively quick and effective classification approach. With access to a large dataset and computational resources, DBNs have the potential to become a valuable tool in addressing the worldwide intestinal parasitic crisis. Given the abundance of medical images, this dataset can further advance the development of effective diagnostic tools. Ultimately, the goal is for DBNs to enhance the accuracy of parasitic classification, contributing to improved diagnosis and treatment of intestinal parasitic infections. In our investigation, we examine the constituents of nuclear spatial contracts at extremely close distances.  Utilizing advanced numerical tools, we discover that experiments involving high-energy electron scattering exhibit significant short-range interactions characterized by a spatial range of approximately 1 fm, with an energy dependence that increases as the square of energy.  Notably, at the highest energy levels studied (approximately 1 GeV), nearly all of this short-range correlation involves pairing of nucleons; however, a notable proportion of this short-range correlation involves non-adaptive components, with implications for our understanding of nuclear matter at extremely high densities and in topologically entangled structures.  Our findings have direct applications for efforts seeking to employ in-depth electron scattering to dissect and create exotic nuclear states.  A novel scheme is proposed for decomposing short-range interactions into distinct, meaningful components, with potential for wide-ranging use beyond the specific case of electron scattering, in scenarios where spatial allocation is significant.  Importantly, our study reveals that while some forms of short-range structure are rooted in conventional understanding of nucleon-nucleon interactions, others require novel, non-conventional explanations.  Specifically, our study demonstrates that conventional understanding of nucleon-nucleon interactions can only account for a small proportion of short-range structure at high energy;  in contrast, non-conventional explanations, specifically topological spin, yield a substantially larger contribution that closely matches experimental data.  Furthermore, our study reveals the following allocation:  40% of short-range structure at high energy is due to nuclear density, 30% is due to nuclear coherence, 15% is due to nuclear collectivity, 40% is due to nuclear pairing, of which 20% lies outside the conventional $S_{\frac{3}{2}}$ channel.  A general framework is established for connecting the phase-space allocations of various nucleon-nucleon reactions and spectroscopic observations.  Our study provides a series of challenges to experimental groups, making the case for further investigations into this previously under-explored area of nuclear physics.  Importantly, our study holds far-reaching implications for how we understand and manipulate exotic nuclear states using advanced electron scattering techniques.  A comprehensive list of open questions associated with this work is provided in Ref. [27].  Importantly, our study reveals a fundamental connection between short-range structure and advanced topological spin structures, providing key insights into the intricate relationships between nucleon-nucleon interactions and nuclear matter at extremely high densities and in topologically entangled structures. In deep learning, especially in speech synthesis and other complex-valued applications, choosing the co-domain of complex numbers is a crucial decision. Two potential domain choices for complex numbers are cis-notation system, where the co-domain is the upper plane, and car-notation system, where the co-domain is the lower plane. Each choice presents a distinct approach, denoted as UP and LP in this study. By incorporating the use of up and lp in the deep representation learning of complex-valued maps, the concept of co-domain equivalence is established. This co-domain equivalence is shown to be a unique extension of the real-valued ReLU activation function. As such, it acts as a key building block for the construction of deep learning maps, whether they are real-valued or complex-valued. Furthermore, the up and lp activation functions are found to fulfill the role of complex-valued proximal activation functions. As a result, they are hybrid versions of the real-valued quantile activation function. If we consider them as activation functions, we can then consider them as components of a class of learning maps known as wide reLU-neural nets, thereby allowing for the application of the universal approximation theorem. However, when it comes to finite-layer deep learning maps, the behavior and differences of the up and lp activation functions need to be examined in more detail. This is because the upper and lower planes have distinct behaviors in the context of finite-layers, particularly with regard to the behavior at the origin and behavior at infinity. Despite these differences, the upper and lower planes present similar behavior when it comes to the finite-layer representation of the up and lp activation functions over a specific set of parameters. This behavior can be visually demonstrated through a two-dimensional representation of the up and lp activation functions. Ultimately, the concept of co-domain equivalence is found to serve as a useful framework for understanding and clarifying the behavior and presentation of the up and lp activation functions, particularly in the context of deep learning maps. This concept further supports the development of a wide reLU-neural network through the universal approximation theorem, which is found to be effective for complex-valued deep learning applications. One such application of this concept is revealed in the design of the first successful, finite-layer-based speech synthesis system that utilizes complex-valued functionality, thereby providing a crucial contribution to the field of deep learning. This system is found to surpass the performance of existing speech synthesis algorithms, particularly those that utilize real-valued functionality, thereby presenting a significant advancement in the field of complex-valued deep learning

A major challenge in understanding the formation of our galaxy lies in determining how the masses of its constituent stars are distributed. Through a groundbreaking study using detailed mass spectra of hundreds of thousands of stars from the Gaia-ESO survey with varying levels of metal content, we examined the density of these distributions. The data supported two distinct models: an exponential curve for less metal-rich stars and a bell-shaped normal distribution for more metal-rich stars. The findings suggested a lower mass threshold below which star formation ceases and a rate at which existing low-mass stars die, resulting in decreased low-mass star populations over time. The data supported the theory of galaxy growth through the merger of smaller units, particularly for less metal-rich stars. Additionally, we derived key parameters such as the normal distribution's peak mass, the mass threshold for less metal-rich stars, and the death rate constant for low-mass stars. The data further indicated that star deaths contribute around 60% of low-mass stars to the galaxy's mass distribution, while birth rates have a negligible effect on these populations. The findings highlighted that low-mass stars predominantly comprise old, low-metallicity population stars. The data also showed that high-metallicity stars, on the other hand, exhibit more diverse mass distributions with a broader range of properties that largely consist of younger, metal-rich stars. The data further indicated that stars in this group exhibit a strong connection to the galaxy's disk, while older, low-metallicity stars, on the other hand, exhibit a more diffuse spatial distribution. The data supported the theory of the galaxy's evolution through the merger of smaller units, particularly for less metal-rich stars. The findings significantly reduced several significant uncertainties in studies on the galaxy's assembly. The data further indicated that less metal-rich stars exhibit a significantly lower supernova rate in their mass range in comparison to more metal-rich stars. The data support either a galaxy's chemical evolution model characterized by a lack of supernovae from low-mass stars or a binary model where low-mass stars predominantly end their lives through gravitational collapse rather than as supernovae. The data further indicated that less metal-rich stars primarily contribute to the galaxy's overall iron content through the incorporation of heavy elements from supernovae with medium to high masses. The integration of quantum computing and machine learning has given rise to Quantum Artificial Intelligence (QAI). We explore QAI within systems that utilize SQUID as part of ongoing research into applications of thin film superconductors. Due to SQUID's superior single-flux tunneling property, it is particularly suitable for QAI. We illustrate this with a sample QAI implementation using a pair of SQUID magnets in a coherent spin context. We also discuss the potential advancements in QAI technology resulting from advancements in SQUID systems. Furthermore, we present theoretical predictions and supportively cite existing experimental studies. We analyze these QAI concepts in terms of their similarity to established machine learning methods, including how they can be used to solve practical problems. We consider both basic principles and future potential implementations. We assess various QAI strategies and evaluate their feasibility with SQUID systems. We recognize that QAI's current development falls short of achieving "green technology" status due to its current reliance on complex, expensive systems. We conclude by discussing the considerable promise QAI holds for future advancements, particularly when paired with innovative SQUID-based ideas such as inductive learning, ferromagnetic support, and spin readout techniques. We anticipate that future QAI implementations could integrate learning and reasoning processes directly into ferromagnetic materials, resulting in enhanced performance, efficiency, and energy savings, potentially exceeding current state-of-the-art QAI achievements. In this research, we investigate warped products of semi-inclined submanifolds within nearly contact manifolds, focusing on their geometric and topological characteristics, with particular emphasis on a critical condition that maintains their warped structure. Additionally, we create a critical examination of various types of warped products, such as minimal, geodesic, and normal curves, as well as their isometric and homothetic counterparts. Furthermore, we delve into the relationship between principal curves and a fundamental topic in differential geometry, namely, the classification of distances. We also establish connections between our findings and existing concepts in geometry and physics, such as Killing vector fields and Einstein metrics, and explore how they can be applied to specific spaces, such as three-dimensional spaces and their hypersurfaces. Lastly, we provide supporting examples of the results presented. Overall, this research serves as a comprehensive introduction to the topic of distorted product warped products of semi-inclined submanifolds within nearly contact manifolds. It integrates various branches of mathematics, including differential geometry, topology, and complex analysis, as well as physics, for those interested in the study of event horizons and gravitational potential. With the emergence of new mathematical definitions and concepts, such as distortion, as a primary focus, we hope to contribute to the study of the topic. (Note: This work has been expanded from the first author's master's thesis.)

This study proposes a novel nonparametric approach to identifying distinct groups within interconnected populations, characterized by disease outbreaks, network propagation, and information diffusion. Unlike existing methods, which often rely on specific models or parameters, this geometric method is based on a single nonparametric metric. Building on the idea of minimizing intermediate mixing between distinct groups, which is often referred to as modularity, this method utilizes geometric concepts such as medoids, convexity, and separation to iteratively refine and define nonoverlapping groups. Furthermore, this method preserves the inherent structure of the input data and is characterized by its lack of sensitivity to small-sized groups. Additionally, this method can be tailored to accommodate varying theoretical and empirical perspectives on modularity. Notably, unlike methods that rely on the number of expected edges per node, this method does not require the specification of parameters or edges per node profiles. Instead, it is based solely on the weighted adjacency matrix of the network, making it suitable for large-scale network analysis. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method using artificial and real-world examples, highlighting its ability to detect non-symmetric groups and handle non-symmetric networks, as well as its applications in nonparametric geometric analysis. Notably, this method is particularly suitable for networks characterized by differing levels of density and separation. For example, it is effective in detecting seed nodes and identifying non-symmetric groups in Twitter-related networks. Similarly, it is effective in detecting distinct disease outbreaks and non-symmetric groups in healthcare-related networks. Furthermore, this method is applicable to applications such as clustering time series data, defining geographic regions, and defining categories based on network similarity. In researching foreground emission from Galactic sources, we develop and apply a novel methodology centered on analyzing around key sources in Galactic maps with emphasis on their characteristic 'X'es' patterns. This approach is particularly significant because it offers a universal framework, unaffected by the specific form of the channel's representation. Previous studies have established that understanding a quantum channel is achievable with polynomial complexity when working within the shadow space, but the problem remains unresolved regarding how to achieve such understanding. This work delves into three related problems. First, we developed a technique using random unitaries to nearly perfectly reconstruct any quantum channel's representation with polynomial complexity. Next, we determined that perfect reconstruction of a channel's representation is not feasible with limited resources, as it would necessitate an excessively high precision in the order of the channel's dimension. However, we do suggest a method for achieving this level of precision with a feasible number of measurements. Our third contribution involves the problem of understanding which specific pairs of matrices can represent a channel's input and output, as these pairs possess unique properties. We successfully transformed the problem of understanding these pairs through shadow representation into a problem related to understanding which pairs constitute contractions, a problem that has been studied and understood by other researchers. Using this well-established knowledge, we demonstrated that understanding these pairs, and consequently the problem of channel understanding, can be solved with polynomial complexity. Our paper presents an algorithm utilizing this approach and shows that it offers a polynomial solution, but first it validates that understanding these pairs is necessary for channel understanding. We also provide additional applications, including the problem of state understanding, using the established method, and we reveal that understanding certain specific channels, such as the depolarizing channel, can be solved with linear complexity only, whereas other channels require a polynomial solution. Our paper completes its analysis by presenting an open problem regarding channel understanding and presents supporting numerical demos. Drone path optimization for swift movement is uniquely challenged by obstacles, wind resistance, and gravitational force, necessitating precise trajectory planning to minimize travel time.  Unlike automotive routes, drone optimal velocity paths often diverge from straight lines due to the significant impact of their weight in determining their flight path.  A new, adaptive algorithm is proposed here for generating optimal drone paths in a given environment with a focus on minimizing flight time.  A small unmanned aerial vehicle model is developed from physical principles, enabling the identification of its dynamics and the creation of a cost function guided by near-optimal solutions to the Belmann-Hamilton-Jacobi equation to approximate the optimal trajectory.  Simulation results confirm the algorithm's efficiency in finding optimal solutions in a reduced number of iterations compared to other techniques such as the Cullen-Liu method and traditional model predictive control approaches with the added benefit of being robust in changing wind conditions.  In addition to time optimization, the algorithm is also adapted to integrate the cost of energy consumption, enabling the identification of optimal velocity paths for drones that use rechargeable batteries with limited capacity.  In this scenario, the algorithm is successful in lowering overall costs by increasing fuel efficiency, which in turn allows the drones to stay aloft for a longer period of time.  Most notably, the algorithm is shown to be capable of handling wind resistance, demonstrating the significant impact of wind on the optimization process and the need for wind modeling and integration in drone path optimization. An investigation was conducted on Sc2TbN@C80 on an h-BN/Ni(111) surface using high-energy X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, providing a detailed and precise understanding of the shift in the Tb 2p levels as temperature changed. Below 150 K, the Tb 2p levels exhibited a 12 meV difference, which gradually grew as temperature increased to 300 K, corresponding to a predicted alteration in the quantum ground state based on theoretical analysis. Furthermore, the calculated results using density functional theory revealed how the surface environment impacts the magnetic behavior of the molecule, indicating a transition from a classical to a quantum magnetic state as temperature decreased. Moreover, the calculated results under ambient conditions showed that the Sc2TbN@C80 molecule exhibits unidirectional magnetic polarization due to the interaction between the molecule and the nitrogen-triplet spin, which may be influenced by noncovalent bonds with the substrate under higher temperature conditions. An analysis of the ratio of the spin-polarized and unpolarized dose components also confirmed that the Tb 2p levels undergo a polarization transition from 0% to nearly 100%, which coincides with the expected result as temperature increased from 150 to 300 K. These findings demonstrate the potential for thermal manipulation of the magnetic polarization of molecular magnets on a surface, offering a foundation for the development of thermally-controlled magnetic phenomena on an atomic scale. An investigation of the magnetic performance of molecular magnets on a surface under various temperature and measurement conditions may lead to the discovery of unique magnetic properties, for example the emergence of antiferromagnetic or ferromagnetic ordering or the appearance of quasiparticles, which may be influenced by the interaction between the molecule and the substrate. Furthermore, the impact of noncovalent bonds and the chemical properties of the substrate on the magnetic performance of molecular magnets as temperature increases or decreases provides an important explanation for the phenomenon of reversible spin polarization. This discovery may also lead to the development of efficient spin-polarized electrons on an atomic scale, which could be applied in various fields of nano-devices, for example the use of Sc2TbN@C80 as a spin valve. Therefore, the calculation of electronic properties as temperature changes may open up a new area of research in the discovery of efficient spin valves on an atomic scale. The internet of things incorporates a device into the network known as a thing, comprising various devices like sensors, cameras, microphones, etc., that are interconnected. The internet of things provides convenience and improved quality of life through services like safety and comfort. The rapid growth of the internet of things has extended to rural and underserved areas, incorporating energy-restricted devices, which often feature restricted resources such as memory, processing power, and energy consumption, all below a specific threshold. Consequently, the applications need to meet these strict resource constraints. The full potential of the internet of things can be realized by implementing post-quantum lightweight cryptographic algorithms that offer high security, even when meeting these resource constraints, despite the rising security threats. The aim is to achieve this while still allowing for the widespread integration of secure services and tools within the internet of things. 

To achieve this goal, several post-quantum lightweight cryptographic algorithms were evaluated based on performance, security, usability, and their respective security proofs. The evaluation included the beyond-beyond post-quantum encryption scheme known as SPHINX/, the MiMC permutation, ROLLO, the MAA protocol, the KYBER key encapsulation mechanism, the SPARTING encryption scheme, the NTRUSign signature scheme, the SARG4 encryption scheme, and the CRYSTAL-II encryption scheme. The evaluation of these algorithms was based on several criteria, and the results revealed that each algorithm excelled in different areas but failed to meet others, resulting in different levels of security, usability, and efficiency.

A new lightweight implementation of the KYBER key encapsulation mechanism was developed, utilizing an Apple M1 processor. The results revealed that the developed implementation met the required level of security, exceeded current levels of efficiency by a significant margin, and could potentially be used at even lower energy consumption levels than previously thought. As a result, the developed implementation could potentially be widely adopted into the lightweight cryptographic tools within the internet of things, leading to a significant boost in security and efficiency levels.

The developed implementation of the KYBER key encapsulation mechanism served as the base for a secure e-mail service known as EMME, that was introduced and demonstrated within the internet of things. We explore the possibility of incorporating Bayesian statistics in the real-time management of high-stakes experiments, specifically Ramsey series measurements searching for oscillating dark matter signals. By using a Bayesian approach, we can update our prior knowledge after each Ramsey measurement and refine the search parameters, potentially increasing the chances of a successful detection. Our study involves simulating a series of measurements with varying detection thresholds to compare the efficiency of adaptive and non-adaptive trial designs. The results demonstrate that an adaptive trial strategy can lead to a significant increase in detected signals, with a 25% improvement over a fixed-frequency search in the dark matter parameter space, and a 3.2-fold improvement in the overall signal rate. Furthermore, an adaptive trial strategy can also be beneficial for closed-search projects, yielding a 50% increase in detected signals. The principles behind our method can likely be applied to other types of particle detector experiments with time-dependent data acquisition. With the rapid progress of quantum computing and machine learning capabilities, our proposed adaptive trial strategy may become even more effective in the future. centrality values to nodes based on the minimal geometric disparities in the triangle

centrality in identifying crucial nodes of the Internet and major airlines in the USA,

The study of $\mathcal D_n$ was initially and significantly contributed by N. K. Bak and B. P. D. A. K. R. R., who specifically examined the case for $n=5$. Our investigation expands the findings of these prior studies, (1) broadens the smoothness conditions to include up to order $m=2$ while simplifying the criteria for interval maps to be elementary; (2) refines and standardizes the definition and description of "widespread behavior" and associated global attractors; (3) develops a theory for weakly separated sets, (4) outlines a general strategy for identifying widespread behavior for odd $n$, with specific applications demonstrating the behavior of widespread behavior for odd $n\leq 49$ and demonstrates the behavior of everywhere transitivity for odd $n\leq 47$. The study also examines the global behavior of certain special classes of $\mathcal D_n$. Lastly, it investigates the problems of finding widespread behavior for even $n$ and everywhere transitivity for odd $n$. The study employs various mathematical and analytical methods, including dynamic system mapping, interval analysis, and Wald's theorem. The accompanying appendix features graphical illustrations of the global attractors of representative systems in $\mathcal D_5$ and shows some numerical results obtained using AUTO, a software package for continuation and bifurcation theory. Additionally, this study outlines a general strategy for performing global continuation and bifurcation analysis and presents several numerical findings regarding global behavior for odd $n$ and everywhere transitivity for even $n$. These analyses were completed utilizing the theoretical underpinnings described in this study, resulting in the visualizations and numerical data presented in the provided PDF document. The accompanying Julia software package 'widespread' models the theoretical findings detailed in this study and serves as a practical implementation of the theories detailed in this manuscript. The study concludes by reflecting on its contributions and the many outstanding problems and questions remaining in the theory of widespread behavior for odd and even $n$. A new quantum algorithm is developed to solve quantum many-body problems on near-term quantum devices by using a adaptive adiabatic simulation method combined with quantum circuit variational approach. To speed up the evolution of the quantum system, an adiabatic simulation method is employed and results in a faster evolution but at the cost of decreased accuracy. To counteract this side effect, an adaptive feedback control is introduced to maintain high precision throughout the simulation. It achieves this by monitoring the gap between energy levels and stopping the simulation when it approaches the regime where energy level gaps become too small, affecting the accuracy of the quantum algorithm. Furthermore, an additional quality indicator is introduced to verify the accuracy of the quantum algorithm by testing the completeness of the basis used in the simulation. With the adaptive feedback control in place, it is possible to speed up the evolution of the quantum system without compromising the accuracy of the quantum algorithm. To illustrate the effectiveness of the modified algorithm, it was tested on the King model which features a degenerate energy level and is challenging to simulate with the quantum algorithm. Simulation results indicate that the modified algorithm is capable of accurately simulating quantum many-body dynamics on quantum devices despite the quantum algorithm's limitations. It is able to successfully replicate experimental findings using fewer pulses on a quantum device and surpass the standard quantum algorithm's capabilities by achieving higher precision overall. In summary, the modified algorithm is an essential advancement for solving complex quantum many-body problems on quantum devices by achieving improved accuracy using fewer pulses, thereby accelerating near-term quantum computing development for these challenging problems. The explanation of effects through mediators has become a widely used method in social sciences to provide deeper insights into how-what factors are involved in causing effects. However, interpreting mediation analysis results is particularly challenging when working with case-control studies. This research paper explores the reasoning and evaluation methods for performing mediation analysis in case-control studies, focusing on situations where the mediator is binary. A theoretical model is developed to evaluate mediated effect size estimates in logistic regression models, including control variable adjustment and scenarios with or without over-adjustment. To assess over-adjustment, we use a categorical equivalent of the F-score and an alternative approach based on Pearson's chi-squared test. Through case studies and simulations, we examine the accuracy of the proposed estimates and test statistics for assessing mediated effect significance. This research finds that relying solely on p-values for mediated effect assessment can be misleading due to over-adjustment influence. By considering control variable impact with the alternative approach, researchers can avoid overly conservative results. Although not extensively validated through simulations, our approaches are based on logical reasoning. This highlights the need for careful examination of control variable impact in case-control studies before assessing mediated effect significance. This research may have implications for conducting such analyses in genetic studies, specifically in candidate gene-case control designs where mediator variables often arise. Such designs often involve large samples, which can increase the likelihood of discovering seemingly significant mediated effects due to the large sample size. Consequently, our approach emphasizes the need for cautious interpretation of such results. This research may also have applications in examining interaction effects between predictors and mediators in influencing an outcome variable. Our approach aims to provide a theoretical and logical framework for assessing mediated effect significance in case-control studies. Through a case study of a well-known genetic association study, we apply our methods to evaluate mediated effect significance. This research demonstrates that even seemingly minor mediators can yield statistically significant results in such case-control studies due to large sample sizes. This has implications for the study, as over-adjustment for control variables may have exaggerated the significance of mediated effects. Since our approach uses control variable impact in assessing over-adjustment for control variables, we can use our method to adjust our approach and provide a more accurate evaluation of mediated effect significance. This is particularly useful in such case-control studies, as it provides a reliable and less biased estimate of mediated effect significance. A related R code is provided in the supplementary materials. This research may have related to various other research projects in candidate gene-case control designs, as it provides a logical and theoretical framework for assessing mediated effect significance. In recent times, Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces have emerged as a highly promising technology for enhancing the resilience of wireless communication systems. Consequently, the focus is now on the design of robust and secure communication networks for multiple users with the aid of RIS. This research investigates a specific network that incorporates an active transmitter, a passive receiver, an RIS located at an enemy location, and an active eavesdropper. The authors developed a two-stage optimization framework for secure and resilient communication. First, the optimal phase shift matrix is designed to null the eavesdropper's signal and maximize the active transmitter's signal strength. Next, the receiver's receive power is optimized using an iterative algorithm. The results reveal that the proposed framework yields superior security and resilient performance metrics, including higher signal-to-noise ratio, reduced probability of error, and higher secrecy throughput, even when the RIS is operating at less than full efficiency. Furthermore, the effectiveness of the phase shift matrix is demonstrated and its adaptability to changing user locations is illustrated. This research shows that the RIS can greatly enhance the resilience and security of wireless communication systems despite its limitations, providing valuable insights into the design of secure and resilient RIS-based communication networks. For vast knowledge bases to offer insightful recommendations, understanding occasions is essential in inferring an individual's personality, thus making Personalized News Recommendation a pressing case for studying occasion-based models. However, current research faces significant challenges due to limited data availability and translation barriers, as news articles often contain occasion-related terms and are published in various languages. To address these obstacles, we have created the Multilingual Event Encyclopedia, a multilingual dataset that categorizes events into their respective domains for 10 million European articles in English, French, and German, covering four different domains. Our dataset is unique because it not only lists event subcategories but also includes synonyms and can be translated to other languages, as the site itself is available in three different languages. Using this dataset, we have developed a Multilingual Event Encyclopedia Transformer (MEE-TR), a machine translation model that can forecast domains, translate terms, and identify occasions in a cross-lingual setting, as our benchmark tests demonstrate. Ultimately, we showcase MEE-TR's potential in creating cross-lingual personalized systems that can seamlessly adapt to users' preferences. We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme entails two primary cryptographic constructions: a new Incognito encryption method and an integrated Sign-Agnostic Ring Signatures, both designed to ensure the anonymity of transactions.
The Incognito encryption method serves as a stealth address wrapper, allowing payments to be untraceable, whereas Sign-Agnostic Ring Signatures, through the integration of Ring Signatures and bulletproofs, provide unlinkable transactions.
Notably, Delegated RingCT offers better performance, especially in the Incognito encryption algorithm, which reduces size and transaction fees by half, making it compatible with existing Bitcoin hard forks.
Additionally, Delegated RingCT maintains RingCT's P2SH compatibility and preserves transactions' public visibility for analysis purposes.
Furthermore, Delegated RingCT's adoption of DPoS enables faster block times, which is complementary to RingCT's P2SH compatibility.
A demonstration POC, in the form of Ethereum contract, has been implemented and is available online. Moreover, Delegated RingCT is being proposed as a solution to mitigate stealth address problems, which has garnered support through a community vote on BitcoincashTalk. 
You can test the Incognito encryption method and Sign-Agnostic Ring Signatures at https://incognito.open-source.io and https://ag-ringsignatures.open-source.io, respectively. 
For more information on the project, visit https://delegated-ringct.open-source.io.  A GitHub repository for Delegated RingCT can be found at https://github.com/open-source/io/delegated-ringct. brightness in an analysis of light intensity can serve as a reliable indicator
of a laser beam's quality. Our study showed that this integral has the ability
to characterize not just Gaussian, but also stochastic and pulsed laser beams.
Using an experimental setup consisting of a High Power Quasi-Single Mode Yb:YAG

different settings of the resonator's cavity. Our data demonstrated that these
beams at their optimal settings displayed the highest value of the mentioned
integral. This method offers a practical way to evaluate the quality of a laser
beam without requiring elaborate measurements of its intensity profile and
temporal characteristics. Our study compared the results obtained from brightness
scans with established metrics like the beam quality factor (BQF) and the

beam's true brightness, while the difference becomes more pronounced as the beam

This paper presents a novel optimization method called AskewSGD to tackle the problem of training deep neural networks with quantized weights and activations. Existing techniques often rely on subgradient approximations or use surrogate loss functions, but AskewSGD directly addresses the non-convex optimization problem derived from the quantized loss. By initially relaxing the quantized loss function and then applying a convex approximation, AskewSGD develops a optimization algorithm with efficient convergence properties. This approach is analogous to the performance-guaranteed optimization method developed by Chouzenoux et al. AskewSGD's efficiency in training quantized neural networks on benchmark datasets such as CIFAR-10 and ImageNet has been successfully demonstrated, yielding results comparable to state-of-the-art approaches both in terms of computational efficiency and accuracy. AskewSGD's implementation will be made freely available on the OpenSource platform GitLab. Reynolds et al. These studies are conducted within the context of a module-based system that efficiently handles computational resources. The state of the art in generative modeling has been enhanced significantly due to the versatility of the Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) architecture. Nonetheless, the instability in training GANs has prompted researchers to create more predictable alternatives. The Generative Confrontational Network (GCN) is one such alternative reported in literature. It introduces a game-theoretic approach to modeling complex distributions by representing data as a result of two conflicting games. While GCN offers more predictability than traditional GANs, it can deviate from generating accurate target data if not properly optimized through the two parallel game solving processes. In order to improve the performance of GCN, we have developed a hidden space conditioning technique that controls the opposing games and adjusts them to fit the target distribution. Experimental results have shown that our method significantly improves the quality of the generated data on various datasets, particularly datasets with multi-modal or intricate data structures such as 3D textures and Lie group-based face-generating applications. The associated code is available for review at https://github.com/jay-kreuter/hsc_gcn. Additionally, we have included a video demonstration of our method at https://youtu.be/y1s_0Sm1K9E. The detailed explanation of our method and its effects is reported in the presented study. It demonstrates how the hidden space conditioning technique reduces model complexity, increases parallel solvers' effectiveness, and improves generated data quality by forcing the opposing games to cooperate in synthesizing target data. Moreover, we have found that the hidden space conditioning technique can be used to model data distributions even in cases where the cost function is not accurately representative of the required data structure. In such cases, parallel game solving produces diverse generated samples, and the dataset is identified as having a multi-modal structure. Ultimately, the technical applications of our method are diverse and extensive, encompassing various fields such as 3D generation, image and video editing, lie group-based systems, protein structure prediction and other intricate data structures requiring accurate modeling. It is anticipated that the presented research will serve as a foundation for the development of future modeling techniques and methods. The quality of the generated data is visualized using high-resolution images and 3D animations within our demonstration video. Our research is a response to several unresolved challenges in the field of generative modeling as discussed in the introduction section. The proposed approach can be applied to tackle similar challenges in a wide array of modeling and optimization domains. A comprehensive review of related work and the relevant background theory is provided in the introduction section.

Machine learning algorithms are often evaluated based on their in-sample and out-of-sample performance. While measures of in-sample performance like cross-validation assess prediction capabilities, those that rely on predictive distributions for out-of-sample data assessment can offer more insight into an algorithm's uncertainty and robustness, particularly when combined with metrics like conservative valid loss or out-of-sample data detection. Here, we show that a distributional machine learning principle can be used to systematically develop such out-of-sample data detection tools. By expanding existing statistical results on distributional machine learning, we derive new, versatile tools for evaluating out-of-sample performance, which we demonstrate with a widely used machine learning method - Gaussian Process regression. Our work enables the creation of an accurate detection tool for this method and its variants, allowing for reliable detection of out-of-sample data even when based on limited in-sample data. Additionally, we propose an improved testing procedure that incorporates the use of conservative valid loss and out-of-sample data detection, while maintaining the preservation of desired statistical properties. Our analysis also addresses the challenge of evaluating out-of-sample data detection uncertainty and, in a new contribution, develops a testing procedure that preserves the desired statistical properties, thus bringing the concept of distributional machine learning one step closer to practical relevance in data science. Our theoretical results are supported by a series of numerical experiments and real-world applications. Importantly, we show that our proposed testing procedures can help identify missing or erroneous data which were previously overlooked within the training dataset, underlining their practical value in data analysis. Finally, we illustrate the effectiveness of our testing procedures in real-world applications with two prominent datasets - the Fletcher Peninsula and the Anne's helicopter data, demonstrating how they can aid scientists in understanding associated complexities. Our analysis confirms that the new testing procedures offer valuable advantages over traditional cross-validation analysis, helping to identify underlying issues in these datasets. Ultimately, we show that the new testing procedures can contribute to knowledge generation in scientific fields by empowering data analysts to accurately recognize and leverage their strengths and limitations. Our analysis and resulting insights have potential far-reaching impacts on a variety of scientific fields and contributes to the advancement of data-driven scientific research and machine learning. Our code is also made available to the public, as described within. A quick summary of our contributions and code is also available at https://michael-zeng.github.io/publications/dgl-out-of-sample-performance/. Following standard academic conventions, detailed mathematical and statistical background information is also provided at https://mathzeng-on-GitHub.github.io/background-material/. (Verified 2023)

Quantum systems displayed in an open environment to external influences experience a persistent heating phenomenon, despite a lack of thermal equilibrium. This leads to the irreversible spread of a quantum system's density distribution over all possible states. However, if the system is initially confined to a narrow set of its states, this spreading may occur gradually. We examine this phenomenon in a two-dimensional system composed of bosons located within an optical lattice structure that is periodically driven and interacts with its surroundings. Although the system is initially simplified to a single stable path, known as a "Floquet Florens Normal Mode", a study reveals how the surrounding heat influence breaks down its unique behavior and disperses it among adjacent states. This complex scenario is explored using a combination of theories that take into account the surrounding environment and the driven nature of the optical lattice structure. An experimental approach based on existing technology is proposed to verify the occurrence of the described unique phenomenon. This study successfully connects distinct concepts, including Floquet systems and Bose-Einstein condensation in environments, to the broader field of disorder-driven phase transitions. It provides valuable insights into the behavior and dynamics of quantum systems under distinct influences. An anticipated investigation of this remarkable phenomenon could greatly contribute to the development of novel quantum driving strategies with the potential to create stable, long-lasting states. This could be achieved by closely examining "echo packages" of repeated stable states, as well as their interactions with environmental noise, using the principles of coherences and temperature-dependent dissipation. An enhanced comprehension of the interplay between quantum coherence and environmental dissipation could possibly lead to the creation of stable, localized states resistant to environmental influences - a crucial requirement for the creation of stable, localized bosonic modes through quantum driving strategies. Such methods could offer a new approach to the creation of stable, localized bosonic modes with potential to be used in the development of quantum computing algorithms. An example of this approach involves employing a multi-domain phenomenon called Dirac-Weyl point with the potential to create stable, localized bosonic modes at extremely high temperatures. An investigation of this strategy in the experimentally feasible 2D optical lattice structure is also presented. It is shown that despite system complexity, a systematic and rigorous theoretical approach can be developed to accurately describe the phase transitions between distinct states. This can be achieved by closely examining symmetry-breaking in the optical lattice structure, as well as the behavior of density fluctuations under distinct influences and environmental noise using the principles of dissipation and quantum coherence, which further complicates the environment-dissipation model. The discovery of quantum clock clusters, specifically non-repeating ones, has given rise to new optical clocks with enhanced performance capabilities. These quantum clocks break away from traditional repeating frameworks, offering a wide range of exciting characteristics. This study develops a probabilistic time-domain representation tailored specifically for non-repeating optical clocks to better understand and analyze their unique behaviors within this framework. By leveraging a statistical description, we identify key features of the non-repeating optical clock spectrum and connect them to an existing Hamiltonian model. Our proposed representation serves as a versatile analytical tool, providing a clear and explicit link between the spectrum and underlying system dynamics. Furthermore, this representation offers a comprehensive and unified framework for interpreting spectral data across various regimes of the non-repeating optical clock. As such, it has significant implications for theoretical analyses and experimental interpretations alike. Additionally, we apply this statistical description to the Drude-Lorentz model, a fundamental approach to describing optical clocks, and gain valuable insights into its underlying systems. This study significantly expands the theoretical understanding and practical utilization of non-repeating optical clocks. It not only aids in Slepian band decomposition but also enables direct modeling of the non-repeating optical clock spectrum using a probabilistic description. Therefore, it has far-reaching implications for interpreting spectral data across different regimes of the non-repeating optical clock. Finally, we use our proposed representation to explore the unique properties of the non-repeating optical clock at the Planck frequency, where quantum gravitational effects are expected to emerge, and the dark energy and dark matter regimes. Our study significantly advances the theoretical analysis and practical utilization of non-repeating optical clocks, opening up exciting new avenues in quantum optics and gravity research. Using our framework, we establish a groundbreaking connection between the non-repeating optical clock representation and miniaturized quantum gravitational clocks, enabling a deep understanding of the complex interplay between these concepts for the first time.
