The rising demand for edge computing in 5G networks has led to the creation of Software Failure Correction (SFC), a general framework for managing edge devices. This paper focuses on three key strategies for SFC: first, it introduces a mathematical optimization model for real-time failure correction in distributed systems; second, it develops an online collaborative recovery approach in conjunction with fault detection and mitigation in decentralized networks; third, it designs an energy-efficient asset management model for fog nodes to support SFC and validate the strategies through various experimental tests under diverse network conditions. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of the strategies in achieving near-optimal failure correction and fault mitigation performance. Notably, the online collaborative recovery method achieves a 90% reduction in control plane overhead, and the energy-efficient asset management approach saves up to 60% of fog node utilization, thereby leading to significant reductions in network delay and overall performance improvement. Additionally, the strategies have been evaluated in terms of computational complexity and have shown varying levels of complexity, ranging from O(n) to at least superlinear complexity. This study is the first to explore SFC in fog-assisted software-defined networks, and the experimental results have outperformed baseline benchmarks in failure correction and fault mitigation tasks. However, the strategies have exhibited limited performance in dynamic network conditions and require further investigation in this area. One potential direction for future research could be the exploration of the fundamental limits of failure correction in fog-assisted software-defined networks, and the development of decentralized control systems could potentially mitigate latency issues in such dynamic environments. Following a comprehensive analysis of the strategies, this study has identified areas for improvement and suggested several potential research pathways for future development. These include extending the fault tolerance analysis, investigating distributed optimization methods that do not rely on central optimization frameworks, improving collaboration and asset management in fault mitigation tasks, and most challenging of all, testing the strategies under real-world network conditions. In summary, the strategies introduced in this paper have demonstrated near-optimal failure correction and fault mitigation performance in real-time failure correction tasks, but the collaboration and asset management aspects of fault mitigation require further improvement and dynamic failure correction remains an open area for future research and development. In terms of social impact, this study has explored the use of edge failure correction as a form of community-based disaster relief effort, and the potential applications of edge failure correction in non-profit organizations and disaster relief initiatives could be a valuable area for further investigation and development. With this premise in mind, we introduce the concept of Hyper-invariant MERA as an approximate holographic error-correcting code, which is predicated on the existence of well-defined quantum systems exhibiting two distinct types of scaling behavior. Furthermore, the proposed framework is easily generalizable to higher-dimensional systems characterized by higher-order power-law associations. The Milky Way's central fibers consist of dense, synchronized magnetic loops spanning 0.1 to 3 solar radii in diameter. Analyzing 111 fibers required evaluating over 17,000 diameter measurements to determine their spatial distribution and properties. We found a statistical relationship linking fiber density to their separation, explaining 47% of variance with a correlation coefficient of 0.685. The probability of two fibers sharing the same or overlapping areas is 12%, and their separation follows a Poisson distribution with an average of 1.8 fibers per unit area (approximately 0.07 solar radii^2). We found no correlation between fiber density and their separation, but the likelihood of a fiber sharing the same or overlapping areas with another depends on its density and the distance to its nearest fiber. Using a simulation, we verified that the structure of the fibers' population could explain our observations, suggesting the presence of a critical distance of 0.7 to 1.3 solar radii when evaluating the population's density, depending on the neighboring fiber's distance. However, traditional concepts of the fibers' origin fall short, and we require new hypotheses to explain our findings, particularly the separation characteristics of the fibers' population. We discovered that nearby double fibers or a fiber and its neighboring fiber (in a circular arrangement) could play a significant role, especially when evaluating their separation. Moreover, the separation characteristics of the fibers' population can be utilized as an indicator to evaluate and modify established concepts of their origin and formation. We intend to build upon our previous study by analyzing the angular separation distribution in the plane tangent to the stars' rotation and apply our data to evaluate and modify the formation models of the fibers and the star formation process. The project will complement our findings by identifying the geometric shape and dimensions of the disks where the fibers originate, and it will allow us to calculate the statistical characteristics of the disks' population instead of individual elements. Moreover, the project will enable us to compare the statistical characteristics of the disks' population with those predicted by existing formation models. To efficiently manage distribution networks and meet rising energy efficiency demands, smart grids have been introduced, and they often operate in an open-access model, requiring automatic and seamless services behind the meter. 

However, the integration of many resource-sharing options and time-of-use pricing in smart grids creates new challenges for voltage regulation, as it facilitates the connection of voltage-dependent load and the deployment of distributed energy resources.

This letter presents a distributed control strategy that maintains voltage stability without requiring centralized decision-making in networks featuring capacitors that can lower voltage. 

The proposed strategy uses a distributed online predictive control approach, ensuring voltage levels at network bottlenecks stay within set limits while maximizing energy storage efficiency. 

The method's key benefit is its ability to adapt to network topology changes in real-time, in the absence of a detailed model, making it particularly suitable for networks with frequent topological variations. 

Simulation results using PSAT confirm the strategy's capacity for online implementation, efficient voltage regulation, and significant energy savings for network operators and resource owners. 

This approach demonstrates a reduction in energy consumption of up to $\mathbf{5.81\%}$ in test cases and eliminates the need for central management or network expansion, providing substantial economic benefits. 

The code for implementing the strategy and demonstration results can be accessed at \url{https://github.com/cooper-ml/did}.

Specifically, calculations of the parton distribution functions and polarized structure functions, results for quark masses, color density effects, the interaction strength between quarks and gluons, and thermal phase transitions in heavy, relativistic hadrons will be examined. Moreover, numerical data for isothermal, anisotropic lattices concerning the pressure's dependence on the spatial correlation length will be analyzed and plotted for comparison with theoretical predictions. Additionally, the implementation of the Ward identities in lattice QCD at non-zero temperature and density will be discussed in detail. Predictive physical modeling for the dynamics of offshore wind turbines is an
essential tool for evaluating their reliability and optimizing their design.
Although computational models of turbine dynamics create valuable datasets
for investigating stress and fatigue, they are costly and time-consuming.
Combining meta-analysis of existing datasets with surrogate modeling enables
the creation of high-fidelity simulation models that can efficiently estimate
the effects of unknown variables on stress and fatigue. We developed a method
for building such models by linking multiple Gaussian processes and demonstrated
its effectiveness in generating synthetic datasets and conducting probabilistic
analysis for offshore wind turbines. Compared to current approaches, our
method produces more accurate predictions of stress and fatigue, utilizing
high-resolution computational models, while maintaining a comparable computational
cost. The method relies on maximizing approximate Bayesian inference and
utilizes variational inference and message passing to scale to large problems. 

Our method for modeling offshore wind turbine stresses and fatigue yields
results that closely match the actual stress and fatigue levels observed in
experimental testing, while predicting fatigue levels remains a challenge.
Despite this limitation, the proposed approach demonstrates significant
improvements in several other metrics, enabling researchers to explore the
effects of various design and optimization strategies on the reliability of
offshore wind turbines. 

Using the modeled dataset, we investigated several strategies for
incorporating the surrogate model in a probabilistic analysis and
contingency table calculation. 

Our approach can be adapted for applications in computational structural
engineering and other fields involving the modeling of complex, 6DOF offshore
wind turbines with nonlinear loadings. 

Merging meta-analysis and surrogate modeling addresses two key limitations
of current probabilistic analysis methods, which often overlook the influence
of unknown variables on fatigue and failure and are too slow for practical
application. 

The surrogate models enable the efficient simulation of unknown variables,
while linking them to the known dynamics of offshore wind turbines using
gaussian processes allows the extraction of valuable insights from the
synthetic dataset.

Social media platforms provide valuable data for research on public health, economics, and natural disaster recovery by offering access to tweets containing relevant information. We conducted a quantitative study of Turkish Twitter users' behaviors and sentiment patterns in response to the Izmir earthquake (June 24th 2020) by analyzing their tweet creation and deletion habits and categorizing their posts using sentiment analysis. The data set consisted of 188,882 eligible tweets and our research explored the effects of account longevity on their posting habits, as well as the sentiment patterns of users who remained active and those who discontinued tweeting about the earthquake. Furthermore, we investigated which emotional sentiments (e.g. positive, negative, neutral)) dominated the Izmir earthquake tweets. It's noteworthy that this study was carried out solely with publicly accessible data, adhering to the terms set by Twitter for research use. The results of our research revealed interesting insights into the behaviors and emotional states of Turkish Twitter users in response to a significant natural disaster. Ultimately, this study has significant implications for digital marketing efforts by highlighting which emotional sentiments are effectively used by Turkish Twitter users and providing valuable insights for crisis communication and digital brand management. The study's findings and data analysis results are presented in detail, accompanied by a sample Twitter data set for researchers to replicate and extend our research. We investigate the rational cohomology of nilpotent quotients of generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups, specifically their free nilpotent and solvable variants, analyzing their fine structure and computing key R-infinity characteristics. For the free nilpotent groups, $GSN_f \mathbb{Z}^n$, we find that their R-infinity characteristic $R_\infty(GSN_f \mathbb{Z}^n, \mathbb{Z}[t])$ has a simple, prime-free form, and propose a more complex description when the domain is based on a rational number. In contrast, the R-infinity characteristic of $GS_n \mathbb{Z}$ exhibits a more complex, prime-dependent structure. Nonetheless, the $t$-primary component of $R_\infty(GS_n \mathbb{Z), \mathbb{Z}[t])$ can be precisely defined as the integral homology of a generalized solvable Higman's group, $H_n(\mathbb{Z})$. Furthermore, the R-infinity characteristic of torsion-free groups can be directly deduced from their continuous cohomology computed by Borel's bivariant cohomology theory. In the case of $GS_n \mathbb{Z}$, the first Borel cohomology $H^1(X, \mathbb{Z})$ can be seen as the 'Maximal abelian $1$-dimensional' cohomology of the unit circle $S^1$ in the complex Banach-$\mathbb{Z}$-space $\ell^1(\mathbb{Z})$, offering a novel geometric interpretation. In a complementary approach, the R-infinity characteristic of $GS_n \mathbb{Z}$ can also be computed via the 'compactification method', which may be extended to the more general case of $GS_n \mathbb{Z}^m$ in the accompanying article. This paper presents a new, unsupervised dataset for naturalistic driving scenes, called the Scene Classification in Naturalistic Driving Dataset (SceNDD). This dataset categorizes critical driving moments into six distinct types. Each instance in the dataset is a frame from one of four distinct traffic situations: collision risk, inclement weather, rear obstacles, or unexpected events. The proposed model incorporates inaccurate channel estimation and imperfect RF components into the channel model to improve accuracy in the least squares problem, thereby enhancing the estimation outcomes. Recently, significant interest has been generated by quantum neural networks (QNNs), which aim to harness the advantages of quantum computing for machine learning purposes. Unlike conventional neural networks, QNNs employ quantum mechanical principles, including superposition, entanglement, and interference, to modify the input data. This different approach is reflected in the way QNNs process data, with recent research focusing on exploring quantum properties in neural networks and its potential benefits for solving complex problems more efficiently than classical neural networks. This work outlines the fundamental concepts underlying qubits, reviews current QNN design approaches, explains how they process data, and explores the unique characteristics of quantum data in the context of QNNs. Additionally, a novel quantum circuit is proposed for solving MNIST, which demonstrates that accurate results can be achieved with significantly fewer quantum operations compared to conventional networks. This outcome highlights the promising prospects of QNNs for extra-fast and efficient computation on quantum hardware. Before delving into the main topic, a concise overview of quantum mechanics, the qubit system, and the concepts of entanglement, interference, and expectation value are provided to facilitate understanding of the underlying quantum principles. Furthermore, a review of circuits is provided, including the explanation of expectation value, along with the description of the measurement process. Additionally, a brief summary of the development of QNN design methods, including the description of quantum realizations for perceptrons, convolutional layers, and fully-connected layers, is provided. Finally, the unique characteristics of quantum data in the context of QNNs are examined and exploited to develop new ideas. This work also acknowledges the distinct characteristics of quantum data in the context of QNNs and explores its potential to shape the design of future quantum circuits. In particular, exploration into non-linear quantum data processing is conducted, and subsequent investigation into the application of unsupervised learning for automatic quantum data processing and label assignment is carried out. Finally, the promising prospects of future quantum data processing are discussed. The focus is specifically on the determination of a solar luminosity as a function of depth, Luther and Kippenhahn function, and radial temperature profiles. The required integrals involve complex functions with strong variations due to the dependence on temperature and radiative opacity. To achieve high computational efficiency, a Gaussian quadrature method with weights based on solar flux distributions is developed. The first part of this study provides a mathematical definition of the problem, while the second part presents an implementation of the proposed method using Gaussian quadrature. The accompanying code is also made accessible through a GitHub repository, facilitating its utilization by researchers in the field of stellar astrophysics. Additionally, a comparison with the existing adaptive quadrature method, Fortran implementation of Kyreau V. Chard (2016), is conducted to demonstrate its superior performance in handling the specified integrals. The resulting implementation is further showcased by its application in updated versions of the programs PMSmodel and Luminal, used for the calculation of model atmospheric profiles and theoretical solar models, respectively. The developed quadrature method has also been successfully incorporated into the program MESA. The presented approach is anticipated to improve the precision of solar-model calculations with the current generation of the MESA software. The work's primary contribution is the development of a novel solar quadrature method, complemented by its integration into multiple widely-used stellar physics codes, thereby facilitating its use by researchers in the field. The accompanying GitHub repository contains the relevant implementation, while MESA has been updated with the development on their website [http://mesa.sourceforge.net.html]. However, working directly with these values is computationally impractical due to their massive size and the necessity to eliminate noisy and irregular entries. In optimization, the Hessian matrix's structure has been beneficial, and this paper discusses how the Gauss-Newton matrix's low-dimensional profile can be utilized in optimization problems, specifically in deep learning where the Jacobian matrix is factored. This low-dimensional structure, comprising only the critical columns, allows for efficient and reliable curvature estimation, and at an even lower dimensional level, the Jacobian's nullspace. These findings are illustrated through an analysis of solving systems of equations and the application of nullspace-based techniques in inverse problem regularization and neural architecture design. Compared to other techniques, such as spectral methods, this approach demonstrates equivalent performance with significantly reduced computational effort, and in a series of experiments, successfully discovers innovative architectures, notably a 94-layer network that surpasses the previous state-of-the-art in MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100. Furthermore, this approach exhibits superior performance on the conceptually more demanding task of fill-in reduction in the sparse matrix completion problem. These results demonstrate that by retaining only the critical columns of the Jacobian matrix, and specifically the low-dimensional critical entries, the ViViT of a function's generalized Gauss-Newton matrix becomes accessible, enabling efficient and reliable curvature estimation and analysis. These entry points enable not only the efficient computation of the Hessian but also the direct application of optimization techniques, such as the Levenberg-Marquardt, without the necessity to invert the entire matrix. This is in contrast to the traditional limited-dimentional structure, typically found in optimization problems, the log-det regularizer, which only allows for efficient row operations. We demonstrate that certain finite subgroups of the general linear group cannot be generalized. In the specific case of $GL_n(\mathbb{Z})$, this particular issue was addressed by B. Brainerd in 1933. Our own contribution involves a collaborative set of rings, focusing on those obtained by reducing $\mathbb{Z}$ modulo a prime number, denoted as $\mathbb{F}_p$ for $p$ being a prime. Despite the distinct nature of $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{F}_p$, the same principles apply in this context. Our proof is constructed upon an earlier concept known as Artin's Autumn Topology, proposed by E. Artin in 1947, describing the configuration of the group's character sphere. In our case, the character sphere represents a tensor product of $\mathbb{F}_p$ with itself, resulting from a square matrix of rank $n$. Our characterization relies on a clear division into two parts: the geometric characteristics on the group's character sphere, showing points of degree 1 forming a non-trivial covering of a sphere with a singular, highly symmetric topology, excluding the identity from its composition. The second component focuses on the group's isomorphism to its given representation, showing that the character sphere's connection with the group's isomorphism is highly rigid and unique. Our contribution serves as an extension to a recent work by the first author, initially applying these principles to the specific case of $p=2$. Our results, however, generalize these findings, making them applicable to the entire set of prime numbers, thereby revealing new and advanced characters for the group's representation in this context. These characters specifically exhibit an even permutation of the group's non-identity elements, resulting from an odd number of these elements. Our characterization addresses a long-standing open issue in the specific case of $p=2$, originally proposed by Brainerd in 1933. Our results, however, go beyond this specific case, resulting in a highly unique and general characterization of the group's representation in this context. Our findings further extend the group's isomorphism to its given representation, showing that the group's character sphere's connection with the group's isomorphism is highly unique and general. The geometric characteristics on the group's character sphere, resulting from a square matrix of rank $n$, show points of degree 1 forming a non-trivial covering of a sphere with a singular, highly symmetric topology, excluding the identity from its composition.

Estimating the position of objects within an image has many practical uses in tasks such as action recognition and vehicle navigation. Unlike object pose estimation, which requires estimating precise 3D characteristics, our focus is on estimating the position of objects within images, which in this study we call object position estimation. By differentiating between object pose estimation and object position estimation, we were able to develop a method that can predict positions for unfamiliar objects and performed well on challenges using datasets COPO, CLEOP, and PASCAL VOC. The success of this study reveals that, by harnessing visual data and incorporating class-level information, it's possible to achieve valuable results in vision, a field where a long-time goal has been to develop robust 3D object pose estimation algorithms. Our proposed approach, which leverages a latent variable and uses a single neural network to accurately predict positions for all objects within an image, recovered effective results for objects at multiple scales and was efficient to implement. The source code of our method has been released for use by other researchers at this link: https://github.com/alexander729/ZERO.git. Additionally, the object position estimation challenge is hosted online at https://competitions.au scope.org/post-zero-shot-object-position-estimation-show-2021. Our method won first place in the PASCAL VOC ZERO SHOT challenge and second place in the COPO and CLEOP challenges without using any ground truth data during training. During testing, our method demonstrated exceptional accuracy, with a mean position estimation error rating below 600, notably for smaller objects our method showed a notable 100x reduction in position estimation error when compared with current top vision-based methods. Our results seem to suggest that, by leveraging a large amount of data, our method achieved successful outcomes. Our method did not perform as well in terms of data efficiency, unlike current top vision-based small-object pose estimation algorithms. Nonetheless, the outcomes of our study are very much in line with what's typically seen in the field. Our method does not rely on the well-known geometric constraints that have been shown to work well for large objects but rather instead relies more on the visual appearance, similar to how well current top vision-based object detection algorithms work. With regards to future research, our method does not work well in situations where the objects fail to appear in an image. In order to further develop our method, we found that integrating visual detection modules, similar to how well current top vision-based detection algorithms work, could help to further improve our method. Predicting long-term or short-term traffic conditions is essential for both individual drivers and the entire transportation system.
The accuracy of traffic forecasting near the forecast time has drawn significant attention due to the usefulness of early warnings, despite posing challenges to forecasting far in advance.
We have found that traffic patterns are influenced by the traffic conditions at nearby points in time, as well as the relative similarity of these points.
The traffic conditions at these similar points can serve as indicators of the forecasted area's future traffic patterns.
The diversity of traffic conditions at these similar points can also provide a comprehensive view, mitigating overconfidence in predictions. 
We have developed a novel sparse forecasting model, called Sim2Forecast, which incorporates similarity information into the prediction process through both indicators and diversification.
The texture of traffic patterns changing over time serves as additional information, assisting in capturing the evolving relationships between pixels at varying time intervals.
We have also devised a Texture2Forecast module for capturing these relationships and integrated the two modules into a comprehensive model for thorough traffic forecasting analysis.
The proposed method exhibits superior performance in comparison to conventional models on real-world datasets, demonstrating effectiveness in forecasting various traffic indicators and conditions. 
Furthermore, to minimize computational overhead, we have developed an acceleration technique using adaptive importance sampling, significantly reducing computation time while maintaining high accuracy, an improvement of up to 3.5 times over conventional methods. 
The source code of our technique will be freely available for research purposes. 
The real-world traffic data used in this research can be accessed from https://github.com/jarvis-ai.my/tf-forecast.

This approach is particularly suitable for applications requiring communication delays below 1ms and offers a decentralized management system with reduced bandwidth requirements, as well as robust cyber security features. Additionally, token ring networks provide near real-time communication, while the cognitive module architecture enables efficient token passing by pre-allocating them to nodes based on their bandwidth availability and safety requirements. A multi-agent learning strategy is also designed to optimize module placement and ring structure in the network. The system's cyber-physical capabilities are demonstrated through a case study involving a token ring network of industrial robots. Furthermore, enablers are proposed to integrate cognitive modules into existing networks, including cyber-physical token ring networks, by retro-fitting them with a hierarchical, distributed system. The framework's technical validity is further substantiated through an analysis of complex cyber-physical system safety and integrity aspects. Finally, an enabler is proposed to make the system resilient against cognitive attacks, allowing users to distinguish malicious behavior and prevent the network from malfunctioning. This spectral feature cannot be fully explained by the relativistic beaming theory. Although the supernovae and GRB afterglows exhibit UV and X-ray excess that can be accounted for by the Inverse Compton radiation resulting from the interaction of an initial unpolarized large-scale region with a relativistic jet, whether this mechanism applies to AGN remains unclear. In the case of AGN, inverse Compton radiation from the interaction of a partially polarized, external, conventional field with a relativistic jet could provide the required UV and soft X-ray excess due to its alignment with the jet and relativistic jet cone angle. If the polarization of the external field is in the plane of the ecliptic, the resulting Thomson scattering will produce polarized photons within the same plane. To illustrate this approach, I demonstrate its application in establishing the extension of holomorphic functions over arbitrary finite sheets and show that the extension of a single function can be determined by the product of the radii of its singular sets. We've developed a method for identifying whether two-beam interferometer output results from a pure state with symmetry properties. This approach is applicable to experiments using unknown pure states, relying solely on mixed states and targeting specific outcomes that indicate a pure state of symmetry. Notably, this research can be applied to experimental settings where low-precision, cost-effective technology is used. Additionally, we've analyzed the time efficiency of our algorithm, finding that its computational complexity is proportional to the number of possible outcomes, a significant improvement over existing virtual detection methods. Furthermore, this research has been partially implemented, with some results providing new tools for experimental settings to identify symmetric pure states. Although we've focused on detecting symmetric states, our algorithm is adaptable for use in virtual detection of rotation-invariant states. Internal criticism suggests that our algorithm may be modified to apply von Neumann's projection, effectively making it more versatile and applicable to a wider range of settings, including those involving two non-complex particles, a scenario that has yet to be explored in this context. Although we've focused on detecting pure states, a more accurate name for this research would be 'detection of states with symmetry properties'. Moreover, our algorithm is not limited to detecting symmetric states; with some modifications, it can be applied to a broader range of sets possessing symmetry properties. In theory, there are an infinite number of sets with symmetry properties, so there are also numerous data analysis methods that identify these sets with precision, although some of these methods are highly complex and sophisticated. In practice, however, there are only a few significant sets with symmetry properties that are commonly explored, including rotation-invariant sets, which have significant practical applications in experimental physics. demonstrating a pattern of construction. Moreover, this text includes continuous

The significant growth in edge devices has led to the widespread use of Federated Learning (FL), a method that gathers data while ensuring device privacy by avoiding the transfer of raw data. Instead, local models are shared or aggregated. Despite its potential, FL's effectiveness is often compromised due to the quality of data and biases in both the data and the model. Research has primarily focused on the technical aspects of FL's privacy, often overlooking these factors. Our research explores the intersection of FL, data fairness, and model confidentiality, with a primary goal of achieving a confidential model that is free from biases. We found that, although achieving confidentiality is theoretically feasible, it is often impractical due to the unique characteristics of FL data. Furthermore, existing FL privacy enhancements that are based on differential privacy are often ineffective in addressing either model confidentiality or fairness. Our study presents new challenges in ensuring the fairness and confidentiality of FL models, and it highlights potential strategies for creating a fair and confidential model without revealing the sensitive information within the FL framework. Our findings were demonstrated in an FL setting where text-based models were trained for hate-speech detection purposes. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/EdenSt-1/DC4J. Our contribution to this field revolves around three key aspects: acknowledging that achieving both fairness and confidentiality in FL is a complex task; identifying existing FL privacy methods as ineffective in addressing either fairness or confidentiality; and proposing potential strategies for a more confident and fair FL model. Notably, U(1)_X gauge boson's mass can be found within the 10-100 GeV range without violating Baryogenesis requirements, which in turn enables its potential discovery at the LHC in the 5-100 GeV mass range with the construction of a future 100 TeV hadron collider. Furthermore, this model's theoretical constraints can be visually represented through a 'green region' on a 2D parameter space chart, where experimental exclusion limits are marked in red and future sensitivity levels in blue. Its hadron collider discovery potential is the opposite of discovering the U(1)_X gauge boson directly, which in turn highlights potential detection challenges at the current LHC in terms of spin-dependent and astrophysical neutrino constraints. Lexicons or dictionaries are essential resources for identifying objects within texts. While numerous lexicons are freely accessible, they often lack spatial annotation data required for object visual identification within the context of visual object recognition systems. This study presents a novel method that utilizes pseudo bounding-box data to complement existing lexicons, using words associated with each other to simulate bounding-box interactions. This simulated spatial relationship data is then combined with word embeddings to guide a lexicon learning process, resulting in an expanded lexicon with improved accuracy. Our proposed method was evaluated on a range of benchmarks and showed significant benefits, achieving a 7.8% point increase in object identification coverage over a baseline that relied on conventional pseudo labeling techniques. Our comprehensive analysis explores the underlying mechanisms of this method and highlights its potential as a standalone object identification solution, especially when coupled with well-trained language models. This research has significant implications for open lexicon object identification, providing a seamless interface between natural language understanding and visual object recognition systems. The associated code is publicly available on GitHub. Our findings suggest that sophisticated visual object recognition systems can be developed using word-based models, achieving state-of-the-art performance in object identification. This research uses factor models to forecast insurance policyholder mortality. We address the challenge of whether using time-varying or static factor loadings is more effective for making short- and long-term forecasts, which requires considering the balance between model complexity and stability. Our study demonstrates that a dynamic factor model with static factor loadings outperforms one with time-varying loadings in the near term (up to 5 years), but the situation reverses for long-term forecasts (over 5 years). Furthermore, to improve forecasting accuracy, we developed a novel method for predicting parameter evolution, which utilizes non-parametric techniques and takes into account the correlation between factors and observations. This method enhances predictive results and allows for reliable confidence intervals to be generated. Additionally, by employing mortality data from multiple countries and spanning multiple decades, we address issues of limited data availability and non-stationarity. Our findings are consistent with those of the ABI mortality research project, which used combined data from 18 life insurers in the UK. In terms of future research directions, we identify potential applications of the methods developed in this study to forecasting not only mortality, but also other life insurance outcomes, such as policyholder lapse rates and credit risk. Trust in a translator can be defined as trustworthiness, which is trustworthiness's measurable aspect in this study. To measure a translator's trustworthiness, it is necessary to assess not only their familiarity with the source and target languages, but also their comprehension and consistency in rendering the source text into the target text, which aligns with the requirements of the source text. To evaluate a translator's trustworthiness, we examine whether their translated texts meet the criteria specified in the source text. For this purpose, we employ a reliability index that calculates the likelihood of a translator's translated texts adhering to the specified requirements. Furthermore, to determine the translator's level of trustworthiness, we use Bayesian estimation by incorporating the dependence structure of translations. The practicality of this method is demonstrated through a dependency-based Bayesian evaluation of translators' trustworthiness using a real-world Chinese-English translation dataset. Our study reveals that translators' trustworthiness correlates with linguistic characteristics, specifically their native language and the level of their mother tongue proficiency. We also uncover that translators' trustworthiness is closely linked to their translation characteristics, which can serve as essential indicators for assessing their trustworthiness. We develop and publish our translation reliability index and Bayesian evaluation tools on our website for public use. We also hope that our research can inspire the development of a trusted translator certification program. We collect a dataset of Chinese-English translations with associated metadata, which demonstrates that the translators' trustworthiness is closely linked to their language expertise. We also demonstrate that utilizing reliance structure in the translation can enhance the accuracy of the translation and improve translation quality. We combine the translation reliability index and the dependency structure of translations to develop a dependable translator evaluation system. The evaluation results show that our translators trustworthiness ranks accurately in line with our criteria for translator trustworthiness. Furthermore, our study reveals that incorporating the dependency structure of translations has a significant effect on improving translation quality. We also make our translation reliability index and Bayesian evaluation tools available for public use and aim to inspire the development of a trusted translator certification program. The translation reliability index is implemented using the Python programming language and is publicly accessible on our GitHub repository at the following URL: https://github.com/mitopencourse/translation-reliability- index. We also incorporate the dependency structure of translations into our translator evaluation system, which is publicly accessible on our GitHub repository at the following URL: https://github.com/mitopencourse/translation-reliability- index. We evaluate and demonstrate the effectiveness of our translator evaluation system

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) can be seen as pre-trained, using a limited number of trainable parameters, and are then searched for the best performing 'lotttery ticket' subset of parameters through trimming. We investigate how trimming effects intermediate CNN layers as well as their ability to perform better than fully connected models of similar size. We discovered that trimming can improve CNN accuracy and allows them to work with smaller numbers of parameters, similar to performance improvements seen when pruning and training at a lower size. Unlike expectations, the effects of trimming on CNNs were found to differ significantly based on the layer, with later layers resisting trimming and performing better under trimming, whereas earlier layers were found to have reduced accuracy and a smaller optimal trimmed size. These findings reveal that CNNs have an built-in advantage making them more resistant to trimming and potentially a superior choice over similar sized fully connected models. We found that common data augmentation methods in CNNs, such as translations, are unbeneficial when applied to the trimmed models, whereas methods such as training on distorted pixels are a good fit. Ultimately, the optimal trimmed size for maximum accuracy and a detailed analysis of the effects of trimming on the structure and performance of CNNs and FNNs is determined. The source code for these experiments can be found at https://github.com/GrzegorzSkrobot/Learning-to-Trim-CNNs.

Our research examines how new mechanisms of electron-phonon interaction affect valley dynamics in two-dimensional materials. To do this, we have developed a comprehensive theoretical framework that includes finite electronic temperature, collective bosonic modes, and various electron-phonon interaction mechanisms. This framework enables us to derive a set of microscopic equations, including Boltzmann and Fokker-Planck equations for electrons and phonons, from which we obtain an effective optical Bloch equation by focusing on weak coupling and employing a perturbation approach. By analyzing the optical Bloch equation, we have numerically investigated how different electron-phonon interaction mechanisms affect valley polarization, relaxation, and decay within a Feynman-Bogoliubov path-integral framework. Our research reveals that (i) the screening effect of electron-phonon interaction mechanisms on valley polarization is negligible, (ii) collective phonons have a notable impact on valley polarization, relaxation, and decay, (iii) the role of collective phonons is similar to that of intravalley phonons, (iv) the impact of nonequilibrium and collective phonons on valley polarization is significant, (v) the impact of nonequilibrium and collective phonons on valley decay is substantial, and (vi) the impact of nonequilibrium and collective phonons on relaxation is considerable. Our research was performed without employing approximations such as the single-mode coupling approximation, the parabolic band-phonon model, or the adiabatic approximation. The visual domain adjustment problem is a critical concept in computer-aided medical imaging. It refers to the process of adjusting a healthy subject's image to match a diseased subject's image, often to create more accurate simulations or by mapping healthy values to diseased values. The goal of the NanoEDU's VDA: TransVas Imaging Quality Assessment track was to develop a method for evaluating transvascular imaging quality, providing a crucial link between research and clinical trials for cardiovascular diseases. Through statistical analysis, we identified the top two ranked solutions from the nearly 30 participants in the challenge. Ultimately, our team achieved first place out of 27 submissions with the solution outlined below. The solution utilized an encoder-decoder architecture, incorporating spatial and categorical attention to handle varying image resolutions, domains, and hypertensions levels. By doing so, it ensured attention was focused on relevant image segments on a per-pixel basis. We utilized the UNet++ encoder, accompanied by a custom-devised spatially-activated category-wise cross-attention layer, to improve training efficiency. We further improved this approach by introducing an adversarial network trained with cycle consistency, mean IPL values preservation, and adversarial regularizers to address domain adjustment constraints. The reported results reflected the improvement from fine-tuning pre-trained LDA models to more recent high-performance architectures. We found that our estimated IPL values demonstrated high consistency with actual IPL values, and through the cross-implementation and cross-device testing, we demonstrated robustness and generalization of our solution. Furthermore, we demonstrated its applicability to various cardiovascular diseases such as cardiovascular diseases and diabetic retinopathy. Our research utilizes ALICE detector data from high-energy lead-lead collisions to measure how electrons produced from heavy quark decay move in a curved path. By assessing the average displacement of these electrons from their expected trajectory based on their momentum, we can better understand the path they traveled. A significant trend in these electrons' movement indicates that those with higher momentum experienced greater displacement, suggesting they originated from decays of beauty hadrons. Additionally, we have used specialized software to reconstruct the history of these beauty hadrons, resulting in a statistically significant finding. Specifically, we have made the first measurement of the production of direct beauty hadrons, those that underwent no significant change in momentum, in lead-lead collisions at a certain energy level. Our results can serve as a tool for further investigations into the interactions between heavy quarks and the surrounding matter in quark-gluon plasma. Furthermore, we have used statistical models to assess the likelihood that the observed trend in these electrons' movement originated from interactions between heavy quarks and the quark-gluon plasma. According to these models, it appears the observed trend can be fully accounted for by the effects of this interaction. However, we have also measured the movement of electrons from certain types of heavy quark decay, providing the first independent confirmation of previous measurements. Our results show that the effects of this interaction are no stronger in more central collisions, indicating that heavy quarks may resist the effects of quark-gluon plasma. Auditing financial transactions involves checking the correctness of each exchange to ensure it follows established rules. Due to the immense number of daily transactions, experts cannot process them individually, and the rules are too numerous to be applied manually. Moreover, individual transactions may involve multiple regulatory requirements, making it difficult to determine which laws apply to specific exchanges. We present a method for deciding which financial transaction rules apply to particular exchanges based on experts' general understanding. This approach uses formal concept analysis to create connections between groups of transactions and the rules that apply to them, while experts review the resulting concepts and add their comments in context. We employ formal concept analysis and Dempster-Shafer theory to address issues related to incomplete or ambiguous expert feedback. By combining comments from various experts, we obtain a comprehensive model of agreement and disagreement, which, together with the understanding of experts, enables us to evaluate the relevance of financial transaction rules to particular exchanges. We demonstrate that our method is adaptable, meaning that in the second step, new comments from experts can be added to the existing model, leading to changes in the assessment of relevance, which in turn facilitates the selection of the most suitable concepts for auditing. We illustrate the effectiveness of our method using a practical example drawn from the field of auditing. We believe that our method could be used as a starting point for the development of decision-support systems for auditing, which could make the auditing process more efficient, leading to better quality controls for financial institutions. In 1927, Heisenberg introduced the generalized uncertainty principle as a consequence to consider the uncertainty of non-commuting observables, measuring each other successively.  This concept is centered around a rectangular hyperbola and has far-reaching implications for the field of quantum measurement theory.  Building upon this framework, Buisman-Henriksen and Heisenberg revisited the relativistic transformations of length, momentum, and energy in special relativity and found that the relativistic transformations of length and momentum can be achieved with minimal error when the uncertainty principle is satisfied.  This letter provides an in-depth analysis of this concept, focusing on its application to the transformations of length, momentum, and energy under Galilean and Lorentz transformations.  The results demonstrate that the error in length transformations is solely dependent on the uncertainty of the Lorentz gamma factor, whereas the error in momentum transformations is directly linked to the uncertainty of the momentum itself.  Conversely, the energy transformation exhibits an exceptional behavior in that the error in energy is directly related to the transformation of length and momentum.  These findings are further exemplified by considering different states of matter, including the human body, proton, electron, and neutron, highlighting the practical implications of this concept for the conversion processes between rest frame and the laboratory frame.  Furthermore, the findings also demonstrate that the error in length transformations can be compensated for by moving at a speed slightly less than the speed of light, thereby providing new insights into the relationships between length, momentum, energy, and speed.  These insights are also applicable to the Lorentz transformations.  Ultimately, the results show that the error in Galilean length transformations can be corrected to the ambiguity limit by choosing an appropriate state of matter, whereas the error in length transformations under Lorentz transformations can be brought in line with the ambiguity limit, but cannot be corrected to the ambiguity limit itself due to the constraint imposed by the Lorentz transformations of length and momentum. The concept of the hyperbola plays a central role in this matter.  The hyperbola may be looked upon as a kind of a quantum of action.  The results presented here may have potential implications for our understanding of quantum geometry and the properties of quantum black holes. In multitasking management, we're dealing with an scheduling problem where multiple tasks can be executed concurrently and have distinct deadlines. Some programming languages allow for task creation through a single operation, but at a basic level, tasks are separate entities with unique code execution paths. This study investigates the cooperation potential in multitasking management when tasks share computation, by utilizing a framework that facilitates task convergence and allows for simultaneous execution. Theoretical calculations demonstrate how to implement the shared computation framework, leading to a new model called the multitasking management with shared computation (MMSC) model. Theoretical analyses were conducted to establish the conditions for the creation of cooperation, the amount of cooperation, and the schedulability of tasks under fixed priority (FP) and dynamic priority (DP) scheduling algorithms. The study also introduces a cooperation management strategy to manage cooperation and proves the closed-loop nature of the system. The study also introduces heuristics for setting deadlines to ensure improved system performance. The study's experimental results validate the theoretical findings and provide insights into the practical use of cooperation in multitasking management. A comparison with existing work showed that shared computation can lead to improved system performance compared to previous methods. This paper examines the dynamics of a one-legged walking and jumping system on deformable ground. To account for the changes in terrain resistance and the resultant forces exerted on the system, we employ a simplified model of ground behavior. Using the pole-vector method, we derive an analytical model for the system's stability and motion, focusing on the effects of stance phase changes and ground properties on one-legged locomotion. To extend our analytical model to more realistic scenarios, we develop a numerical simulation framework. However, using this framework reveals that utilizing simple control strategies can be insufficient to overcome complex challenges in unstable environments. To address these limitations, we propose a novel control strategy that incorporates learning and feedback adjustments, demonstrating its efficacy in stabilizing the system's motion through simulation results. Moreover, we explore the system's capability to exhibit diverse gaits through incremental authority transfers over time. To ensure the system's practicality, we optimize its control parameters using a genetic algorithm. To validate our model and results, we also present experimental findings on a physical one-legged jumping robot called NINJA, showing agreement between simulated and real-world data. By achieving stable long-term operation, our approach enables extended flight times for the jumping robot. To achieve the system's ultimate goal of dynamic movement, we use the simulated tool to create and test various flight control strategies. Ultimately, the system achieves the ability to perform a 30% more efficient forward flight compared to gliding. The entire process from modeling to optimization takes around 30 hours, encompassing all time-consuming tasks, including genetic algorithm iterations and genetic evolution. The proposed control strategy also allows the system to execute the desired motions smoothly and accurately, reflecting the importance of optimized control parameters for achieving representative gaits in the system. Our approach enables the system to surpass the existing state-of-the-art by accomplishing tasks at a 10% higher level of performance. Additionally, the system's capability to adapt and respond effectively to changing resistance conditions gives rise to the potential for agile and rapid-controlled flight in the future. The accompanying movie depicts the system's dynamics and the results of the experiments. The system's source code, including the modeling, simulation, and control strategy, is publicly available at the specified repository, used in conjunction with the reported findings. The related physical robot's source code and 3D model are hosted on the Git repository as well. The research was supported by the grant number 152 052 305 from the Russian Science Foundation. The underlying data for the graphical figures in the paper can be accessed through the provided DOI.

The growing IoT landscape is characterized by significant scale, density, and dispersal. As these devices increasingly rely on software-based services, they generate a substantial amount of network traffic. Consequently, IoT systems need upgrade mechanisms that are not only flexible and efficient but also highly available and resilient to failure. One such mechanism is mesh network-based IoT software upgrades, which has garnered considerable interest. Nonetheless, evaluating this approach at the large scale and density found in IoT is a significant challenge. In our research, we evaluate the feasibility of carrying out software upgrades in high-density IoT settings using 18,000 mesh-based routers by controlling the network traffic and introducing controlled failures into the device pool. Our evaluation reveals that IoT software upgrades are not only technically feasible but also relatively swift and resilient to failure. In particular, we found that: (1) only 2% of mesh devices experience upgrade issues, with the majority of problems stemming from controlled failures; (2) the upgrade process is highly available, with zero-effect on 95% of meshes; (3) the upgrade process is remarkably fast for the large pool of devices involved; and (4) the network is largely unaffected by the upgrade process, with only a minimal increase in QoS. Our study not only investigates the large-scale feasibility of IoT software upgrades but also provides the necessary empirical evidence to support the deployment of this approach in real-world IoT settings. Moreover, our evaluation showcases a novel, high-density mesh network testing platform that allows for the controlled experimentation and testing of IoT features in densely populated urban environments. The study's findings have significant implications for a range of IoT deployment scenarios, encompassing the upgrade of critical IoT systems, deployment strategies for IoT services, and design choices for IoT software. Our research offers valuable insights into the development of large-scale IoT systems by contributing to the reliability and efficiency of software upgrades, a process which underpins the overall dependability of these complex systems. In doing so, we open up a range of promising research avenues related to the development of large-scale IoT systems, encompassing cutting-edge technologies like IoT upgrades, network traffic management, and related topics. During the critical point, where localization transitions occur, the fractal dimensions of eigenstates change continuously, correlating with critical exponents derived from the scaling of the propagator's local average as a function of system size and convergence rate. In real-world operations, military and law enforcement personnel frequently encounter complex situations involving multiple critical objectives. To effectively accomplish these tasks, they need to gather relevant information about each objective, often generating a substantial amount of irrelevant data that hinders decision-making progress and needs to be efficiently eliminated. This research defines the problem of interacting with information to achieve objectives within a specified budget as a variant of decision-making known as the k-search problem. To address this issue, we developed two cost-effective algorithms based on the principles of entropy and proximity, demonstrated in experiments that outperform existing approaches under various budget constraints and multiple objective scenarios. The findings also reveal that the underlying characteristics of the resulting information distributions contribute to successful goal achievement. The implementation of these algorithms, named info-k, is currently available online. The results of our studies demonstrate that, with limited interactions, the entropy-based algorithm delivers superior performance, while the proximity-based algorithm excels in high-resource environments. We have further enhanced the entropy-based algorithm to prioritize the most crucial objectives and developed a variant with improved results in multiple objective scenarios. We anticipate that these developments will contribute to goal-oriented information gathering in real-world applications. The online repository for the work, including the code and results of the experiments, can be found at https://github/com-arg-info-k/). The related demonstration can be found at https://info-k-demo.com). Highly accurate quantum machine learning algorithms are being developed to tackle complex classical problems.  Unlike their classical counterparts, these quantum algorithms are forced to operate in a completely controlled environment, making them vulnerable to unexpected disruptions and challenging to adapt to changes in their surroundings.  Our investigation focuses on the ability of quantum classifiers to identify instances of disease based on magnetic resonance images when subjected to various disturbances and adverse conditions.  Our results show that even the smallest uncertainty can significantly impact the performance of these quantum classifiers, with the introduction of disturbance introducing unexpected errors and reducing their effectiveness by up to 95%.  Our study also demonstrates that quantum classifiers are unable to defend themselves against purposefully constructed adverse conditions known as smart attacks, with the difficulty of detecting these conditions scaling exponentially.  To mitigate these limitations, we propose strategies that enable quantum classifiers to better withstand disruptions and adverse conditions, including the use of bootstrapping techniques and adjustments to the training process.  Our findings highlight the importance of addressing these limitations in order to fully leverage the potential of quantum artificial intelligence.  Our work includes multiple experimental and theoretical trials supporting the validity of our conclusions.  The associated code is available at https://github.com/alexkic/disease_classification_QML. A comprehensive formal model for time-sensitive and restricted multi-agent planning has been introduced, taking into account a well-established theoretical framework for evaluating the validity of plan representations and a proven approach for checking consistency within those representations. By applying this established method, the model's planning domain syntax can be fully substantiated, ensuring the formality and accuracy of subsequent validation processes for generating plans. Unfortunately, the traditional model is ineffectual in describing certain sophisticated planning scenarios, such as domains with restricted agents' actions and multi-agent coordination, as they necessitate incorporating temporal relationships and agent interactions into the model. Additionally, the initial version of time-sensitive and restricted multi-agent planning with temporal relationships and agent interactions does not allow for a complete and rigorous validation of plan representations, resulting in only limited conditions being applicable for verification. However, by integrating temporal logic for defining agents' perspectives and domain characteristics, the complete and rigorous validation of plan representations for the extended planning model has been achieved. Furthermore, the planning process within this extended model can also be thoroughly validated and justified. A detailed and step-by-step explanation of the key concepts, including the formal model and subsequent validation processes, is presented, utilizing clear and concise language to ensure the definition and interpretation of these concepts are uncomplicated and unambiguous. Some models, like the growth models studied here, attempt to forecast future energy development by projecting key characteristics of energy providing and using devices under given constraints.  Although previous models have been shown to accurately predict the growth of specific energy-related variables, the influence of individual model parameters on model outcomes remains unclear.  Using established growth models as the foundation, this study employs an algorithm to determine the optimal parameter values that minimize discrepancies between model predictions and real-world data.  With a focus on models involving two variables, namely energy-converting and energy-storing technology, the results indicate that the best-fitting models are highly susceptible to changes in model parameters, particularly those related to technology advancements in the underlying components.  Notably, the best-fitting models show nearly infinite precision when rounded to two significant figures, suggesting that small changes in model parameters can yield significantly better fit outcomes.  Furthermore, the findings indicate that as the growth models mature and look further into the future, their parameter sensitivity increases, potentiating slight adjustments to these parameters based on current market conditions to accurately forecast future growth.  Ultimately, this study reveals that high precision in modeling does not necessarily translate to high accuracy, as the best-fitting models are often overly complex and therefore flawed.  As a result, this study offers recommendations for accurately assessing and presenting model outcomes, taking into account real-world data and the economic feasibility of the projected technologies.  In doing so, the study provides essential insights for model refinement and offers a clear framework for evaluating growth models in the field of energy system growth modeling.  Specifically, the study provides a new metric, the Model Prediction Index (MPI), which enables model outcomes to be rigorously assessed and compares them to real-world data.  With the MPI, the study demonstrates that even slightly biased models can still provide highly accurate forecasts of future growth, thereby offering valuable practical insights.  Furthermore, the study reveals that there is a natural equilibrium among models that accurately forecast the growth of specific energy-related variables, suggesting that such models tend to converge and become highly consistent as the growth models mature and look further into the future.  In doing so, the study provides a clear explanation for this phenomenon and shows that the equilibrium among models is influenced by the underlying components involved. This paper presents a data-driven approach to conceptualising search phrases through a retrieval-based framework, aiming to expand existing concept dictionaries by associating defined concepts with unlabelled search phrases. Despite the inherent subjectivity of concepts and search phrases, we establish a viable comparison framework through sentence embeddings and propose a robust retrieval-based model called STRICT that adapts to the inherent variability between concepts and search phrases. The proposed method is evaluated on a substantial dataset and outperforms existing baseline models made of sequential models. Furthermore, we highlight the practical applications of this approach in concept placement and demonstrate its potential in concept-driven search and recommendation tasks. The proposed framework, including source code and accompanying dataset, is available for further exploration at https://github.com/thesmithy/stRICT. Extensive experiments and findings are documented on the website at https://thesmithy.github.io/stRICT. The conceptualised search phrases are compiled into a comprehensive dataset at https://concept-earch.github.io. The associated application, Concept Search Phrase, is accessible via https://concept-earch.github.io/search/. Furthermore, users are encouraged to generate concept definitions and associate them with search phrases on the crowdsourcing platform https://thesmithy.github.io/stRICThedge/. The research demonstrates that the proposed approach is adaptable to varying concept and search phrase embeddings, paving the way for future crowdsourcing-inspired concept expansions. The research highlights the practical implications of this approach in concept placement and search operations, which may be limited by existing concept definitions. The study also demonstrates the potential benefits and drawbacks of data-driven concept expansions. The research could be extended by exploring the feasibility of search phrase evaluations in the context of transfer learning, noise reduction, and pseudo-labels. The potential applications of this approach in concept-driven search and recommendation tasks are not limited to this study and can be extended to other domains, potentially requiring adaptations for regularisation, demodulation, and fairness. The research also raises important ethical considerations for data-driven concept creations and search operations. The proposed framework is compatible with other concept creation methods and can be used in combination with existing approaches, suggesting novel fusion techniques as possible directions for future research. The Collatz Conjecture is a mathematical hypothesis that has withstood testing for over 80 years, having been proven true for nearly all numbers within its realm, with the exception of a set of unproven statements referring to sequences of 2 and 5. This hypothesis suggests that if a number is subjected to a series of operations - specifically, a specific sequence involving doubling the number and replacing it with the number's half - it will ultimately reach 1. While this conjecture has been largely confirmed through its wide-reaching applications and the success of many supporting theorems, a definitive proof or contradiction remains pending, with the conjecture continuing to captivate mathematicians' interest. Historically, this problem has been proposed by David Collatz in 1937 and has since become one of the most prominent unsolved problems in the field of pure mathematics. This paper, titled "Collatz Conjecture," provides an in-depth examination of the conjecture itself, along with the theoretical foundations and supporting theorems underlying our work. We have also successfully applied computational methods to further test and validate the conjecture for an extensive range of natural numbers, with our software and findings being made publicly accessible for download at the specified URL. While our findings contribute nothing new to the body of known work supporting the conjecture, our work serves as an added affirmation of its validity and the necessity of a definitive proof or contradiction. We have specifically focused on expanding the known applications of the conjecture itself, rather than presenting new theorems related to the conjecture, in an effort to more thoroughly establish the conjecture's significance and relevance to the field of pure mathematics. This paper's comprehensive nature is intended to serve as a single, in-depth resource providing an extensive examination of the conjecture and the theoretical supports underlying our work, with the conjecture's potential applications and the conjecture itself being made accessible to readers who may be new to the subject. We have also included a related problem, the Odd 3n+1 Conjecture, in an effort to more thoroughly explore and explain the nature of the conjecture and its broader implications. While our related problem is not an integral component of the conjecture itself, it does serve to more effectively demonstrate certain properties and the conjecture's applicability to related sequences, with the problem also being an additive extension of the original conjecture. In various STEM fields such as physics, engineering, and mathematics, there are two main types of documents - instructional and research-based. Differentiating between these document categories is essential for understanding the preferred presentation of information, with instructional documents requiring conceptual explanations, and research documents needing evidence from experiments. Previous studies attempted to distinguish between the two document types based on linguistic features, but their approaches have been limited by ignoring the underlying structure of the text and relying solely on surface-level words. Considering that mathematical concepts play a crucial role in both instructional and research documents, we propose a method that combines the presence of both general and domain-specific mathematical entities with their connections to determine document categories effectively. The proposed approach has been tested and validated on a combined corpus of educational and research texts in physics, and the results suggest that incorporating the relationships between the two types of mathematical entities can improve document categorization. Furthermore, our study also highlights the need for a more comprehensive understanding of the organizational patterns in the 'why' research domain, where mathematical entities play a pivotal role. The various benchmarks and analysis tools used in this study are accessible through an open-source repository at https://github.com/aliyanm7/MATH_Categorization. The research dataset is publicly accessible at https://www.dropbox.com/s/a7n9k0k0qk0ln0/CORPORA.zip. The implemented method has achieved an overall accuracy of 66.6% with a 65.9% accuracy in instructional documents and 66.5% in research documents. Although the results are still inferior to the state-of-the-art performance of 72.1% achieved by the benchmark model, our method demonstrates the potential of combining the presence of mathematical entities with their connections to improve document categorization in STEM fields. The research findings indicate that further development of organizational patterns in the 'what' research domain could greatly contribute to understanding the underlying structure of the text and may complement current document categorization approaches. The research was conducted to answer the query 'How can we utilize the organizational structure of the 'what' research domain as well as the underlying structure of the text to demonstrate the role of mathematical entities in document categorization in STEM?' Self-referential theories of reliable knowledge make knowledge ascriptions dependent on the speaker's own knowledge, creating a recursive problem when applied to knowledge claims about matching (one's knowledge being matched by another's knowledge). We introduce a new solution to this challenge that avoids circularity by distinguishing between direct and indirect reports. This distinction led us to the proposal of 'indexical reliability', where certain situations, including matching claims, are considered reliable only if the speaker has first-hand experience describing them. Our analysis also addresses challenges related to generalisation, anchors and negative statements, offering novel explanations for familiar phenomena through this new lens. Ultimately, the new theory provides fresh insights into the nature of matching and makes novel predictions based on the distinction between direct and indirect reports. A specific empirical demonstration of this distinction can be seen in the case of 'know that'- and 'know how'-ascriptions. The new theory is tested against a range of linguistic data, including speaker intuition and meaning judgment. The most significant finding from our analysis is that the distinction between direct and indirect reports gives rise to a visible 'indexicality shift' in matching claims, revealing an underlying structure to the matching relation. The theory's applicability extends beyond the domain of knowledge ascriptions, encompassing other epistemic logic formulas such as belief claims. Possible extensions of our analysis to the realms of attitude and modality are also explored. The entire project is made accessible through an accompanying Jupyter notebook at github.com. The analysis challenges previous work on matching, including Peacocke (2004), and offers an alternative to the dominant approach to the matching problem, differing significantly from the recent solution proposed by Rabern (2020). Furthermore, our analysis diverges from the discussions found in the recent publications by J. Genzler, M. Peters and S. Rabern in 2019. Our analysis also provides an opposing view to the solution offered by Hand (2018) on the indexing approach to the matching problem, although, interestingly enough, our analysis shares some similarities with the solution provided by S. Yaghi in 2018. Ultimately, our analysis provides an original and standalone contribution to the existing epistemological discussion on the nature of matching between knowledge states. The empirical significance of our work is expected to invite further research, specifically a large-scale experiment designed to confirm the distinction between direct and indirect reports that underpins our analysis, particularly the indexicality shift in matching claims. Existing evaluation metrics for summarization models are limited in several ways:
\emph{(1)} they do not consider what the model is actually doing -- how well the summary's meaning aligns with the original text's meaning? \emph{(2)} they do not assess whether the summary provides new information not found in the original text. To address these issues, a new cross-encoder architecture, called SummScore, is proposed to evaluate summarization models in a more comprehensive manner. Cross-encoder models, like BERT, can capture semantic meaning by paying attention to all words in the input, making them ideal for analyzing summaries. A large corpus of 999 summaries from the Wikipedia dataset was used to train SummScore, allowing it to assess the performance of other popular summarization models. The results show that SummScore outperforms existing metrics in several aspects: it can tell the difference between high and low quality summaries with 95\% accuracy, it can identify originals and non-originals with 91\% accuracy, and it can identify abstractive and selective summaries with 87\% and 85\% accuracy respectively. To promote its use, SummScore is made available as a web tool. Furthermore, it's shown that by combining SummScore with other existing metrics, a more accurate picture of the model's performance can be achieved, highlighting their collaborative potential in assessing summarization models' capabilities. Ultimately, SummScore's extensive evaluation of the models enables prioritization of the development and refinement of those that perform the most complex tasks -- generating the most informative summaries with the most accurate meaning. To facilitate adoption, SummScore's code is shared publicly on GitHub and I'd be delighted to share any of the pre-trained models for other use cases. Furthermore, a demonstration of SummScore is available through this Colab notebook. To facilitate discussions, a dedicated Google Forum is established where concerns and suggestions can be shared. By leveraging SummScore, it's anticipated that it can streamline the detection and rectification of summarization tasks' shortcomings, ultimately leading to the advancement of the field's progress. Despite significant advancements in this area, existing integration frameworks are often plagued by inaccuracies, inconsistencies, and computational bottlenecks. In response, we introduce BEVFusion - a novel, adaptable approach for fusing LiDAR and camera data, characterized by simplicity, robustness, and efficiency. By leveraging beam representations in a beam-view feature, we propose an aggregate method that provides superior overall performance and can withstand component failures. To test the effectiveness of our framework, we develop the Beacon Dataset - a comprehensive collection of 3D scene data created through integrations of LiDAR and cameras. As demonstrated by our experiments using widely utilized 3D detection models, our framework surpasses existing integration frameworks and 3D detection models in terms of overall performance.
