We suggest that the hydrodynamic representation of the quantum vacuum of a thermal bath may induce turbulence in the dissipation range of a fluid. This concept is grounded in the stochastic hydrodynamics of the Bogoliubov theory, which describes a weakly-interactive boson gas in terms of the fluid's velocity field and its fluctuations. Given that the thermal disturbance introduces random changes into this fluctuation field at a rate influenced by temperature and wavenumber, it can cause the fluid's velocity field to deviate randomly within local areas of the fluid. As this random deviation propagates at the speed of sound, it can give rise to high-frequency fluctuations within the dissipation range, thus providing an alternative explanation for the scaling laws of turbulent flows. We examine and support this idea through calculations and analyses of liquid turbulence and quantum fluids such as helium-4 and superfluid helium-3, also considering the potential implications of the thermal disturbance on the statistical properties of turbulent velocity fields. Our findings suggest that the average energy density at scale 'k' in a turbulent fluid is proportional to 'k' to the '-5/3' power, consistent with the theoretical expectations and experimental observations in various turbulent fluids. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the average square of random deviation associated with the stochastic hydrodynamics in the vicinity of 'k' follows the 'k''(-3)] power law, contributing significantly to the statistical properties of turbulent flow. This idea of turbulence in terms of thermal disturbance may open up novel avenues in the study of turbulent dynamics, allowing for a deeper understanding of the quantum fluid dynamics and possibly providing answers to longstanding problems in the field of turbulence research. Moreover, the thermal disturbance concept has the potential to address fundamental questions in geophysical, biomedical, and other fields of study where cold thermal baths play a crucial role. Finally, the thermal disturbance idea can serve as a link between microscopic quantum dynamics and macroscopic turbulent flow, highlighting the significance of the quantum vacuum as a thermal bath in the understanding of turbulent dynamics. The idea presented here is an extension of our earlier work, which was published in the 'Chaos, Solitons and Fractals' journal in 2021, titled 'Low-entropic fractality in quantum fluid turbulence.' The phenomenon of laser-induced modulation diffraction (LIMD) in liquids, which is characterized by the formation of complex, controlled diffraction patterns through modulated laser beams, has significant applications in optics and photonics. Recent studies of LIMD in liquids have revealed various unusual patterns, such as spots, grids, rings, and roses, brought into harmony with the prediction by Scahmndt's equation. Despite this, the underlying thermal effects causing the observed grid patterns remain poorly understood. In our study, we provide a detailed numerical representation of the thermal profiles generated by laser interaction with the liquid, thereby offering insights into the intricate multi- and singularities present within. Through our investigation, we demonstrate that the observed grid patterns result from the superimposition of phase gratings produced by harmonic components, taking into account their respective decays. Utilizing our analysis, we are able to identify the effective modulation depth of the laser beam as well as determine the influence of the reference beam's position and focus. Ultimately, our research and findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the phase-grating formation in liquids, which can be utilized for the development of LIMD techniques in both theoretical and applied settings. This work is intended to provide a foundational knowledge for individuals seeking to implement LIMD methods in their own work, including the exploration of phase grating applications and grid pattern formations. In the design process, the integration of interactive tools is particularly significant due to their direct connection to customer needs and design goals. However, designing interfaces for designing designs is an especially demanding task, as it requires navigating the double layer of abstraction. One such challenge is reaching a stable conclusion regarding the most effective design, which can be described as a design optimization problem. This study focuses on visual design optimization, where an active user involves AI in designing elements based on specific requirements. In the context of generating design conversations, the AI makes suggestions and the user considers these options to form a cooperative strategy in an iterative process. From a theoretical perspective, we classify different patterns of design conversations, classifying them and predicting their likelihood based on the description of the problem and the proposed design, and found that concluding design options based on human judgment is the most common pattern. Additionally, we observed that humans generally agree with each other and that the quality of design suggestions is positively correlated with the model's capacity for design creativity. From a practical perspective, we developed a CONVERGENCE algorithm with a 90% likelihood for leading to design convergence and useful results. Finally, based on our analysis of the frequency and duration of design conversations in a real-world application, we identified an opportunity to further develop the algorithm to enhance design outcomes. Experiments conducted on an autoencoder revealed that it is possible to improve the quality of design suggestions to meet the needs of users who value such results. This study validates the potential for natural language driven mining of design conversations and provides a foundation for future development in this area. In a groundbreaking achievement, scientists have demonstrated the theoretical production of top and bottom quark pairs in high-energy proton collisions through the incorporation of open strings. This pioneering approach deviates from traditional string models utilizing Regge physics, emphasizing a non-resonant mechanism instead. Employing a semi-classical framework with a focus on hard scattering interactions, they observed prominent quark pair production in strings exhibiting rapidity separation. This process was identified as an exceptional example of non-relativistic string dynamics leading to irreducible, non-resonant production of top and bottom quark pairs. Building upon this concept, they formulated a new distribution function for top and bottom quarks to facilitate further investigation into the string theory manifestation of associated quark pair production in high-energy collisions. This research has generated considerable interest among theorists in the string theory community. Furthermore, it provides an innovative illustration of singular production in high-energy collisions of heavy quark pairs through the incorporation of open strings. Associated production in this context refers to the simultaneous creation of heavy quark pairs characterized by distinct rapidity values, large separation, and negative signs of the squared transverse momentum. This production mechanism is distinguished from regular processes, such as $t \bar t$ or $\rm{b \bar b}$ pairs, by the significant overlap of their distribution functions. We have thus proposed a Meta-tuning Strategy to further optimize these pre-trained models for maximum performance on these pre-assembled datasets.  This is achieved by leveraging the Exascale processing power of modern GPUs to conduct a large-scale grid search of the many possible prompts and data configurations, selecting the one that yields the highest performance score. Natural Language Processing tasks are unsuccessful when performed by systems with no prior knowledge of the world, implying that they need to rely on pre-existing information. However, instead of using general knowledge bases, advances in machine learning suggest that task-specific data can provide sufficient insight into human cognition. This study examines how little data is required for successful interpretation in the low-data regime. We developed a framework for representing semantic interpretations that is grounded in psychological theories and adaptable to various visual grounding tasks. Furthermore, our interpreter is unique because it avoids relying on visual recognition tools. We evaluated our approach on a complex understanding task - referring to images with common nouns - and successfully adapted a human-like language generation system with as few as 50 example sentences per class. We also discovered that incorporating task-specific biases and multi-modal interactions significantly enhanced performance, even when training with the smallest datasets. Overall, our results indicate that systems without prior knowledge can outperform human-level performance by leveraging data-driven methods of learning and naturalized semantic interpretation. These methods are particularly effective because they are adaptable to various knowledge domains and can be guided by intuitive principles. Given that our smallest dataset consisted of only 50 sentence pairs, our approach may hold the key to resolving the twin challenges of understanding and interpreting human cognition and achieving a breakthrough in Artificial Intelligence. Finally, our code is publicly available for anyone to access and utilize. We actively sought to eliminate biases in our evaluation and made a significant effort to explain our approach in a clear and transparent manner. We discovered that our system's ability to learn from data could be expanded if we could identify and suppress the underlying biases inherent in all language generation methods. However, our research also raises important ethical considerations, warning that natural language generation systems can perpetuate existing prejudices if the biases in the training data are retained. To address these concerns, we developed a simple technique for removing biases from our approach and conducted an in-depth analysis of the challenges involved in natural language processing and machine learning. We hope that our findings and contributions inspire further research in these fields and contribute to the ongoing discussion about the growing importance of AI in society. Ultimately, our study demonstrates that semantic interpretation can be successfully achieved even when systems have no prior knowledge of the world by relying on task-specific data and naturalized machine learning systems. Unlike other medium-strength magnetic field stars, HD58260's radial field fluctuations do not diminish as the collection of spectral lines increases, but instead, its radial field field strength appears to grow as a result of an average of weaker, narrower-base spectral lines. Knowledge graph completion has become a crucial task in recent years. Many existing studies have focused on completing static graphs, but static graphs are insufficient for capturing dynamic relationships found in temporal knowledge graphs. Previous approaches to completing temporal knowledge graphs often employ a multi-step, resource-intensive process, requiring numerous iterations to find a suitable solution. This method is particularly efficient when dealing with localized search areas but becomes impractical in larger graphs. In contrast, utilizing fixed models for connection prediction yields superior results by constraining possible solutions, thereby improving connection accuracy and efficiency. Building upon this concept, our study introduces an innovative method for completing temporal knowledge graphs, incorporating a constraint that utilizes fixed models to enrich graph representations and optimize multi-hop jump algorithms, ultimately leading to more accurate results. The framework's versatility allows for integration with multiple fixed model structures. Our experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, showcasing its potential as a benchmark for evaluating temporal knowledge graph completion. Wildfires pose a significant threat to global ecosystems and human societies, and their visualization is crucial for effective management and emergency planning. Advanced technology has improved satellite imagery, enabling more detailed observations of fires. However, combining visible and infrared images of fires presents several challenges, including differing resolutions and alignment issues. Existing fusion techniques have been successful in boosting visualization quality, but their capacity to maintain accuracy is limited due to the complexity of aligning co-registered images. In response to these challenges, we developed a novel FIRe-GAN model that utilizes a new type of information flow. By integrating deep learning and attention-based guidance, FIre-GAN synthesizes and aligns fire visuals more accurately and efficiently. Our evaluations of FIre-GAN against competing frequency modulation (FM) radio modulation techniques and other state-of-the-art methods have demonstrated its superior performance in producing high-quality, aligned fire visuals. Additionally, we created an interactive web platform using FIre-GAN for the public to view wildfire visuals. This platform has the potential to enhance public safety and safety emergency planning, and its source code is available for immediate use. Our research makes the following contributions to the field: it presents an innovative, complex neural network architecture for the integration of wildfire visuals; it introduces an efficient, trainable process that is more cost-effective and accurate than other state-of-the-art methods; it develops source code with a simple, easy-to-use interface for interactive visualization, which is currently unique in the scientific community. We've developed a straightforward compartmental model for the COVID-19 pandemic 
which takes into account distinct vulnerable groups within the population, 
enabling the calculation of tailored intervention strategies to minimize 
overall mortality and individual subgroup mortality. This model also 
accounts for the effect of testing efficiency on mortality metrics. What 
matters is not just $R_0$, but how the disease spreads among and within distinct 
groups, influenced by their age distribution and the presence of widespread 
testing. These findings are substantiated by statistical analysis of COVID-19 
death data in the United States. We use this model to explore mortality reductions 
worth considering in real-world scenarios. Finally, some potential extensions 
of this model are discussed. 

Our model results show that, in the context of the United States, 
unrestricted spread of the virus would ultimately claim around 1.47 million lives, 
and that widespread testing worth considering would lower this total to 1.47-1.53 
million fatalities. 

There are several possible expansions of this model. Firstly, incorporating 
testing, contact tracing, isolation, and other pandemic mitigation measures 
exposed to errors. Also, incorporating variables related to comorbidities would 
be a considerable expansion. This model could also explore the impact of vaccination 
efficiency, focusing not just on preventing infections but also with preventing 
transmission, and could be used to explore long-term virus behavior scenarios. 
Lastly, incorporating climate-related factors that might impact human movement 
and virus transmission would be a considerable expansion. 

When discussing these expansions with epidemiologists, it becomes clear that 
incorporating comorbidities, and the impact of climate on human movement and 
virus transmission, would be the most significant additions to this model. 

It's also clear that each expansion adds significant complexity to the model. 
Therefore, any expansions should be motivated by a solid understanding of their 
individual and combined impacts. 

In order to decide which expansions to implement, a sequential process can be 
followed. First, begin by adding the expansion with the greatest impact, then 
evaluate the need for further expansions by determining if there are other 
significant impacts left unaddressed. 

The model results presented serve as a starting point for this process, 
providing initial insights into various potential expansions. 

Ultimately, any expansions should be guided by the principle that they 
improve our understanding of their effects, not their simplicity. 

And, as always, the devil is in the details.

A mathematical study on stick-slip oscillations in systems governed by Coulomb friction is conducted. The system's motion is analyzed through a singularly perturbed analysis, considering a characteristic time span: (i) a long-time regime where persistent homoclinic trajectories dominate, leading to oscillatory behavior, and (ii) a shorter time regime where non-sticky, convergent trajectories of small amplitude emerge from these homoclinic structures. The study reveals the system's dynamic response to varying parameters as a smooth transition in the long-time regime from stick-slip to smooth, periodic motion. The research develops asymptotic solutions for both regimes and investigates the system's behavior during the sticking phase, evaluating its dynamic response to parameter changes. The study also demonstrates that the sticking phase can significantly impact the system's motion, influencing its trajectory and computational stability assessment when accounting for Coulomb friction versus using viscous friction in its place. Furthermore, system designers have the flexibility to tailor the system's dynamics through the choice of parameters, allowing for the optimization of the system's motion for desired outcomes. As an example, a force-generation system is analyzed, with the study demonstrating the feasibility of using Coulomb friction-based systems to produce oscillating motion if smooth motion is not achievable. The study's findings on the system's behavior during the sticking phase have also contributed to a new understanding of the system's convergence properties when using Coulomb friction versus viscous friction in its model. The study's results reveal the presence of conjugate pairs of unstable limit cycles, indicating that the system's motion can exhibit persistent, long-time existence of these limit cycles, unlike in systems with viscous friction where such behavior is generally absent. Consequently, system designers should implement certain feedback adjustments to the system to increase its convergence towards asymptotic states, particularly when using Coulomb friction in its model. The study's results on the system's behavior during the sticking phase and convergence have also been further quantified through numerical simulations, analyzing the system's behavior during the sticking phase and assessing its convergence properties in a comprehensive manner. We focus on improving the performance of Bellman Risk Management (BRM) in addressing high-dimensional reinforcement learning tasks by identifying significant subspaces within high-dimensional observation spaces and applying BRM to them. First, we represent the high-dimensional observations as graphs and find the optimal subgraphs by calculating the risk associated with each subgraph as a whole system and then reducing it into a series of more manageable local subproblems. This approach allows us to efficiently use both theoretical and practical approximations to reduce computational complexity and facilitate rapid exploration within the subgraphs by selectively choosing action sequences. We have successfully tested our method on a variety of complex problems, including the evaluation of large-scale dynamic systems and the analysis of high-dimensional video footage in an autonomous drone navigation task, resulting in noticeable performance enhancements. We have also provided empirical evidence demonstrating that our algorithm is capable of finding the most adapted subgraphs from a wide range of possibilities, underscoring the significance of subgraph search in BRM. Importantly, our method remains compatible with BRM-based reinforcement learning techniques and extends their applicability to a broader scope of tasks involving complex high-dimensional interaction settings. The associated software is publicly available at https://github.com/laurenceturetz/Profound-BRM. Our study is an important step towards enabling BRM algorithms to effectively tackle a wide array of challenging reinforcement learning tasks involving intricate temporal and spatial interrelations. As a result, we propose the name "Profound Bellman Risk Management" for our developed algorithm. Furthermore, we plan to contribute the development of graph search algorithms as a new chapter in the recent Handbook of Reinforcement Learning. This chapter serves as a comprehensive reference on the fundamental concepts, properties, and applications of Bellman convergence in reinforcement learning. We are committed to sharing the updated version with our readers upon its completion. Our method's practical implementation is another key contribution as it has been successfully tested on the LIGONN drone, an autonomous system with 240 sensors, as well as the LIGOT car, an autonomous vehicle equipped with 7 sensors, both designed by Christof Krähenbühel and Jüri Petus. In particular, we have successfully applied the search algorithm to estimate the dynamic behavior of a large commercial jet aircraft, a task that had previously been considered intractable. Notably, the used code is interleave with the one written by another researcher, Alexey Dosovitskiy. We have also participated in the new AI sports league, LAIAA, as described in a related paper.

One major challenge in explaining recommender systems output lies in uncovering the real intentions behind users' historical behavior. This is made harder by the fact that a single user can have multiple motivations for viewing or interacting with recommended items. While some approaches focus on modeling item representation and user preferences as a whole, we developed a new framework called Hidden User Intent (HUI) that tackles the problem by modeling user intentions as a set of structured concepts. This framework provides a dynamic system for exploring and predicting user interactions, and we designed it specifically with sequential recommendation in mind. Our framework effectively extracts and captures the varied intent patterns from user data and simultaneously uses these intent models to forecast interactions. We implemented HUI using an innovative technique that integrates a concept extractor with a collector, and we combined the results with a collaborative filtering model. Our experiments with Amazon datasets revealed HUI to be superior in terms of predicting next items, and it successfully extracted distinct intent patterns at different levels, such as item, sub-category and category levels. Additionally, we found that HUI produced better results when compared to an explicit tagging system, and it effectively adapted its intent models to accommodate changes in user behavior over time. Overall, our research demonstrated the potential of uncovering complex user intentions at varying levels, and we found that HUI is a useful system for explaining and monitoring user behavior over time. One of its key capabilities is providing ex-post explanations for items in the recommended list, and recovering abandoned user intentions when the system fails to predict the next item correctly. Finally, our research revealed that HUI's intent models can be applied in various applications, like suggesting related items, predicting item popularity and developing marketing strategies. As a result, we hope that HUI motivates the development of more advanced explanation techniques for uncovering the real motivations behind users' historical behavior. We are releasing the code and data for HUI, and it's available on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/Mayx/Hidden-User-Intent. We also created a demonstration video of our approach, and it can be accessed at http://youtu.be/video. For the sake of convenience, we have made the related data and the Amazon datasets used in our research available via this download link: http://mayx.io/data. Furthermore, we have made the developed techniques as platform-independent as possible, and it runs smoothly on platforms such as Windows, Linux and macOS. The properties of the solvable double confluent Heun equation are examined, including its derivation, fundamental properties of its solutions, and associated invariant spaces within the $sl_2(\mathbb{C})$ Lie algebra. Furthermore, this equation is shown to be an unfolding of a special universal form, which has significant applications in Lie theory, especially through the process of generalization and the concept of $sl_2(\mathbb{C})$-module unfolding. The latter method has its roots in the work of G. Segal, though it is there that the concept was referred to as 'generalization'. Here, its connection to the 'uncoupling' method is outlined in detail, but it's worth noting that the work of C. Freyre and M. Rodriguez in 2014 was the first to equate 'generalization' with the process of removing couplings in a representation. The current work builds upon this notion by providing a perspective that combines, in a rather non-obvious way, the 'uncoupling' and 'folding' methods. The equation in question can be viewed as a special form of the universal unfolding of a nilpotent sl_2(\mathbb_ C) -module operator, which is particularly noteworthy since the universal forms of Lie algebra actions are essential in the study of the critical aspects in integrable systems. The properties of these spaces are explored, including short chains of invariants, nilpotent actions, and Schur Polynomials in a millennial notation. The latter serve as classic examples of universal invariants. The work also delves into the relationship between the value of Schur polynomials at the point (1/2, 1/2) and the volumes of moduli spaces of harmonic maps from a 2-dimensional disk to a CP^1. This connection is part of a larger thread that links moduli spaces of non-linear systems to their corresponding Lie algebraic properties, which is particularly significant in the study of universal critical aspects in integrable systems. The current research represents an advancement in the work of T. Szabados. The properties of the solvable double confluent Heun equation can also be applied to the study of quantum mechanics, especially in the context of the factorization of systems as proposed by E. Balażs and the second author. The research into this area is set to continue in a forthcoming study, which will delve into the properties of the universal 5-parameter cubic monster in Lie theory and its Lie algebraic properties

Topological properties are a fundamental part of a physical system's description, as they are entirely independent of model details and easily interpretable in different models.  Topological characteristics are known to endow systems with distinct attributes such as fractional quantum hall effects and topological quantum biomolecules. We introduce a novel concept of topological feature 'lack of symmetry' (LOS), which defines the inherent properties of points in symmetry-lacking systems. We provide a geometric illustration of this property using the sample density function of a continuous family of maps on a topological space. This serves as a visual representation of LOS. We apply the Atiyah-Patodi-Singer theorem to demonstrate the connection between a system's non-ergodicity and its lack of symmetry. We also use the Hilbert space model and the matrix regular representation to define and explore LOS. This approach aids in understanding the properties of systems lacking symmetry and sheds light on the role of initial conditions in this system. We further use Los function and Hilbert space model to effectively illustrate topological features of three key systems: rare-earth terbium, triplon, and quantum biomolecules. Theoretical calculations of Los function for these systems reveal distinctive characteristics that can be experimentally validated. We propose a general method for topological feature detection in experiments as well as symmetry detection in cases lacking it. The experimental validation of topological properties is highly sought after due to their theoretical significance. In decentralized networks, a new approach to distributed regulation is developed for channels with interdependent connections and locally available data, focusing on optimization for the complete network. The proposed distributed strategy does not require global channel information, is activation-based, and features channel-independent, decentralized control laws with plug-and-play capabilities. For networks with identified connection patterns, necessary and sufficient conditions for convergence are defined using graph principles and optimization, and for all other networks, a gradient-based method is provided to determine ideal connection patterns. Numerical simulations demonstrate the proposed strategy's efficacy in achieving regulation, and compare favorably to existing solutions for fully-informed distributed regulation. Furthermore, the simulations illustrate the proposed strategy's ability to adapt to changing network configurations without requiring updates to the local or global data, resulting in significant computational resource savings by eliminating the need for channel identification. Ultimately, the proposed strategy outperforms existing solutions in terms of computational efficiency, as proven through complexity analysis. The proposed strategy's efficacy is validated through experiments on multiple distributed-mass systems. The presented research builds on comprehensive distributed-control theories, and offers contributions to decentralized-control literature, as well as practical solutions for real-world applications involving distributed systems with interdependent connections and limited global information availability. The proposed distributed-regulation method, featuring decentralized control laws with plug-and-play capabilities, significantly improves computational efficiency by reducing complexity by a factor of N compared to existing fully-informed distributed regulation solutions for networks of N nodes, and further improves efficiency by eliminating the need to regularly update the local data. The proposed strategy's efficacy in achieving regulation and reducing communication frequency in scenarios with incomplete network information and dynamic system and network configurations is demonstrated through simulation, and proves to outperform existing solutions of local information. The proposed strategy has been successfully tested on a network of N=8 distributed-mass systems, and the presented results in this work indicate that this strategy can be extended to much larger networks without difficulty. The problems of incomplete information, dynamic system and channel data, incomplete network information, and limited global data availability, and efficiency in network communication, will be addressed in future research. The proposed strategies and the research in this work will likely have a significant impact on the design of distributed systems with limited global information availability. The research in this dissertation has been supported by a grant from the National Science Foundation, and the results in this work will likely contribute significantly to the research community in the future. A related MATLAB project is available at: https://github.com/mariusmuhle/Distributed-Regulation-Decentralized-Multichannel-Networks

The global fight against COVID-19 hinges on understanding its progression, which drives research, hospitals, and policy-making. We outline a two-phase method to categorize COVID-19 severity through clinical modifications and attribute analysis. In the first phase, patients are sorted into critical or non-critical categories based on clinical symptoms. In the second phase, attributes of patients without symptoms are evaluated for probable, latent, or asymptomatic cases. We apply BERT attributes in both phases, utilizing a unique dataset from 1880 patients in a government hospital in Hyderabad, India. Our study demonstrates the effectiveness of a two-phase framework over existing models for assessing COVID-19 severity using standardized attributes only. We highlight that the first-phase classifier outperforms the second-phase classifier, indicating early symptoms are more predictive. Moreover, probable cases are easier to spot than asymptomatic or critical cases. Notably, the second-phase classifier's performance improves when given the first-phase model's predictions, suggesting the value of combining both for accurate results. This study showcases the practical application of BERT attributes in real-world medical settings and highlights their utility for COVID-19 severity assessment and categorization. The study's findings and code are available on GitHub at https://github.com/ashwinkumar/BERT-COVID19. Our analysis reveals a rich diversity of eco-evolutionary patterns, ranging from simple to complex long-term outcomes, within and across these models. Our research demonstrates that complex life histories and interconnections between duration and rate regulators are essential for achieving dynamic stability at long timescales, which is crucial for understanding and achieving persistence within these ecosystems. We've also developed a theoretical framework that outlines the dynamics of duration and rate regulators, providing insights into the intricate relationship between eco-evolutionary dynamics and life history. Ultimately, our work highlights the importance of temporal complexity in understanding the evolution of co-existing species, which is essential for developing effective conservation strategies. We've also created an online platform where users can interactively explore the dynamics of eco-evolutionary models, which will facilitate the development of innovative and pragmatic conservation approaches. By connecting theoretical developments with empirical knowledge, we're hopeful that our research can serve as a springboard for future investigations into the dynamics of ecosystems. To ensure that our platform is accessible to a wide audience, we've used clear and concise language and added interactive elements that make the models easy to understand and use. We encourage other researchers to build upon our work and collaborate with society to integrate eco-evolutionary thinking into conservation and sustainability practices. By effectively applying eco-evolutionary principles, we believe that it's possible to achieve long-term sustainability and resilience in complex ecosystems. We're committed to continuing this research path, which is characterized by the dynamic and iterative process of theoretical development, empirical exploration, and interactive simulation-based investigations that foster cross-disciplinary connections and innovative thinking. mechanisms are still not fully understood. To further develop these systems, it's
essential to clarify how they operate and what factors influence their performance.
To address this gap, we investigate the antagonistic susceptibility of SSL as an
ideal framework for characterizing how SSL models adapt features from the input
material to enhance task-specific performance. By using a normalized measure, we
determine that the SSL training process introduces unique features with distinct
lifetime dynamics that are highly indicative of SSL's antagonistic susceptibility.
Furthermore, our parameter-free estimate of antagonistic susceptibility allows
us a deeper understanding of SSL's inner workings and helps us anticipate
classification performance based on this factor. Interestingly, our estimates show
that the dependence on this factor is negligible, which aligns with existing evidence,
but surprisingly, our quantification reveals that the effect is even weaker than anticipated.
To support our theory, we conducted two experiments verifying that decreased
dependence on this factor leads to enhanced generalization of speech features during
SSL training and increased task-specific performance after fine-tuning. Our study
implies that the antagonistic susceptibility of SSL is a critical determinant and
that developing methods to decrease its value could greatly improve performance. 
Moreover, our quantification provides valuable insights for guiding future research
in understanding the dynamics of speech self-supervised learning. We make our code
available for other researchers to reproduce our results. The study was implemented

feature extraction during speech self-supervised learning. Therefore, it is crucial
to investigate and characterize this aspect to foster better understanding and
more accurate predictions of speech self-supervised learning outcomes. We hope
our contribution promotes generalized results in other areas of supervised learning

Digital currencies like cryptocurrencies and tokenized securities have experienced rapid growth since the emergence of Bitcoin. Traditionally, CFDs and digital currencies were served through Centralized exchanges like FX, but they faced drawbacks such as a single point of failure, vulnerability to hacks, and the trust-based model's limitations. The introduction of Decentralized Exchanges or DEX has mitigated these issues through the utilization of Blockchain technology and the application of Cryptographic methods. Yet, DEXs still face their own set of challenges, including trading challenges like high latency, a limited selection of trading instruments, and others. This dissertation aims to explore alternative solutions for digital currency trading. It begins by defining key terms including Distributed Exchange Platforms or DEPs and Blockchain technology, before highlighting the benefits and drawbacks of decentralized trading. Following this, it presents possible solutions to the challenges faced by DEXs that could potentially enhance their offerings and make them more competitive in the market. Ultimately, this research recommends the development of decentralized platforms that integrate Blockchain technology and Cryptographic methods to create more robust and responsive trading systems. The potential outcomes of this research could include increased adoption of digital currencies through the expansion of accessible and reliable trading platforms, leading to accelerated digital currency adoption. Furthermore, this research could contribute to future studies on decentralized digital asset trading by establishing a standardized framework for the development of Digital Exchange Platforms or DEPs. These potential outcomes could be verified through practical testing of the proposed trading method, which could be applied across various digital currency markets to assess its effectiveness, before finally reflecting on the practical implementation challenges presented by real-world market conditions. Despite potential technological solutions being put forth, it is crucial to note that DEPs face significant practical hurdles that necessitate further exploration and resolution before they can effectively replace traditional exchanges in real-world digital currency markets. Ultimately, this research seeks to contribute to the expansion of digital currency utilization through decentralized digital asset trading, while also raising essential practical considerations that necessitate attention from academics and practitioners working on related topics. In various fields, including epidemiology, medicine, and genetics, researchers often encounter data gaps, making it challenging to draw conclusions. We developed an approach that employs Bayesian analysis to determine how missing information affects the accuracy of binary conclusions by utilizing the E-value methodology. This approach includes a function to calculate the 'absent data E-value', representing the upper limit of the true effect size, and a statistical power metric. We tested this approach using data from 25 to 30% complete, generated under different true effect sizes and two different distribution types. Results showed that the absent data E-values provided overestimations similar in magnitude to those obtained with the standard E-value, indicating minimal impact of missing information on the accuracy of the E-value in this scenario. However, the statistical power metric demonstrated that the amount of required data to achieve a certain level of precision varies significantly based on the underlying effect size strength. When the data is sparse, collecting large datasets to strengthen the evidence against a hypothesis is necessary to lower the statistical power metric, thus minimizing the effect of missing information on the analysis. This approach is presented along with an implemented R software package titled 'absent-e' that enables users to determine the absent data E-values and the statistical power metric in multiple experimental comparisons, including Bayesian and frequentist hypothesis testing for means and medians. The corresponding software package can be accessed at the link provided. Furthermore, the supplied data is part of the 'absent-e' package. As part of the grand narrative of humanity's journey, the Internet of Things is crucial for bringing together the physical and digital worlds. The Internet of Vehicles, an aspect of the Internet of Things, involves vehicles acting as active elements within this hybrid world. Despite the growth of the Internet of Vehicles, concerns surrounding the confidentiality, integrity, and accessibility of data continue to persist. To address these issues, learning has emerged as a key solution for Internet of Vehicles, where edge learning at the vehicle level, federated learning at the network level, and transfer learning at the device level helps mitigate these problems. However, the emergence of new technologies such as Blockchain and Distributed Ledger Systems has further compounded these challenges through questions surrounding data ownership and privacy. Considering these factors, learning has become a vital component for Internet of Vehicles. A systematic literature survey on Blockchain Enabled Federated Learning for Internet of Vehicles is presented, covering research from 2020 to 2021. A majority of the surveyed papers have cited notable challenges, including data security, privacy, and ownership, as key hurdles for Blockchain Enabled Federated Learning. However, few papers have explored the practical applications of Blockchain in Internet of Vehicles. As a result, a comprehensive understanding of the current state of Blockchain in Federated Learning for Internet of Vehicles is achieved, along with a proposal for a action plan in this field. A comprehensive map of the subject matter is achieved through this survey, allowing researchers and practitioners to gain valuable insights in achieving successful FL within the internet of vehicles. Additionally, a list of recommended reading is provided at the end of this survey. Furthermore, several challenges associated with this field are highlighted, including the practical implementation of FL, the validity of provided metrics and results, the level of agreement between researchers, and the need for case studies and field experiments to support delving into the remaining challenges of FL in IoT. A comprehensive understanding of the remaining challenges is achieved, including the practical applications of Blockchain in Internet of Vehicles. A framework for formulating research within this field is proposed, along with several potential research directions. Ultimately, a thorough analysis of the field is achieved, offering valuable insights to researchers and practitioners in achieving successful FL within the internet of vehicles.

Topological quantum systems have shown promise due to their natural resistance to electrical interference.  Our research involves constructing an experimental platform for isolating a superconducting circuit from electrical noise using advanced quantum management techniques and sophisticated cryogenic design.  This study outlines the progression we've made so far in establishing a substantial millikelvin platform at Fermilab, allowing for the development of a topological quantum computer.  We present a comprehensive description of our laboratory setup, including the components such as the variable temperature stage, the 3D bonder, and the assembly of the superconducting circuit.  This experimental platform achieves a remarkable cooldown rate of about 600 thousand degrees per second, allowing us to reach a target temperature of 50 millikelvin in under six hours and maintaining it with high precision.  The successful demonstration of our laboratory's capabilities paves the way for further advancements and showcases the application of state-of-the-art cryogenic techniques and technology to develop a topological quantum computer.  Using established quantum management strategies, we've characterized the resistance of our laboratory's components and the surface insulation, thereby evaluating its suitability as a quantum processing environment.  Furthermore, we've developed a sophisticated analysis technique based on the nonlinear response of the laboratory's components and the associated input output calculus to accurately determine its performance and pinpoint any potential issues.  Our laboratory's measurements indicate a remarkably low fluctuation level of about 390 nano-kelvins when the laboratory is at a steady 50 millikelvin target temperature and the circuit is in a stabilized state of equilibrium, thereby providing valuable insights into the development of a topological quantum computer.  Our laboratory's fluctuations are dominated by the photon occupation number at the 50 millikelvin target temperature, thereby pushing the development of a topological quantum computer to the quantum regime at about 60 decibels below the white noise floor, and facilitating further breakthroughs to reach the quantum superiority regime at about 68 decibels below the white noise floor.  The presented research develops a set of universal techniques and strategies to establish a precise and stable millikelvin platform and contributes to the ongoing advancements in developing a topological quantum computer. Our research discovers and categorizes overlooked security features in Python's
implementation, exposing vulnerabilities in popular cryptocurrency libraries.
Since 2015, we've been analyzing open-source misuses of security features
involving Python, a language widely used for cryptocurrency development.
Our study covers 106 identified vulnerabilities in 10 widely-used libraries,
out of 15 surveyed, without requiring prior knowledge of the underlying code.
Fifteen percent of the assessed libraries contained implementation vulnerabilities
such as unauthorized access to data or functionality, undetected by static
analysis tools, with a library's user base ranging from a few to more than
500,000 developers. To exploit certain vulnerabilities, attackers only need to
infiltrate a project's domain name, IP address, or network connection.
We've discovered six critical vulnerabilities that could lead to financial loss,
together with nine less severe ones that still pose a risk to cryptocurrency
users, with a potential impact of at least $5.8M in losses, primarily due to one
of the critical vulnerabilities.
Additionally, we found non-technical barriers preventing some project maintainers
from applying security features effectively, such as resource limitations and
human language barriers.
Based on our research fee-only model, where experts compensate us to identify
security issues, we found that the average cost for resolving a misuse was $2.5M.
In conclusion, we've taken action to notify the project maintainers, either by
disclosing our findings publicly or by cooperating with them, leading to the
resolution or partial resolution of seven misuses.
Furthermore, we've collaborated with relevant organizations to either cease
or reduce two misuses, which involved cryptocurrency libraries listing us as
required security features.
Our study highlights the significance of security feature misuse in the
cryptocurrency ecosystem, justifying the allocation of resources by project
foundations and organizations to address such misuses in their codebases. Our
research provides the first systematic analysis of security feature misuses in
Python and showcases applicable methodologies and policies to assist in the
discovery and remediation of such misuses in cryptocurrency projects. Moreover,
the study initiates discussion on the market failure in the cryptocurrency
ecosystem, contributing to social sciences research. Our work offers the first
public list of security features in Python with related misuse types,
illustrating a comprehensive taxonomy. Our study provides actionable advice to
project maintainers on how to prioritize their security features and address

track daily routines including eating, sleeping, and exercising. Despite these

effectiveness of our approach. Additionally, this study provides open-source code

behavior under various phases of the city's daily routine including work,

Building on this concept, we develop a novel deep learning approach, named NuSPAN, a Proximal Mean Network that enables our network to approximate the proximal map of the given non-uniform $\ell_1$-norm. Through the analysis of the network structure, we demonstrate that our model retains the essential properties of the non-uniform sparse model and we also prove the convergence of the learned model parameters. Furthermore, we test the effectiveness of NuSPAN in recovering seismic reflectivity using the Slim Tiger 2D Seismic Inversion dataset, demonstrating superior results compared to the uniform sparse model, and we provide theoretical justifications for the observed outcomes. The massive linguistic riches of historical texts are locked away in annotated corpus formats that were established in the 1980s, rendering them inaccessible to modern machine learning techniques. In particular, part-of-speech annotation, a crucial dimension of linguistic understanding, is hindered by its discrete set of possibilities and the partial labeling present in many ancient texts. In this paper, we employ a forecasting technique known as Set-Valued Forecasting to address the challenge of predicting part-of-speech tags in the COCO corpus, which contains partially annotated texts. Our experiments show that SF-based models outperform traditional deep neural networks and achieve a similar level of performance as a state-of-the-art template-based method. Additionally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of SF within a semi-supervised learning framework. Our findings highlight the potential of SF to enhance part-of-speech annotation in historical collections, a necessary step in unlocking the semantic potential of these texts. This article explores the application of Set-Valued Forecasting to achieve reliable part-of-speech labeling in linguistic history. In contrast to standard machine learning methods that typically involve single-valued outcomes, Set-Valued Forecasting models can accommodate a discrete set of possible outcomes. A key strength of SF lies in its ability to accommodate partial labels, which is uncommon in traditional machine learning challenges. In this study, we apply Set-Valued Forecasting to the part-of-speech challenge in historical texts, which often exhibit incomplete part-of-speech annotations, often due to the labor involved in creating these annotations. Our proposed approach integrates Set-Valued Forecasting with a top-3 output constraint to achieve this challenge. Our experiments with the COCORUS corpus, which contains French texts from the 16th century, demonstrate the effectiveness of this challenge. Our study has a particular focus on advancing French historical corpus analysis. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/MichaelAllemand/set-valued-forecasting. A preliminary version of this work was presented at the ICML 2021 workshop on Set-Valued and Multi-Label Prediction. This article demonstrates the semi-supervised learning potential of Set-Valued Forecasting through part-of-speech challenge in historical texts. Our study employs a semi-supervised self-training framework to achieve this challenge. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/MichaelAllemand/set-valued-forecasting. This work develops a theoretical framework for non-smooth integrability and
examinines its underlying principles, varying from smooth integrability which
has a well-established mathematical foundation. The new theory is applied to a
range of nonlinear control systems that have components with kth order
derivatives. The study includes analytical investigations into the necessary and
sufficient conditions required for integrability in this context, including
the creation of a novel distributional derivative. A key finding is that the
sufficient condition for Caratheodory integrability in smooth systems retains
its validity in this non-smooth scenario. However, the necessary condition is
no longer equivalent to this case. Instead, it is only applicable when the
kth order derivative is equal to zero. Additionally, the study delves into
chordal integrability and uses the theory to clarify any confusing notions
arising from a prior study on this topic. A range of examples serves to illustrate
the practical implications of this theoretical framework. The non-smooth
integrability theory is further applied to a dynamic programming problem where
the challenge is to find the longest possible reach of a nonlinear control system
with kth order derivatives. By converting it into an integrability problem, it
is possible to establish a piecewise Ck+1 solution that can be used to calculate
the longest possible reach. Lastly, the study incorporates the theory into a
computer algorithm which can be used to visualize the reach of the control system. Further research directions are also proposed in the study. Ultimately, the study demonstrates the significance of non-smooth integrability theory in various fields of control systems. Through the application of our proposed concealed inverses protocol, the influence of errors on quantum states is eliminated without invoking the principle of reciprocity. This proposal is substantial because it presents an independent solution to the problem of mitigating errors caused by phase fluctuations. We also develop a mathematical representation, in the form of a spin operator, to describe the phenomenon of errors induced by fluctuations. This error model can potentially be extended to address broader issues, thus offering a significant contribution to quantum research in the development of reliable quantum computers. Furthermore, our protocol does not rely on the principle of reciprocity and is applicable to systems lacking inversions, thereby offering an additional tool for error correction, with supporting simulations also being carried out. The validity of our approach is demonstrated through the performance of qubit operations with nearly error-free results using a superconducting circuit. This confirms that our protocol is a reliable method for eliminating errors and can play a vital role in the development of quantum computers. The possibility of reducing errors and achieving a stable quantum state has also been explored. The theoretical framework of our protocol is suitable for the development of diverse quantum systems and may find potential applications in the development of reliable quantum computers. We examine the relationship between significant events, average levels and spatial patterns in various fields such as oceanography and geology. Our proposed method integrates a multivariate spatial scan statistic and a density estimation technique to identify extreme events' conditional spatial patterns simultaneously. The approach involves first identifying extreme events through a multivariate spatial scan statistic, and then using kernel density estimation to determine the average levels and spatial patterns of those events. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method using simulated data and real-data sets in oceanography, including satellite altimetry data and buoy wind speed data. Our analysis reveals consistent results: extreme events tend to occur under favorable average conditions and these events are dispersed across the study area. Additionally, we provide spatial density estimates for each variable, and find that extreme events' locations do not always align with areas of heightened activity. Our study sheds light on the relationships between significant events, average levels and spatial patterns, and contributes to understanding extreme phenomena's dynamics in complex systems. We publicly share the spatial analysis code using open-source tools and data repositories. Our research has practical implications in identifying locations most vulnerable to extreme events and in informing infrastructure planning in extreme environments. We apply the method to data from the Agulhas Current and find that extreme events' locations are related to the Western Gulf of Bahrain's ocean currents, which supports a previous hypothesis, and we also investigate the dynamics of events in that region. Our analysis shows that extreme events' conditions in terms of currents and temperature do not consistently align with regular ocean patterns, and we explore the potential causes of this discrepancy, which could be linked to the presence of oil platforms in the area. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in identifying consistent spatial patterns of extreme events in a complex and dynamic environment characterized by high economic values, which have important policy-relevant implications for data-driven hazard mapping and infrastructure planning in similar environments. Our analysis code can serve as a model for analyzing other complex and data-sparse environments worldwide. We publicly disclose in our repository our analysis code used to generate the results in this study. Recently, vision-language models have shown significant progress, but their performance in tasks like image captioning and VQA is still limited due to a combination of visual and textual confusion. To address this issue, we propose VT-CLIP, an innovative framework that leverages contrastive learning of visual and textual signals to enhance the cross-modal understanding of VL models. Specifically, we utilize visual cues to stimulate text processing and enhance textual semantic representation, while also utilizing textual cues to stimulate image processing and narrow down the image-search space in conjunction with CLIP. By integrating our proposed pre-training scheme with two-directed multi-modal attention, VT-CLIP is able to elevate the fluency and accuracy of image captions and raise the accuracy of visual question-answering by approximately 1 point from its existing counterparts. Moreover, VT-CLIP's visual-directed texts, obtained through the integration of visual and textual signals, surpasses current state-of-the-art image search performance by 2 points. To further facilitate future research, we create a new dataset called VT-CLIP's visual-directed texts, available at https://github.com/liuwenhan/NanoCTLIP. The VT-CLIP code is available at https://github.com/whwu1995/VT-CLIP. Our work is influenced by Prof. from Antgroup Feiyue Xu. The final version of this paper is published at Findings of ACL-IJCNLP 2021, with a significantly revised version published at NeurIPS 2021. The visual-directed text demo is shown at https://clipsort.sortflight.github.io. The VT-CLIP's performance on image captioning and VQA is outperformed by current state-of-the-art models, with an improvement of 4 and 1 points respectively. To further investigate the efficacy of visual-directed texts, we conduct a human study that demonstrates the value of visual guidance in natural language understanding. The human study reveals that human observers can accurately answer visual questions with minimal prior knowledge and that visual cues alone can yield accurate answers. The human study also shows that visual-directed texts facilitate better comprehension of multi-modal content in tasks like image captioning and VQA. The human study is available at https://sortflight.github.io/human-study/CLIP-guided. A novel approach to this problem is presented, capitalizing on the opportunity presented by the expansion of deep learning to broaden the scope of available reductions and make it easier to find effective reductions.  Unlike other approaches, this method bypasses a detailed analysis of the system dynamics and instead uses a machine to identify reductions that are effective in practice, thus promising a significant improvement over existing reduction techniques.  Two variants of the method are proposed, one involving the application of a universal operator switch to simplify problems with noisy matrices, and another involving the creation of an optimal operator switch.  A universal operator switch is shown to be effective in a variety of systems including quantum gravity and Hawking radiation, and an optimal operator switch is shown to be effective in solving systems of linear equations.  Our source code is available at https://github.com/TimGarland/operator_switch.  Experimentation results indicate that the method is highly practical and produces results that make theoretical sense, and the code has already been shown to produce useful reductions for complex systems. In recent years, interest in applying machine learning methods to analyze medical images has been increasing. Research has been drawing parallels to industrial sectors, where data-driven innovation is prevalent. However, examining medical image data necessitates adherence to specific imaging standards to ensure interoperability and accuracy. The DICOM protocol serves this purpose by establishing a set of rules, but implementing these requires technical expertise and familiarity with the standards and image analysis. By utilizing Highdicom, researchers can access a user-friendly Python library that simplifies the process of converting image data into a standardized format compatible with DICOM specifications. This article highlights key aspects of the Highdicom library, specifically focusing on its application in image annotation and model output within the context of medical imaging. A step-by-step tutorial is provided to guide users in installing and utilizing the Highdicom library to achieve standardized image annotation and model output. Moreover, the section includes information on the conventional practices within the medical imaging field and discusses how the Highdicom library addresses these requirements. Finally, the section includes examples of applying the Highdicom library in actual medical imaging use cases. We establish a precise relationship between standard Bergman spaces and their scaled variations, demonstrating hypercontractive behavior. This leads to the derivation of uniform norm estimates for operators between these scaled spaces, assuming a certain condition on the weight function $w(\lambda)$. Specifically, we show that for weights that grow at a logarithmic rate, operators between scaled Bergman spaces with weight functions $w_\varepsilon(\lambda)$ can be bounded uniformly as $\varepsilon$ approaches zero. Our findings are complemented by a counterexample illustrating the optimal conditions for the weight function. Furthermore, we apply these results to develop invariant norms for multi-sectorial operators in weighted $\ell^p$ spaces. Finally, we apply our methodology to establish hypercontractive behavior for multi-sectorial Bergman spaces and provide an exemplar counterexample. Our methods and conclusions are anticipated to facilitate the study of weighted multi-sectorial operator theory. The research is inspired by the work of Weiss and Zhai on hypercontractivity in weighted Bergman spaces. Mesh coarsening is a process that reduces a detailed mesh created for computational purposes, like solving partial differential equations (PDEs), to make simulations more efficient. To maintain accuracy, it's crucial to retain key features of the original mesh. In mesh coarsening systems, particularly those based on Riemannian metrics, high-order quadrilateral meshes offer advantages due to their stability and robustness. To achieve this, we utilize linear programming to optimize directional derivative coefficients to minimize the L2 norm of the Laplacian operator on the mesh's Riemannian metric. By incorporating whole number constraints on variable values, we employ the linear programming algorithm to generate coarser meshes from high-order quadrilateral meshes. To validate our method's effectiveness, we apply it to mesh models in CAD and verify the mesh topology to ensure the quality of the resulting coarser meshes, even at a coarseness of 16 times the original density. Additionally, our method outperforms a reference approach in L2 Laplacian error and approximation vector L2 norm, making it suitable for use in mesh coarsening and refinement applications. Relevant source code has been made publicly available on the GitHub repository 'lsb-mesh-coarsening'. Following rigorous numerical testing on various meshes and problems, we visually illustrate the performance of our method in mesh coarsening and refinement on the 3D CAD model of the Tesla Model Y. With our method, it's possible to efficiently solve complex computational problems and generate high-quality visualizations of the resulting solution. To demonstrate this, we execute a mesh-based finite element analysis (FEA) of the Tesla Model Y to visualize and validate the resulting solution. Our mesh coarsening method shows promise for use in computer-aided design and engineering simulations, complemented by our mesh coarsening and refinement video showcasing the Tesla Model Y. Furthermore, we execute a mesh-based Monte Carlo simulation in fixed-income analysis to illustrate the effectiveness of our method in reducing L2 Laplacian error and retaining the accuracy of the resulting solution. To facilitate reproducibility, we include relevant supporting data in the Dropbox folder '201121 LB Whole Number Optimization Mesh Coarsening'. Our method does not support handling meshes with isotropic Riemannian metrics, nor can it efficiently solve PDEs on the resulting coarser meshes. In the field of recommender systems, EXPLAINABLE RECOMMENDER SYSTEMS have gained prominence as they provide users with transparent decision-making by outlining the factors influencing their personal recommendations. However, interpreting black-box models is often hindered by the lack of user-centric features and over-reliance on instrumental variables. Furthermore, users expect explanations to be consistent with their past behavior and informative. To address these concerns, we propose LIME-RS, a practical approach that uses optimization techniques to provide intuitive and consistent interpretations for complex recommender systems. Our study evaluates the efficacy of LIME-RS through explanatory and informative reflectiveness, and its applications are discussed below. We investigate the impact of changing explanation modes on user trust, examining the LIME-RS explanations in a user study involving Amazon Electronic Devices. Our research reveals that instrumental variable-based explanations are preferred over saliency-based ones, and users trust explanations focusing on item similarity and user interaction more than those focusing on semantic attributes. We also demonstrate the utilization of LIME-RS for optimizing top-list displays and discovering new item categories based on user feedback, and we reveal that instrumental variable-based explanations are less susceptible to manipulation. To the best of our knowledge, our research is a first breakthrough in understanding the stability of explanatory models in recommender systems, and our studies were conducted without participating humans in the case of Amazon Electronic Devices. We hope that our research will inspire future advancements and facilitate human-centered advancements in the field of explainable recommender systems and human-computer interaction in general. When training deep learning models, common practices such as data augmentation and regularization help mitigate overfitting due to large training datasets. However, these methods aren't applicable when dealing with biased or limited labeled data, and an alternative approach is using regional queries to improve model robustness and generalization. A region query is essentially a large batch of samples drawn from the full training set, differentiated from traditional batch training by its size and the fact that it's not uniformly mixed. By incorporating regional queries into the training process, recent studies have achieved notable improvements in state-of-the-art benchmarks. Despite this, the underlying reasoning behind successful regional query techniques remains poorly understood, and these methods suffer from a lack of clarity in terms of hyperparameter selection and reproducibility. In our work, we develop a coherent framework for regional queries, and through theoretical analysis, we identify scenarios in which regional queries outperform traditional training methods. A thorough experimental evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of our proposed approach, confirming that regional queries can significantly aid in achieving robust and resilient learning outcomes. Moreover, by exploring the theoretical framework, we derive principles to help inform the selection of key regional query hyperparameters, thereby providing practical recommendations for practical application. Ultimately, through both theory and practice, we highlight the importance of considering regional query techniques as a viable solution for overcoming limitations associated with large and varied training datasets. Our proposed algorithm, Rapid Sinkhorn II, is designed to compute the optimal transport (OT) plan between two distributions rapidly, where the OT problem is formulated as a convex optimization with a doubly stochastic constraint. By first approximating a matrix with the collinear triangular array (cta) structure, we are able to significantly decrease the number of matrix-doubling operations in the OT problem, from O(n^2) to O(n). Additionally, we discovered that using the cta array to compute the inverse of the cost matrix in the OT problem results in the majority of partial sums being eliminated, leading to a significant reduction in the complexity of the OT problem from O(n^3) to O(n). We have optimized the OT problem solution to require only one pass through the data, achieving a time complexity of O(n) with the cta structure and an efficient OT solution in closed-form, precision guaranteed, with local convergence facilitated by the triangular array's structure. We have validated the performance of our algorithm through the execution of self-developed C, CUDA, and OpenMP programs, where the algorithms' scalability has been examined through real-data OT problems with up to 50,000 data points. Furthermore, our algorithm outperformed existing OT algorithms in efficiency, achieving a runtime of only 0.049s for the 50,000-data-point problem. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of our algorithm's OT solution for knowledge discovery in image data, where the algorithm successfully detected highly aligned structures in the OT solution's scalar weights. We plan to utilize this algorithm in the knowledge discovery domains of OT in the future. We have made the algorithms public and available for download at the website https://github.com/TuomasSipola/Rapid-Sinkhorn-II. When charged particles from space interact with Earth's radiation belts, they transfer energy and alter the environment's equilibrium. Reciprocal action from the environment, in the form of drag, counteracts the particle acceleration, ultimately counterbalancing the effect. This active radiation drag phenomenon has largely been understated due to the prevailing focus on the driving force, namely accelerated particles. We now shift the perspective and instead emphasize the environmental response as the primary physical process involved. We investigate radiation drag within the resistive magnetohydrodynamic model of the radiation belts' interaction, utilizing a simplified approach with both thin and full shell representations of the Earth's dipole magnetic field. We demonstrate that, as expected, the magnitude and rate of drag generated by a fixed driving force greatly depend on both the chosen coordinate system and electron density. We conduct an exhaustive examination of drag generated in response to varying field lines, driving force intensity, and electron density within the inner radiation zone, focusing on toroidal and poloidal currents. We find that an approximately linear relationship exists between the poloidal current and generated drag, regardless of variation in electron density and magnetic flux. We further perform an identical analysis for the full shell model and confirm that, despite differences in geometry, the principles remain largely unchanged. We propose a new drag coefficient representation that reflects variation in environmental response, adaptable to scenarios involving multiple driving forces. This framework serves as a methodological template for describing radiation drag under varying conditions and can serve as a baseline for theoretical modeling and model construction. This study provides the foundational knowledge required to develop models that accurately capture the effects of radiation drag and environmental response across various fission and fusion systems. We outline relevant applications involving drag-coupled particle and fluid systems in low Earth orbits, offering implications for systems management and design. Ultimately, the effects observed suggest a need to reconsider equilibrium equations that solely account for particle acceleration, incorporating environmental response as a critical counterbalancing force. This study provides an essential mathematical and conceptual framework for understanding and addressing radiation drag across relevant systems and processes. We examine potential applications of this principle in astrophysics, including planetary magnetic field remodeling and neutrino-driven accretion disks, showing how drag can function as a self-regulating mechanism to prevent plasma collapse. We also explore the effects of drag in gravitational disk systems, including spiral density waves and a tetrahedral planetoid, where we find that local drag can develop into a long-range interaction mechanism despite reduced particle density. This exploration leads to a demonstration that the HS equation's solution group has a certain robustness property, tied to the $L^{2}$-norm of the velocity map. Moreover, the paper introduces a concept called semi-robustness and shows that HS flows share this semi-robustness property, while displaying robustness for specific types of velocities. To confirm these findings, the paper provides a direct proof for the robustness of left translation flows and, similarly, the semi-robustness of right translation flows. This exploration also extends to the continuous time HS equation and its connection to Robustness, via the $L^{2}$-norm of the velocity map. A unique aspect of the paper's findings is the separation of left translation robustness from semi-robustness. To the author's knowledge, the idea of semi-robustness is another novel concept introduced in the paper. Semi-robustness is defined in the context of discrete time PDEs and it implies robustness for specific types of velocities. In turn, the paper's findings suggest that the $L^{2}$-norm of the velocity map is the natural choice for robustness considerations of PDE flows. The evaluation of scoliosis using ultrasound imaging requires precise measurement and detection of the spinal curve's maximum deformation. However, the reliability of robotic ultrasound technology for this purpose has not been established in clinical settings. This study compared the reliability of robotic ultrasound imaging against traditional manual scanning for scoliosis detection. Three-dimensional ultrasound data was collected from 15 healthy subjects with no scoliosis at two degrees of freedom. Fuzzy C-Means clustering was applied to determine the vertebral bodies, and the deformation map was calculated through the vactor length, operating in two different modes - B mode and M mode. Two human observers measured the maximum deformation and curvature from ultrasound images, while the robotic system made automatic measurements. Results showed that the robotic system produced data comparable to manual scanning in terms of accuracy and reliability, indicating its potential as a reliable tool for scoliosis detection and evaluation. This study forms the basis of a clinical trial to assess the detection capabilities of this technology in patients with scoliosis. In a subsequent clinical trial, the robotic system was found to effectively support the evaluation of scoliosis by physical therapists. The results indicated no significant age-related bias in the robotic technology for scoliosis detection. Finally, the feasibility of using ultrasound imaging for real-time, non-invasive spinal curvature assessment in individuals has been established. Deep learning-based MIMO models exchange features effectively by incorporating
a spatial constraint into their training, but adding Feature Exchanging (FE)
modules during training can be costly and time-consuming. To address this, we propose
a modified MIMO architecture that integrates FE modules by default, placing no
extra computational demands on the training process. Our experiments demonstrate
that this modified MIMO model exceeds the performance of the standard MIMO with
FE modules in several key datasets, achieving comparable results to state-of-the-art
models in STL10, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 with fewer parameters. Notably, this
modified MIMO model also performs competitively in training times, showcasing its
efficiency. Furthermore, through ablation studies, we investigate the effects of
dropping individual components of our model, which confirms the importance of
each component in the model's success. We also successfully apply our approach
to a more complex dataset, demonstrating its generalizability to larger datasets.

A review of publicly accessible databases and collections of historical manuscripts is provided, followed by an analysis of their strengths and limitations.  It becomes evident that the development of extensive, benchmarking databases similar to those available for natural images is crucial for establishing new benchmarks in the document analysis community.
