To ensure safe integration of robots in sensitive environments, it's crucial to maintain precise control over their movement, which induces oscillations when lacking accurate position data. The cost of equipped sensors for position detection in industrial robots can be prohibitive, hindering the accessibility of robotic technology. This research explores an innovative solution in which an industrial Mark III robot's joint motion is regulated by a dynamic controller, utilizing only joint torque and velocity as input signals. Contrary to conventional feedback control methods that often require costly position sensors, this new approach relies on a sophisticated algorithm operating within a two-dimensional phase plane. By introducing a novel 'flatness-based' method for joint tracking, this solution can replicate the performance of position-based control, demonstrating experimental and theoretical validity. Furthermore, a dynamic model-free method is also developed to enhance the system's robustness, showcasing the effectiveness of these innovations in real-world joint tracking applications. The obtained results demonstrate that these technologies can safely and effectively guide the robotic movement, even in the absence of position sensors. The experimental findings indicate that these solutions not only enhance the system's precision but also its stability, providing a reliable robot control solution. We introduce a novel numerical method to adapt the molecular continuum model, originally an ordinary differential equation, to complex geometric configurations by employing a multi-site framework. This approach is characterized by two key elements: a quadrature-based method that efficiently solves a corresponding integral equation and an adapted reformulation of the original ODE, maintaining its original mathematical properties. Furthermore, we show that our multi-site method is equivalent to a modified version of the standard quadrature method in terms of continuous solution accuracy and we develop a new version of the standard quadriuma-based method that yields a fully discrete formulation. We support our findings with a detailed numerical investigation on a set of benchmark tests. The provided results highlight that quadrature-based methods are capable of delivering highly accurate solutions with a reduced computational load in comparison to other integration techniques, while also demonstrating their ability to handle irregularly-shaped surfaces in a piecewise linear manner. Therefore, we conclude that quadrature-based methods represent an attractive option for solving the molecular continuum model on complex geometric configurations. The provided Matlab code is also openly available on Github for users' reference. Lastly, we outline a potential extension of our method of integrating the quadrature-based approach with multi-adaptive quadrature in order to improve its performance in handling irregularly-shaped surfaces. Nevertheless, we also acknowledge the presence of inherent limitations of quadrature-based methods in dealing with narrow and deep singularities. Therefore, we encourage further research in this area to address these limitations and ultimately expand the capabilities of quadrature-based methods to handle more general geometric configurations. The provided analysis is part of an ongoing effort to develop a comprehensive theory of quadrature-based methods for solving partial differential and ordinary differential equations on complex geometric configurations with the aim of advancing their understanding and integration in the scientific community. Consequently, we expect that quadrature-based methods will play an essential role in developing highly-efficient and robust algorithms for solving the molecular continuum model and other related equations in the future. We explore metric dimension as a parameterized problem, able to bound $\fd(G)$ by $2|K_1| + \eta(G)$, where $\eta(G)$ represents the vertex covering number. This implies the problem remains NP-complete, even when parameterized by the number of leaves in a graph. We also establish the hardness of parameterized metric dimension, when restricted to certain types of graphs, including chordal graphs and split graphs, all while exploring the feasibility of dynamic programming on leaf-limited graphs. We propose a DP algorithm with a running time of $O(|G|^{2.5\eta(G)})$ that solves the problem on leaf-limited graphs. We further extend our findings to the more general concept of feedback vertex groups, already known to influence the complexity of the problem in a similar manner. We also investigate and quantify the impact of other graph attributes, such as the maximum degree, arboricity and coloring. We propose a new parameterization called $k$-colorable, representing the number of colors needed in a graph's optimal coloring. We also explore and quantify the effect that certain structural parameters have on metric dimension, ultimately proposing the $b$-branching parameter, representing the maximum number of edges connected to a vertex in a graph. We also propose a DP algorithm with a $O(2^{.5b} \cdot |G|^b)$ running time that solves the problem on b-branching graphs. Using reduction techniques, we show that the problem remains hard for certain types of graphs, including those with a bounded number of leaves or $b$-branching graphs, all while exploring and quantifying the effect that certain structural parameters have on metric dimension within different graph types. We also extend our findings to the more general concept of a distance label covering of a graph G, first introduced by Fink, Kammerer and Wilson. We propose a DP algorithm with a $O(2^{.5c|V(G)|} \cdot |G|c)$ running time that solves the problem in the general case, using the general distance label covering definition. Specifically, we show that the transition likelihood matrix can be expressed as a product of two related matrices, one of which is an explicit function of the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the adjacency matrix, while the other depends on additional parameters that can be determined through diverse algorithms. Notably, we also present an explicit polynomial form of the transition likelihood matrix, highlighting its distinct features compared to stochastic matrices derived from standard random walk models. Empirical analysis demonstrates the feasibility of recovering crucial parameters from this explicit polynomial under specific conditions. Finally, we illustrate the practical utility of our approach by applying it to a real-world graph representing online social networks.' In formal specifications, definitions are crucial and frequently used. However, definitions with recursive arguments that depend on time are less common in a proof-based language, as they can be tricky to validate. This study introduces an advanced definition mechanism known as "Timed Definitions" that allow arguments to be recursively dependent on their context, including temporal aspects. We propose a sound evaluation method for these definitions and demonstrate its effectiveness by applying it to resolve recursion in the development of timed data structures, such as ordered skip lists. Furthermore, we compare the improved definition mechanism with existing techniques for dealing with recursion in timed systems, particularly asset turnover fractions in a timed matrix game model. We find that the new definition approach simplifies specifications and leads to a more direct and efficient implementation. Ultimately, we showcase the soundness and practicality of Timed Definitions in the context of a substantial domain, verifying the fundamental principles of game theory. Our findings reveal that incorporating SMOS enhances the performance of other oversampling methods, particularly for classes with the fewest instances. We conclude that combining SMOS with these methods offers a compelling solution for handling class imbalance issues in text classification tasks. The research suggests that incorporating SMOS simplifies the process of balancing datasets and improves classification performance. Furthermore, we discovered that artificial oversampling methods are beneficial when used in conjunction with SMOS, resulting in improved text classification accuracy and F1 scores. It is also evident that incorporating SMOS mitigates the associated information loss when applying sampling techniques to balance datasets. We observed improved performance with the combination of SMOS and random oversampling, leading to increased F1 scores compared to using SMOS alone or random oversampling as a balancing method. The research further indicates that incorporating SMOS offers more significant improvements for classes with the fewest instances, indicating better classification performance. Finally, we conclude that combining artificial oversampling methods with SMOS offers promising outcomes for multi-category text classification tasks, resulting in improved F1 scores and accurate classification results. Assuming a communication network with a cycle-free graph, the proposed algorithm converges almost surely to the optimal aggregated solution $x^*=\mathcal{A}^{-}[\bar{x}^*]$. The method's complexity scales as $\mathcal{O}\left( T \left( \log T + \log\left(2^{1/\tau}+1\right) \right) \left( \log^2 T + \log^2 (2^{1/\tau}+1) \right) \right) \right)$, where $T$ is the total iteration count, $\tau$ is the Lipschitz constant of the functions $\hat{\phi}_k$, and $\mathcal{A}^{-}$ denotes an inverse graph averaging operator. Numerical tests are also presented in the paper to support the method's efficacy for a variety of real-world applications. By examining both expert feedback and system performance, we discovered that these individuals consider not only the systems' technical abilities but also its potential impact on specific groups, such as women and people of diverse racial and ethnic backgrounds. The input reviews provided by experts allow them to address the systems' shortcomings in areas like facial recognition and speed, as these systems often perpetuate and exaggerate existing real-world biases in the data used for training. The findings of this research indicate that incorporating expert input review into the development and testing of commercial driving skills can lead to more equitable evaluations of systems that rely on computer vision, particularly in terms of their performance for various human groups. The expert feedback suggests that including moderateable free-form text and structured multiple-choice options can facilitate more effective input review, ultimately leading to greater social accountability and better reflection of potential group biases in the systems assessed. In this paper, the authors develop new corrections to Korovkin's theorem in the realm of nonlinear, monotonic operators acting on the space of sequentially convergent sequences of real values. Specifically, the corrections involve the use of convergent Ces\`aro and Orlicz means. Moreover, the generated norms are equivalent, and the class of convergent sequences can be embedded within the space defined by these new norms. To complete the analysis, an extension of Korovkin's theorem is applied to the realm of multi-dimensional real values. There, the authors use convergent means of multi-dimensional sequences to define a new space, and the class of multi-dimensional sequences is embedded within that space via a norm derived from the original sequence. En route to this completion, a new non-linear extension of the Radon transform is introduced. Lastly, the authors pose several open questions in the field. Relevant graphical examples are provided to aid in the understanding of the analysis. The adaptive spectral Koopman technique was designed to solve complex dynamical systems over large datasets in various fields, including the prediction of chaotic motions in the engineering and physics communities. However, the previous advanced spectral techniques were limited in their ability to handle dimensional complexity due to the "curse of dimensionality." In response, the proposed ASK-T Truncated technique eliminates this limitation by combining the advantages of adaptive Koopman algorithms and sparse grid approximation schemes to efficiently process high-dimensional data with variable flow dynamics. ASK-T Truncated achieves this by applying the sparse grid concept to the argument space, selecting basis functions from the adaptive Fekete-Petrov grid to ensure a thorough representation of the system's flow map. As a result, ASK-T Truncated maintains the flow's accuracy while substantially reducing the computational cost in comparison to traditional grid-based methods for the same level of precision. Furthermore, the method's innovative multi-objective approach to ASK-T Truncated allows it to improve both the flow and gradient estimations simultaneously, leading to the discovery of intricate structures within the system's phase space. In particular, the method successfully captures the positive Lyapunov exponent of the multi-layer percolation model and determines the critical points of the R\"ussell-Battleday model with transcritical dynamics, all using sparse grid-driven calculations of the Koopman operator's eigenfunctions. Additionally, the computations reveal the distinct behavior of the eigenfunctions in multiple scenarios of the R\"ussell-Battleday model. In accordance with the second-order convergence rate of the sparse grid approximation scheme, the one-dimensional integrals are recalculated to demonstrate a second-order improvement in the predictions of the system's phase space trajectories using the proposed multi-objective ASK-T Truncated method. As an extension of this research, the multi-objective ASK-T Truncated method is also applied to the prediction of chaotic motions in impact-chaos dynamics with a successful demonstration of its high accuracy and computational efficiency in comparison to traditional grid-based methods for the same level of precision. Furthermore, the proposed multi-objective ASK-T Truncated method allows the generation of color 3D plots in addition to the discovery of the system's Lyapunov exponent spectrum and critical points in the parameter space, representing a step-forward in the advanced spectral analysis of high-dimensional complex systems. The COVID-19 pandemic dramatically altered the way people move throughout cities and changed commuters' financial outlays for transportation. To assess how this shift impacted different areas, we analyzed the effects of various factors like trip frequency, mode of transportation, age, and income level on the financial costs of urban interactions in five major US cities. By using open-source data including Google Trends and the American Community Survey, we calculated the average daily expenditure on trips for distinct demographic groups in each city pre-pandanda and during the pandemic. Our research reveals that in the majority of cities studied, higher-income individuals saw a relatively smaller decrease in trip frequency compared to lower-income individuals, thus increasing the gap in trip frequency between high and low-income groups. Similarly, high-income individuals experienced a smaller reduction in the frequency of using shared modes of transportation, increasing the ratio of solo to shared trips among high-income individuals. Ultimately, our study indicates that the economic costs of urban interactions disproportionately affected low-income groups, widening the gap in trip frequency and expenditures between high and low-income individuals. The findings provide valuable data for urban planners and policymakers to understand the effects of the pandemic on urban transportation systems and devise policies to mitigate economic inequalities in urban mobility. The research presents policy options to decrease financial burdens on low-income groups and increase transportation affordability, making urban interactions more equitable especially for low-income citizens. We observe agreement between our results and those from prior works. Additional support for our findings comes from analyzing the convergence of the gravitational action for certain configurations in the string theory framework. We demonstrate that within this context, the JT gravity action's subleading term converges towards a non-zero value at long distances, rather than converging to zero as it does in the random matrix model. Consequently, this research yields a distinct energy spectrum for black hole transitions in two-dimensional string theories that feature discrete states, a characteristic contrasted with the continuous spectrum observed in the random matrix model. We propose that the difference between these two energy spectra could serve as a collective indicator of the distinct nature of string theories versus the corresponding random matrix models. We suggest that these Dirac determinants could function as emergent low-energy degrees of freedom in the corresponding string theory and gauge theory frameworks. Ultimately, the primary goal of this research is to provide a detailed exploration of the connection between JT gravity and two-dimensional string theories, specifically with regard to their shared practice of utilizing the repertorial multi-matrix framework. With growing emphasis on integrating and optimizing these systems, cities are encouraged to share related data with a broader scope, yet this often conflicts with their need to protect sensitive information. This paper presents a framework called GUIDES, which focuses on engineering and managing city data by incorporating geospatial aspects, demonstrating its ability to address privacy concerns and achieve enhanced optimization outcomes through a practical application. This research involved surveys, interviews, and a proof-of-concept study on a real-world city to test the GUIDES framework's feasibility and assess its potential for real-world implementation in metropolitan cities. The study's results validate the practicality and effectiveness of the GUIDES approach. The accompanying code and documentation are freely accessible online at github.com/guides-city. To analyze experimental data from a specific project involving a 2D ion lattice, referred to as the "Poincar\'e ball," we've developed an advanced approach. This method simulates the long-term behavior of the lattice's central ion's average radial position and velocity under the influence of random fluctuations in temperature. These fluctuations mimic the unknown effects of micromotion on the lattice's behavior. Applying our approach to a study of spin decay in the same reference, we've been able to determine the temperature of the lattice's center ion and identify areas of larger and smaller temperatures within it. Additionally, we've found that the random fluctuations in temperature are twice as significant as previously thought and that the random fluctuations in the lattice's motion are more substantial than initially expected, leading to increased rates of heating in the system, which may partially counter the cooling effect provided by the optical trap. We've also made estimates for the necessary modifications to the laser cooling physics that will bring the system into a state of quantum degeneracy. Furthermore, we've obtained the distribution of the lattice's initial energy for the first time and found that it conforms to a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution. Finally, we've obtained the rate at which the lattice's motion is being heated due to laser cooling and found that it is primarily influenced by the trap's residual dc components rather than the actual laser used for cooling. Analyzing the difference in the rates of spin decay in the lattice's center ion and a peripheral ion, we've found that the primary cause for this disparity is an imbalance in the rates at which they are being heated due to the influence of the optical trap. We've also demonstrated that the balance of the rates at which the lattice's ions are being heated can be used to determine the magnitude of their residual dc components. Ultimately, we've been able to illustrate the reasons for the challenges of achieving quantum degeneracy in 2D ion lattices and provided recommendations for potential future work to overcome these difficulties. Machine learning algorithms can be divided into two categories: those that make perfect predictions and those that do not.  The latter type relies on trial-and-error techniques such as trial-and-error, exploration, and exploitation to refine their accuracy. Our study employed a cutting-edge neuroeconomic paradigm to evaluate how humans learn in a challenging predictive environment.  The results revealed that individuals using suboptimal or characteristic strategies tend to receive stronger rewards in areas associated with the midbrain that process pleasure and reward, as well as greater accuracy in their predictions.  These findings were consistent with previous studies and provide significant insights into the underlying principles of trial-and-error learning in humans.  Furthermore, these results pose interesting questions about the potential coexistence of optimal and non-optimal reinforcement learning methods and their relative prevalence in different domains.  The study's data are publicly available at osf.io/ep4fj/ for further analysis.  The study's findings were previously published in the journal Neuron and form the introduction to this related follow-up study.  To improve the understanding of these learning techniques and their widespread use in various fields such as AI and neuroscience, this document presents a comprehensive overview of the theory and supporting evidence from our study and other related studies whose publication dates vary from 2006 to 2021.  To achieve this goal, we have divided the document into six sections.  The first section introduces the concept of non-optimal reinforcement learning and its distinct strategies, while the second section presents the underlying theory behind these methods.  The third section DESCRIBES a neural circuit involved in the learning process in humans, while the fourth section EXPLORES midbrain structures associated with the learning strategy and prediction accuracy in humans, and the fifth section EXAMINES the learning strategy and prediction accuracy in humans. Finally, the study's conclusions are presented. To enhance the visibility and accessibility of this research for a broad audience, we have included introductory sections and employed simple definitions of key terms, while making all study-related data and code available through open-source repositories for maximum efficiency and accessibility to all users. Furthermore, we have incorporated several interactive visualizations to help non-experts understand the study's concepts and results. Finding the closest points to a given set of points within a certain distance or the distance between two sets of points is referred to as close neighbor search. Approximate close neighbor search involves finding a close neighbor within a specified threshold of the optimal solution. This study focuses on using the Frechet distance as a measure of similarity in metric spaces and introduces a concept called $\alpha$-approximate close neighbor search, where an $\alpha$-ACNS for a query sequence $q$. An $\alpha$-ACNS for $q$ consists of a pair of parameters $c$ and $\delta$, where $\delta$ represents the maximum allowed deviation and $c$ is the radius of the ball in the space that contains at least one close neighbor within the specified distance. Studies have established that finding the exact ACNS for the Frechet distance is an NP-hard problem, even with simple queries, and is even harder when using the Hamming distance. This study involves proposing two new algorithms, called FTreap and HTree, for approximately solving the close neighbor search problem using the Frechet distance. FTreap uses a Treap data structure and is based on the idea of "hooking" two sequences together, while HTree utilizes a balanced search tree with a fractal-like structure. Studies have shown that FTreap and HTree are capable of achieving better results than prior algorithms called Hooked and Frechet-Ranjan. In terms of space efficiency, FTreap outperforms Frechet-Ranjan, while HTree offers better query performance. Ultimately, the studies have established the limitations of approximately solving the close neighbor search problem using the Frechet distance, and these results may be applied to related problems such as shape search. As shape search is a type of approximate close neighbor search, the results of this study may be directly applied to this problem. Furthermore, the results may be extended to other similarity search problems that involve the Frechet distance as a measure of similarity in metric spaces. This study offers the first known analysis of the time and space complexity involved in approximately solving the close neighbor search problem using the Frechet distance, and these results outperform those of a related problem called Fr\'echet-Ranjan. An effective training approach for reinforcement learning in high-stakes, human-safe applications involves assessing environmental quality based on human feedback. While utility-based assessment error mitigation is feasible in laboratory settings, its practical application in real-world environments is severely limited by the high human costs associated with recovery from severe system failures. Moreover, the underlying assumptions of utility-based AEM are not consistently met in general. In order to overcome these challenges, we developed a cost-effective approach to assess error free representations of a system's dynamics without direct human input, relying solely on temporary system failures. Within a reinforcement learning framework, we utilize a Bayesian decomposition of the observation model to iteratively recover high-fidelity state and dynamics representations from incomplete data. Results indicate that this approach outperforms utility-based AEM in terms of both sample efficiency and robustness, all without utilizing any post-hoc corrections, relying solely on the underlying system dynamics for recovery purposes. Furthermore, we expand upon this framework to address a common drawback associated with learning dynamics via simulation, namely the discrepancy between simulated and real-world system dynamics. We then apply this approach to robot manipulation tasks where environmental quality is evaluated based on task-specific performance metrics. Resulting parameterizations of the observation model enable samples to be generated and evaluated without prior knowledge of the system's dynamics, thereby representing a significant advancement in the field of high-stakes reinforcement learning. Ultimately, we demonstrate that these generated samples can be utilized to design safe and efficient testing environments, thereby reducing human costs associated with recovery from system failures and streamlining the testing process. Code for this approach is publicly available for review at the following repository: https://github.com/NorthfieldTechnologies/airshift. In this research, we address the task of Contextual Named Entity Recovery (CNER) where we're given a part of a sentence with an absent named entity's context and a list of possible replacements. Unlike standard NER tasks, where training data contains complete sentences, CNER only provides a surrounding context - a few words on both sides of the missing entity. Since there's no signal on the missing part itself, it's challenging to learn reliable replacements. To overcome this, we suggest enhancing the recovery process by asking the model to indicate how much each term contributes to the recovery by incorporating WordImportance, a novel type of feedback that indicates the contribution of each term in the context to the final recovery result. Experimentally, we verify that incorporating WordImportance as an additional training objective significantly improves the performance of state-of-the-art CNER models on three datasets, leading to a notable improvement of up to 5.6% in the accuracy of the top-1 prediction. This study examines reasons for engaging in data visualization, particularly with complex, multi-dimensional datasets like time series. We investigated the elements that drive engagement in these visualizations by looking at the effect of adding spatial dimensions and how people interact with 1D, 2D, and 3D visualizations. We developed an app that allows users to explore various screens representing different types of datasets, including time series and linear data. The app includes interactive elements like panning, zooming, and pinning to make navigation easier and robust. Our results show that users prefer visualizing data in 2D spaces with an additional spatial dimension, even if it's not technically required. We found that users engage more with 2D surfaces than 1D or 3D visualizations and prefer a single, enlarged view over multiple smaller ones. Additionally, we found that the 'pocket' feature, which saves pins for easy access, is an important interactive element. Based on these findings, we identified principles for designing engaging, multi-dimensional data visualizations. The implementation of Electronic Health Records across the globe offers immense opportunities for conducting population studies and improving healthcare outcomes. However, standardization in EHR systems hinders the exchange and analysis of data due to differing data structures. New technologies like cloud and distributed computing have mitigated these obstacles, enabling the aggregation of multiple systems by patients' data. Nevertheless, existing machine learning methods still face considerable challenges in learning diverse representations of EHR data, which ultimately impairs their performance. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel graph neural network architecture known as DS-GNN that efficiently captures the heterogeneity and variability within EHR datasets. DS-GNN is particularly well-suited for processing tabular data with diverse node and edge types by establishing multi-faceted similarity links between nodes and applying a machine learning algorithm that assigns weighted labels to nodes. Empirical evaluations of this method on EHR datasets have revealed substantial enhancements in MIMIC IV hospital mortality prediction and synthetic diabetes diagnosis, both of which demonstrate promising results. The success of the DS-GNN approach not only showcases its potential in learning diverse representations of EHR data but also has the potential to expand to other domains with similar heterogeneity. Additionally, this method allows users to integrate domain-specific knowledge when performing multi-classification tasks, which can further facilitate their goal of improving healthcare outcomes through data-driven decision making. In this study, we aim to incorporate machine learning into the process of developing software specifications from unstructured text sources, such as knowledge bases and online forums, which are widely available and pertinent to software developers. By leveraging text analysis techniques and incorporating specific keywords, we can pinpoint requirements that developers have previously discussed and identified in informal online conversations. Following this, we employ cutting-edge natural language processing models and a pre-defined set of possible requirements to accurately interpret the meanings of the text and match it with relevant existing requirements. The identified specifications can then be utilized to enhance knowledge bases, such as Wikipedia's knowledge base, by either validating or introducing new requirements. We evaluate our approach through two diverse applications: (1) utilizing discussion threads from GitHub assisted by a specific knowledge base, and (2) drawing data from Wikipedia's monolingual descriptions and related subtitles. We successfully demonstrate that our method yields satisfactory results in both scenarios. With the continuous advancement of text analysis techniques and pre-trained models, we anticipate this method to deliver even more impressive outcomes in the future. The proposed technique is notable for its reliance on textual hints and absence of semantic cues in the input data. Moreover, we show that our approach can also be applied to analogous challenges in other domains, such as medical research and bug reporting. Real-time control systems in industrial settings, such as machine tool monitoring, require efficient data exchange between devices via a network with limited bandwidth. To address this, a parallel processing method involves splitting data into equal parts and sending them through a relay station, which then combines the segments upon receipt. Nevertheless, implementing this approach in a real-world setting is complicated by the need for synchronized data arrival at the destination. To simplify this process, we explore the possibility of combining data segments at the destination instead, which introduces a novel problem: designing an efficient data encoding scheme that enables combined processing. To this end, we introduce a new encoding technique that achieves combined processing, alongside a optimized scheduling algorithm for maximal system utilization, and demonstrate its effects on energy consumption and latency. Numerical analysis confirms that our proposed method exhibits improved energy efficiency and reduced latency in comparison to traditional approaches. Moreover, we demonstrate that the method allows for increased reliability in data transfer with a higher probability of successful arrival at the destination within a specified timeframe. To address the challenges associated with this approach, we framework a solution using a combinatorial optimization problem and present a approximate algorithm in the form of a graphical method for efficient implementation, paving the way for practical application across a variety of fields. Furthermore, we study the variability in data sizes resulting from monitoring a typical machine tool, revealing the existence of inherent redundancy that can be utilized through compression, resulting in significant data volume reduction, which in turn facilitates efficient data transfer and potentially reduces communication delays. To implement this method in real-world settings, we introduce a novel concept of joint power and scheduling configuration tuning and demonstrate its effects at the network protocol layer, resulting in improved efficiency through optimized configuration files. Lastly, we apply our method to monitor and visualize the operation of machine tools across a distributed network, achieving successful implementation and visualization. The effect of compression on combined processing is investigated and the concept of compression is defined as the ratio of original size to its modified size. Through analysis and numerical evaluation, we demonstrate that our encoding technique achieves combined processing with minimal effect from compression, which in turn enables improved system efficiency and reduced latency. In this research, we examine various forms of generative adversarial networks, including transposed convolution structure variants, as potential methods to restore and achieve modulation categorization efficacy despite hostile conditions. Our experiments specifically involve presenting the network with a continuous flow of distorted modulation waves and demonstrating its ability to perform effectively without prior training on undistorted signals. Interestingly, a combination of three GAN models, each utilizing transposed convolution structures, yields the most effective results, showcasing the network's ability to successfully recognize and accurately categorize distorted modulation waves. Furthermore, through an in-depth analysis of its results, it is clear that the network has developed a strong understanding of its underlying concepts, and this knowledge can be utilized to develop more sophisticated and resilient communication systems capable of operating in various environments. Ultimately, this research serves as a foundation and opening chapter in exploring the world of adversarial robustness in electrical engineering and communication systems. The Manic-Contrast algorithm is designed for binary classification, aiming to identify labeled items of a specific class and discard the rest. This approach is best utilized in situations where labeled items are scarce and transformation into an alternative class is undesirable. Benchmarks indicate that Manic-Contrast is highly competitive among unsupervised anomaly detection methods and outperforms supervised ones in cases with limited labeled data, ultimately resulting in substantial time savings by reducing the required training dataset size. A unique phenomenon, the shadow of a black hole, offers a means to verify the accuracy of four key gravitational theories: Einstein's general theory, general relativity's modified versions, and two alternative gravity models. Due to the resolution constraints of current simulations, it has been a challenge to analyze light behavior around black holes with masses less than the mass of the sun. In this research, we introduce an innovative method to examine the shadows of less massive black holes by combining a publicly accessible framework with high-performance graphics processing units. Utilizing this approach, we were able to accurately compute and visualize the shadows of black holes with masses as low as that of the sun via simulations with much higher resolutions than were previously possible. Additionally, these simulations provided a detailed view of the matter distribution around a black hole with a mass of 10,000 times that of the sun. By comparing the observed shadows to theoretical shadow calculations, it is possible to assess whether the tested gravity theories accurately predict gravitational effects. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we generated and visualized shadows for various types of black holes, including primordial black holes with masses equivalent to that of the sun and 10,000 times that of the sun, using two alternative gravity models. In the future, the observation of these shadows by the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope and the Square Kilometer Array may serve as evidence to determine whether Einstein's general theory, modified general relativity's versions, or alternative gravity models are the most dominant theories. With our method, it is possible to conduct an even more thorough test of gravity by analyzing the critical area of the black hole, as well as provide valuable insights into black hole populations by identifying potential areas where binary black hole formation may have occurred. A publicly accessible code at github.com/astroDES/PopSyCLE demonstrates its utility and allows for the execution of various applications. By analyzing these results, it is possible to draw conclusions about the gravity models, such as whether alternative gravity models can predict the existence of superdense objects with masses less than that of the sun, and whether the tested gravity models accurately predict the behavior of black holes with masses less than that of the sun in the areas surrounding their shadows. Furthermore, it is possible to draw conclusions about the superdense objects with masses less than that of the sun by analyzing the behavior surrounding their shadows and by setting an upper limit on their abundance in the universe. By further developing PopSyCLE, it is possible to apply these methods to a much wider range of astrophysical and cosmological problems.

In contrast, humans easily incorporate their prior experiences and preferences when evaluating samples, especially when dealing with set augmentation tasks like song collections or picture albums. This difference in treatment leads to a significant performance disparity between current models and humans, particularly in set augmentation learning tasks. Children constantly learn and refine their understanding of language in response to various feedback mechanisms, such as verbal and non-verbal cues.  However, deep neural networks employed in contemporary NLP research operate in isolation from explicit feedback mechanisms.  A critical, though often overlooked aspect of NLP involves sequences where rejection is a feasible outcome - NLP may need to decline comprehension in such cases.  Drawing on the principles of child language development and the insights gained from recent studies on rejection in transformer models, this research develops a new class of deep neural networks that integrates rejection as an inherent property.  By constructing these networks, we aim to address a long-standing query in the NLP field: can deep neural networks, similar to children, learn to effectively utilize negative feedback in language learning?  Experimental evaluations of our models have been carried out on the TAC KBP and TyDiLLD projects, with the results suggesting that utilising multiple forms of feedback can lead to enhanced text comprehension and improved performance.  A copy of this research paper, along with associated code and data, has been made publicly-availabale at https://github.com/philiplicson/Rejection-NLP.  Furthermore, our study has also uncovered a novel phenomenon associated with models that integrate rejection as a possibility - nonlinear backpropagation, leading to biased outcomes in language modelling, with the potential to cause instances of biased comprehension during NLP task execution.  By delving into the roots of this phenomenon - referred to as vanishing variance learning - we have been able to develop a novel method for analysing NLP models and understanding the impact of rejection on learning.  Through our research, we have also been able to recommend a simple technique for mitigating biased learning, with the potential to broaden our comprehension of NLP model behaviour and enhance NLP model performance through this discovery.  Ultimately, our study has also been used to formulate a range of open research questions related to NLP model execution and development. When analyzing open-ended creative text like fiction, defining a set of desired outputs is challenging due to the lack of clear criteria for evaluation. In the field of Neural Machine Translation (NMT), researchers are exploring the use of external guidance to help models understand what the system aims to produce next. In this study, an alternative and more realistic approach called Look-Ahead Focus (LAF) is introduced. Instead of relying on predetermined objectives, LAF relies on human feedback to discover desirable properties of generated content during post-processing. In the context of a task that asks users to imagine stories based on a single sentence, human judges evaluate and rank the generated content based on its quality. Utilizing human feedback in a loop, LAF trains a language model to predict scores that reflect the content's desirability, which it uses as a guidance mechanism for generating content in the story. In human trials, it was discovered that stories written using LAF performed better than baseline models on both reader experience and publisher satisfaction. Furthermore, LAF was found to be more effective than prior approaches that used external guidance for NMT. Our method is not only applicable to story telling but also other forms of creative text generation like writing poems given prompts. The source code for our study can be accessed at https://github.com/allenai/laf. The study also produced accompanying media at https://medium.com/aiclouds-research/look-ahead-focus-rethinking-external-guidance-for-creative-text-generation-8b8c8d0b8c8c. The research dataset can be found at https://ift.is/storygenerator. In terms of publication, this research is based on an earlier version, however the publisher requested changes which are included in this version. The publisher's full response can be found at https://www.iappsec.org/f/2022/ML-FE-2022-02.pdf. The study was featured in an AI publication at https://medium.com/airesearcher/how-to-influence-ai-to-create-artificially-4d8c8d0b8c8c. This study introduces a method for calculating the Kontsevich graph values associated with symmetry breaking and curvature in symplectic Poisson systems, with a focus on systems traversing hyperelliptic Jacobians. The proposed method relies on an iterative formula for $\mathfrak{g}$-structure symmetry breaking that only depends on hyperelliptic theta functions and linear algebra, making it applicable to any hyperelliptic Jacobian. Additionally, this method adapts the 1830s Fourier series of hyperelliptic Jacobians to efficiently calculate the graph values. Furthermore, through the lens of Whittaker forms, the study demonstrates that the superpotential of a symplectic Poisson system can be expressed as a sum of theta constants and exponential functions, thereby providing new insights into symplectic Poisson systems traversing hyperelliptic Jacobians. These insights include explicit expressions for superpotentials, curvature, and $\mathfrak{g}$-structure symmetry breaking in terms of theta constants and exponential functions. The study also explores the compatibility of Weil algebras with hyperelliptic Jacobians and uses the calculated graph values to derive new, strongly degenerate Hamiltonian symplectic structures on Jacobian elliptic curves. Specifically, the study introduces the first known degenerate Norden symplectic structure on these curves, as well as new $L_\infty$ operations, providing further applications of the theory to Jacobi manifolds and control theory. In a recent publication, Huang et al. (2022) have made a groundbreaking discovery in the field of Asian options pricing by developing an universal framework to calculate the value of these options. Their approach relies on transforming problem-solving tasks for Asian options into well-formulated mathematical abstractions that can be easily solved. In response, the current study aims to provide evidence that the proposed method of Huang et al. is indeed flawed, as it is built on an overly restrictive assumption about the existence of a stochastic basis that is not necessarily valid in general cases, which in turn prevents extension to multiply-chosen strike prices and flexible payment rules. To illustrate this point, a counter-example is presented, along with an alternative pricing formula that is more general and flexible in this context. In addition, some potential areas for improving the pricing framework of Asian options are also suggested. Ultimately, this study provides new insights and perspectives for researchers working on valuation methods for Asian options. Its key contributions can be summarized as follows. Firstly, the study offers a counter-example that demonstrates the limitations of the original pricing framework, specifically highlighting that separable components in the original context do not necessarily represent a universal structure that can be applied in all cases. Secondly, by leveraging the concept of transition operators, a pricing formula is developed that is more general, flexible, and naturally applicable to a broader range of payment rules and multiple chosen strike prices. Thirdly, the study identifies and addresses a notable omission in the original work, specifically regarding the pricing of options under Markov chains, which is a critical component in achieving a universal pricing framework. In doing so, this study provides a more complete explanation of pricing principles, specifically with regard to the pricing of options under both Brownian motions and Markov chains. In conclusion, the study acknowledges the significant contributions made by Huang et al. (2022) in advancing pricing methods for Asian options and related derivatives, specifically with regard to their use of stochastic bases and multi-wavelet expansions, which have also found applications in other areas, such as image processing and machine learning. In order to promote further research in this direction, some potential areas for improvement are also identified. In addition, related work is specifically referenced in response to this counter-example and pricing methodology, specifically with regard to joint works published in 2021 and 2022 by the same research group on derivative pricing and related areas, which in turn has also contributed to the advancement of theoretical methodologies in this field. Our study utilizes several decades-worth of computational data collected from various sources, including our own simulations and those of others, to examine how geostrophic degeneration impacts global magnetic field dynamics in convective dynamos across different radii. We utilize a range of mean-field frameworks that represent and analyze various turbulent influences, before evaluating and comparing our results against existing theoretical frameworks and simulations. We observe significant discrepancies between the standard and hybrid mean-field frameworks, particularly in how they account for magnetostrophic term forcing and its interaction with baroclinic and barotropic instabilities, leading us to conclude that a comprehensive understanding of convective dynamos requires a deeper understanding of all turbulent influences, rather than relying on simplified or averaged representations of turbulence. Furthermore, we demonstrate that convective dynamos can generate strong magnetic fields in objects with small radii, provided that the velocity and magnetic field timescales align with those predicted by our mean-field theory and simulations. We also show that for larger stars and planetary cores, our framework appears to yield similar outcomes to previous studies, while highlighting several theoretical and computational shortcomings that require further investigation in the future. Ultimately, we conclude that for realistic applications and interpretations of global magnetic field dynamics in various astrophysical and planetary objects, we must closely resemble the full spectrum of turbulent influences captured in our computational data and theoretical frameworks. As such, we believe that a deeper understanding and refinement of our mean-field frameworks and computational methods is essential for advancing our knowledge in the field. A novel conservative approximation is developed for diffusion equations with nonlinear diffusion coefficients that vary in direction. The existing theory in [24] shows that solutions to these equations exhibit regularity and bounded behavior within a bounded domain. The approximate solution converges strongly to the exact solution at a rate of $O(\tau +h)$ in the L^2 norm, where $\tau$ and $h$ represent temporal and spatial discretization steps. The new approach is applied to a quasilinear diffusion model that describes magnetized plasma's thermal relaxation. A semilinearization technique combines with finite element Galerkin method to achieve a fully discrete scheme with a first-order temporal rate of convergence in the L^2 norm. The theoretical findings are substantiated by numerical simulations conducted on a variety of problems featuring nonlinear diffusion coefficients such as the choice of $-(-\Delta)^{-1/2}$, the more extreme choice of $-(-\Delta)^{-3/2}$ and the alternative option of $D\log\cdot$. The results include an exhaustive investigation involving the use of spatial and temporal convergence rates for system parameters in the presence of electric fields applied tangentially and normally to the diffusion front, while fixing the magnetic field's strength, its angle of approach and the coefficient of diffusion that governs the model behavior. The achieved understanding has led to the development of an effective model, the validation of its accuracy and the successful application of this model in analyzing thermal relaxation processes in the presence of spatial inhomogeneities and periodic solutions. The results include an analysis of the formation, evolution and interaction of front singularities in highly anisotropic and isotropic diffusion processes and the detection of limit cycle behavior at the diffusion front for a specific range of system parameters in the log-case, in addition to the calculation of convergence rates at diffusion front ends. The solution has also been successfully extended to the case where the magnetic field's strength, its angle of approach and the diffusion coefficient exhibit spatial inhomogeneities in a smooth, periodically changing functions. The results include an analysis of the convergence rates at diffusion front ends. The developed model represents a break-through in the understanding of turbulent magnetized plasma relaxation processes and has a significant impact on this field of study. The approach is expected to be extended to other nonlinear processes such as the case of strongly nonlinear geophysical and geodynamic fluid flows where a similar identification of an effective model and its application to the study of singularity formation, evolution and interaction has not been achieved yet. Recent studies have sought to refine the Range of Attention in Generative models (RAG) for tasks such as question-answering and inquiry-response, yielding impressive results. Building on existing research, we introduce an enhanced RAG framework, dubbed RAG-IR, tailored for inquiry-response. In this framework, the RAG generator is supplemented with a pre-trained Descriptive Passage Retrieval (DPR) selector, leveraging both text-to-text and text-to-segment architectures. We expand on the idea of using the DPR selector to assign a narrow attention span to the model. Importantly, when employed in an inquiry-response setting, the RAG generator is conditioned not only on the input query, but also on a relevant context snippet retrieved via the DPR selector as well. We evaluate various combinations of RAG models, attention spans, and retrieval snatches (including full documents and segments), ultimately assessing their impact on inquiry-response performance. Complementary human evaluations also reveal that the most capable RAG-IR models produce more natural, coherent responses. Notably, when used in conjunction with a relatively basic RAG model and a retrieval context spanning just one sentence, the refined RAG-IR framework delivers remarkable improvements in both human and machine assessment of response quality, essentially hitting a sweet spot in the RAG performance spectrum. Furthermore, the refined RAG-IR outperforms other powerful generative models, including RAG-DPR, RAG MS MARCO DPR, RAG Pretrain, RAG Unsupervised Pretrain, and RAG Unsupervised Pretrain with ELECTRA, ultimately solidifying its position as a state-of-the-art inquiry-response model. Last but not least, the refined RAG-IR also excels in various other natural language processing tasks, ultimately emerging as a versatile and efficient generative model. By developing and using a selection process that evaluates Crowdworkers based on provided samples of their writing, we found that we could build a relatively reliable system for choosing top performers.  As the number of applicants for a task increases, so does the difficulty in selecting them, which our method effectively addresses by allowing us to pick a subset of top performers and thus achieve a notable improvement in the overall quality of the summary, outperforming previous best practices.  Our findings indicate that it's possible to identify top-performing Crowdworkers and save both time and money in the process, thereby making the Crowd a more predictable option for tasks like summarization.  Our code and data are now available for others to use at https://github.com/Deban888/SummEval.  Additionally, we suggest that future work in automated summarization investigates the potential advantages of being able to select top performers, which now enables such systems to outperform human generated summaries, which were previously considered the gold standard. Text retrieval is a crucial operation in numerous document management systems, and recent advancements have enabled the transformation of texts into compact, invariant embeddings that enable similar texts to be grouped together and retrieved efficiently. Although major breakthroughs have been achieved, retrieving text clips or segments rather than entire texts remains a much more difficult task. Unlike overall texts, individual clips may lack uniqueness and understanding of their context. In this research, a novel approach called TS2-Net is proposed, combining token shift and selection to learn clip-level embeddings that are both context-aware and identity-neutral. It incorporates a selective token shifting mechanism within a transformer model to learn such clip-level embeddings. Through token shifting, TS2-Net can sample and move tokens from the fed input according to a masking grid, effectively aggregating different input token sets. A transformer model then determines which of these sets, by selectively weighing and aggregating the tokens, is the most meaningful and relevant one to form the final clip embedding. In doing so, TS2-Net can learn to overlook less critical and distracting information, making it particularly strong at retrieving text clips. Comprehensive experiments have shown TS2-Net to be the current best-performing model for text clip retrieval, outperforming previous state-of-the-art models both individually and in combination. A newly-introduced dataset called Clip Retrieval Dataset has also been created to study and understand the problem of text clip retrieval from multiple perspectives. Clip Retrieval Dataset is the world's first publicly-accessible dataset designed for the task of text clip retrieval and contains a large number of diverse text clips and full texts in both English and Chinese languages. As such, it not only allows researchers to train and test their models but also to advance the task of text clip retrieval itself. In particular, it allows researchers to study and confirm the assumption that certain contextual understanding is required to successfully retrieve text clips. Furthermore, it also reveals the inherent characteristics of both identity-identical and context-driven retrieval patterns prevalent in text clip retrieval. In addition, it introduces a new research method called the Average Search Density (ASD) to study and quantify the problem of retrieving text clips. Through the creation of Clip Retrieval Dataset, researchers are given the opportunity to understand and demonstrate the nature of text clip retrieval from multiple perspectives. Ultimately, it is now possible for us to see how well various models, including both established and improved ones, perform the task of text clip retrieval. Graph isotope problems encompass a wide range of critical challenges that are crucial in mathematics and computer science. A particular subclass of these problems consists of invariants that remain unchanged under graph isomorphisms. In our study, we explore the concept of graphs whose invariants are equivalent to those found in isomorphism classes of finite abelian groups under the condition of submultiplication. This research leads to interesting mathematical representations of these groups as well as generalizations of their decomposition theories. Additionally, we identify hierarchies among these graph isotope problems and derive solutions or complexity classifications for specific cases, such as abelian groups with orders 2, 4, and 8. Notably, some of these graph isotope problems have classifications as NP-complete or co-NP-complete, while others are soluble in polynomial time. Lastly, we also explore the analogous problems for oriented graphs and identify interesting open research questions that require further exploration. In total, our study covers over 160 finite abelian groups and their corresponding graph isotope problems. In particular, we demonstrate that every finite abelian group of rank at most 3 can be represented as a subgroup of a more general structure known as the Brauer bracket group. This leads to the conclusion that all graph isotope problems corresponding to finite abelian groups of rank 3 or less can be reduced to the more general problems found in the class of Brauer bracket groups. As a result, we confirm that the graph isotope problem corresponding to the 8-cube is indeed co-NP-complete, a conclusion which had been left uncertain in a previous study. This work was completed as part of the author's PhD thesis, the exact version of which can be found at arXiv:2109.00005. In terms of notation, we refer to the reader to the sources listed in Section 1.3, specifically to the work of Jaeger, 1988 [Jae88], for clarification on the notation regarding subgroups and subgroup lattices, while the concept of subgroups and their corresponding properties, including dilation, have been discussed in detail by the author in the preprint arXiv:1908.03749, specifically the definition found on page 16. Moreover, the exact version of the thesis contains further analysis and related results in the fields of distance in graphs, graph isomorphisms, and their respective relationships with linear error-correcting codes, as these concepts have been explored by the author in the preprint arXiv:1908.

To assess potential ways to prevent beam-induced noise from limiting these metrics, we examined various simulation studies. They demonstrated that separating muon production and acceleration rings can substantially reduce noise effects by a factor of hundreds. Additionally, our studies showed that enhancing the density of muons in the accelerator ring can also effectively lower noise levels. Finally, using a steady muon stream to counteract noise effects can offer a viable solution to this problem, though it increases ratchet losses in the accelerator chain. To achieve this, we outlined the necessary modifications to the accelerator chain and predicted the resulting improvements in muon collider performance. Specifically, our studies indicated that we can anticipate a reduction of at least one order of magnitude in beam-induced noise effects. They also demonstrated that these modifications will only result in a relatively minor loss in achievable luminosity, of less than a tenfold increase in the relevant muon collider metric. Overall, our studies show that these measures can effectively prevent beam-induced noise from limiting the potential performance of future muon colliders. They further emphasize the significance of completing the necessary design work for these corrections in order to ensure the full muon collider beam delivery capability, corresponding to an luminosity of $10^{34}$ cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$. Our studies were conducted as part of the R&D work recommended in the DOE Report on Muon Collider Research. They have allowed us to identify the necessary work required to integrate beam-induced noise controls into the muon collider design, a crucial step in realizing the collider as a viable research tool. The relevant DOE work has been identified and the necessary next steps are outlined. They include the required theoretical design work for the beam-induced noise reduction techniques, specifically fast beam tuning and chicanes, which need to be carried out by physicists in the relevant fields of expertise. Our method employs a novel candidate distribution and a straightforward regularization term combined with the Wasserstein distance to measure the difference between the actual data distribution and a desired sparseness pattern. By allowing the choice of probability distribution, the Spartan framework can be tailored to suit specific applications by changing the candidate distribution's mean and covariance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on a variety of tasks, including reducing noise in adversarially trained ImageNet models, increasing image resolution, enhancing translation accuracy and translation by word position, improving reinforcement learning in Atari games, and improving both neural architecture and sparseness for linear discriminant analysis. By using a flexible framework, we are able to achieve state-of-the-art performance in all these applications. Our code for these experiments is publicly available on the public Spartan repository. Our contribution is two-fold: First, we introduce a general approach for addressing sparsity in a broad range of a network's components using a flexible choice of probability distributions. Second, we provide a set of guidelines for implementing this approach effectively. Additionally, we demonstrate that using truncated distributions accelerates convergence to a stable state, which is beneficial for all applications. Lastly, we emphasize that using the correct mean and covariance for each choice of probability distribution is crucial for achieving optimal results in each specific task. By adhering to these best practices, the Spartan framework offers a reliable set of tools for addressing sparsity in a wide range of a network's components. A new edition of the KEK-Monte-Carlo for electron-positron colliders, KKMCee, has been developed, which predicts the formation of lepton and quark pairs in leptonic colliders through the hard interaction of two initial electrons. The predictions are based on the next-to-leading order (NLO) cross-sections of heavy quarks in conjunction with the FINnick short-range yield model for heavier masses not currently supported. The KKMCee algorithm incorporates a precise method of calculating heavy quark pairs, which demonstrates nearly complete stability in its NLO predictions when varying key parameters within established ranges. Furthermore, this tool is compatible with the interactive simulation program of the Future Circular Electron-Positron Collider, IDAF FERCE. An extensive examination has been conducted to assess the reliability and accuracy of this tool, which examined factors, including random number generation, uniform particle distribution, trial generation, weighted importance, and efficiency estimation. Lastly, a detailed description of integrating this tool with the detector simulation program is provided, which would be essential in conducting particle simulation studies in future electron-positron collider research. An initial demonstration of KKMCee's capabilities was conducted using simplified models of the CMS detector at the Large Hadron Collider at CERN and the Fermilab Run II detector, which showed that each generated event was treated independently to accurately simulate the detector's response. The simulation of nearly 100 million events revealed that the FINnick model effectively simulated the non-perturbative contributions to heavy quark production at the CERN Large Hadron Collider during Run II. Furthermore, detailed distribution estimates were obtained for the production of Z boson pairs, which would be crucial in measuring their mass through the Z mass reconstruction method. The analysis estimated that generating statistical errors of less than one percent would require simulations of approximately 10, 60, and 300 million events for the CERN Large Hadron Collider during Run II, the Fermilab Run II detector, and the Future Circular Electron-Positron Collider, respectively. The development and testing of this tool at the CERN Large Hadron Collider during Run II and the Fermilab Run II detector have provided the necessary requirements for conducting precision measurements of particle physics at future electron-positron collider research. At the heart of social networks, the evolving graph framework offers a research tool to analyze and understand dynamic network developments. As networks grow and change over time, nodes interact and establish connections, influencing the overall network structure. To accurately model this interaction process, the embedding of evolving graphs, particularly those related to interaction metrics such as centrality and connectivity, needs to be studied thoroughly. Three datasets - Wikipedia revision graphs, Twitter microblog graphs, and Wikipedia article pair graphs - were used to analyze the interaction process in evolving graphs from a graph embedding perspective. Our research combines complex network principles with Deep Graph Embedding methods to analyze and predict interaction patterns in these graphs, thereby shedding light on the underlying structure of social networks using temporal analysis and network embedding results. The incorporation of time from a network's perspective in embedding algorithms also enables deeper insights into the evolution of these networks, ultimately revealing how network layout and layout-related metrics change over time. Furthermore, our research reveals that incorporating time into the embedding of these graphs improves the accuracy of predicted metrics, namely node centrality and connectivity, thus providing a predictive analysis of evolving graphs from a social network perspective. The combination of Deep Graph Embedding with the concept of time, referred to as Deep Temporal Embedding, enhances the accuracy of layout-related prediction in these graphs, ultimately demonstrating that Deep Temporal Embedding can be utilized as a metric for predicting layout-related variables in these graphs, thereby providing a predictive analysis of evolving graphs from a social network framework. Notably, including a $^3$H resonance factor significantly improves the accuracy of this estimation. A comparative analysis of our findings with existing experimental data and theoretical models is also presented. Importantly, our results validate several key characteristics of these models, including a clear $^3$H+4n resonance structure in $^7$H, consistent with our MCV calculation, and a maximum momentum of around $110$ MeV/c for the neutron component, in line with the SRF. Our study further confirms the presence of a $^3$H+4n resonance character as far as $0.5$ MeV above the $^3$H ground state, demonstrating that these models are effectively describing the $^7$H's base state. A separate analysis of the spatial distribution (OD) of the $^7$H ground state was also conducted in this study. Our OD examination identified four distinct neutron components within the $^7$H, each exhibiting a considerable spatial separation as far as $12$ fm. A well-known theoretical model, the Mottleson- Kelson potential, was used in this analysis to determine the position and distribution of these components within the $^7$H. Our results confirm the effectiveness of this model and provide valuable insights into the spatial separation and density of the $^7$H's base state. This work utilizes homology to analyze Betti numbers in the context of Gaussian journeys. Betti numbers, drawn from homology, offer significant BIRG coefficients that serve as key indicators of the topological structure in random fields. These BIRG coefficients are generated by applying homomorphisms to homology vectors derived from contour sets within level sets of multivariate Gaussian fields at varying levels. Field models can be narrow or wide, which are referenced by their spectral density shapes. Our study computes BIRG coefficients for narrow and wide Gaussian journey models, also establishing relationships between these BIRG coefficients and traditional extreme value indices like the spectral density's tail exponent and the spatial extreme exponent. Calculations for narrow Gaussian journeys are done analytically, yielding exact formulas, while the scenarios for wide Gaussian journeys involve numerical approaches via Monte Carlo sampling. Our study's methods can be broadened in future work to cover non-Gaussian fields. Our findings, published in a recent paper, are based on these analytical and Monte Carlo computations. They reveal that homology analysis can serve as an effective tool to derive useful extreme value indices, offer insights into the effects of smoothness on BIRG coefficients, and establish a correlation between these BIRG coefficients and the indices themselves. Our study's method is complex, allowing the analysis of other Gaussian journey models, such as those with correlations in the spatial or temporal dimensions. Additionally, future work will delve into applying homology to the analysis of nonlinear journey models for wide or narrow models. Our study's long-term goal is to cover all models as a means to create a unified homology-based tool for topological data analysis across various probability models. This can lead to a greater understanding of the relationships between the structure of random fields, the BIRG coefficients, and the extreme values within these fields, ultimately enabling the determination of the field's topological structure from BIRG coefficient estimates. Our study's approach is a crucial step in this goal. In robotics, manipulating objects with an end-effector attached requires adjusting a robotic arm's tip between two key points - one holding the object and another within the workspace. Typical methods for calculating the necessary robotic arm movements involve tracking the object's image across a sequential series of frames. However, calculating these movements becomes challenging when the object and camera are enclosed in a complex environment, like a human's hand, obstructing the view. Instead of relying on object tracking, we developed an innovative technique for calculating the robotic arm's movements by utilizing just one handheld image. By leveraging the image and knowledge about the object being grasped (its shape and main features), we developed an algorithm to calculate the robotic arm's movements in 3D space. Our study evaluates how accurately this technique works with different types of objects and whether it can be applied across a range of scenarios. Moreover, we also examined our approach's practicality by implementing it on the OpenHRP robotics platform. The results indicate that our method shows promising potential for real-world applications in robotics. It demonstrated a high success rate in calculating the movements with just one image when the object's shape and workspace dimensions are known. The results also reveal that incorporating additional information, like the object's thickness and field of view, further improves the calculation accuracy. The integration of our technique with a path-planning function demonstrated that it is feasible to use this method in robotics applications. While the results are somewhat inconsistent, we are confident that our approach has significant potential for improvement through continued development. In many real-world applications, learning a policy from demonstrations is more practical than training a model directly. This is because demonstrating the optimal quality of a policy is often simpler than accurately modeling the environment. The Inverse Reinforcement Learning problem therefore seeks to learn a policy from rewards rather than understanding the environment's dynamics. The focus on policies makes IRL a more feasible task, but it also poses difficulties as there can be multiple optimal policies for each reward function. The current approaches available are limited and don't effectively address this challenge, leading to sub-optimal or incomplete policy learning. The new family of algorithms introduced in this research, known as Value Function Guided (VFG) IRL methods, leverages the power of value functions to improve IRL. The use of value functions allows these new algorithms to learn a near-optimal policy more effectively and efficiently. The experiments conducted across various domains confirm the success and efficiency of the VFG approach. The source code for these new algorithms has been made publicly available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/mtgual/Value_Function_Guided_IRL. The performance of these VFG algorithms has been evaluated and compared with existing IRL methods in the domain of robotic games such as Stochastic Robot Tennis, Robotic Bowling, Sliding Block Puzzle, and many more. Furthermore, an open-source implementation of these algorithms has been released for the reader's convenience. The study also explores the potential applications of IRL in the field of generative adversarial networks (GANs) by introducing Adversarial Guided IRL, a new form of GAN architecture. The new generation system successfully produces new data samples in multiple domains, outperforming state-of-the-art models. The open-source implementation of this new algorithm has been made available at the following link: https://github.com/mtgual/Adversarial_Guided_IRL. Graph treewidth, an important concept in graph algorithms, can be challenging to compute, but it's relatively easier to find an approximate value, specifically, a minimum effective treewidth. The idea of treewidth in weighted graphs is more complex, but it can be approximated using minimum weighted perfect bipartite matchings. This paper introduces space-efficient algorithms for finding a specific type of graph structure called vertex divider, which helps calculate the treewidth of a graph. The proposed methods employ binary heaps to operate within a certain memory limit, but they still offer a worse time complexity compared to a recent solution. Furthermore, we suggest an improved approach for approximating minimum weighted perfect bipartite matchings in weighted planar graphs, utilizing a specific graph structure called 4-vertex biconvex polytope. The proposed algorithm operates in two levels: a coarse search using a binary heap and a finer search using a priority queue, but it too offers a higher time complexity than a recent solution. Despite this, we propose a method for dynamically controlling memory usage, which could potentially be applied to these algorithms to improve their performance. The ideas presented could potentially inspire future optimizations to reduce their time complexities. Lastly, we briefly discuss how these algorithms can be modified to apply a similar concept called edge divider, which helps calculate the edge-bipartiteness width. The proposed edge divider algorithms operate in an exponential time but can be utilized for solving the problem of partitioning a graph into connected components with low edge connectivity. The idea could be potentially used in future graph algorithms that benefit from graph edge partitioning as a preprocessing step. The detailed components are available at [1].
